- Alberta Premier Danielle Smith visits Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago
Strathmore, Alta.-based political analyst Deidre Mitchell-MacLean says the premier’s inner circle finds it challenging to criticize a government they feel politically aligned with.
“We're seeing every other premier come out with their — let's say — elbows up and Danielle Smith is not,” Mitchell-MacLean said.
However, with an October referendum looming on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a binding referendum on separation, and polling suggesting most Albertans support national unity, Mitchell-MacLean thinks Smith has little leeway to take a strong stance on the issue.
Smith is caught, she says, between a political base that favours the idea of Alberta independence, and wanting to win a provincial general election in October 2027.
Consultant Deron Bilous, who served as a minister of economic development and trade in Rachel Notley’s Alberta NDP government, said there’s little political risk to Ontario’s premier proposing counter-tariffs that would cause his province minimal harm.
“It’s quite easy to negotiate with somebody else’s poker chips, which is what Doug Ford is doing,” Bilous said.
He said tariffing oil and gas exports would have “massive” implications in Alberta, blowing a multi-billion dollar hole in the provincial budget, and causing the industry to halt any expansion or investment plans in the province.
Although oil tariffs may be Canada’s biggest trump card, Bilous questioned the wisdom of playing that card so early when Alberta is so reliant on the U.S. as a customer. Bilous said Smith knows this, which fuels her reluctance to support such a move.
Bilous said he supports Carney’s decision to take other counter-measures against Trump.
“Bullies only respond to people that stand up to them,” Bilous said. “And the challenge with not imposing any kind of counter tariff on him — my fear is that it makes Canada look weak.”
Evan Menzies, vice-president of Crestview Strategy, who has worked for both the United Conservative Party and the former Wildrose Party, said Smith’s diplomatic approach has been effective so far, as Alberta exports remain less affected by U.S. tariffs.
The provincial leader has to maintain positive relationships with any U.S. administration, given the importance of the American market, he said.
Separation referendum is a bigger risk: analysts
While Ford says a lack of unity among Canadian premiers is a liability in U.S. trade negotiations, the analysts CBC News spoke with on Monday are far more concerned about the Oct. 19 referendum as a perceived weakness in the federation Trump can exploit.
Alberta voters will cast ballots on 10 referendum questions on Oct. 19, including a question about beginning a process to hold a binding vote on becoming an independent nation.
“The timing is awkward, for sure,” says Menzies, who added that Smith has been clear she will campaign to remain in Canada.
Bilous said the nuances don’t matter to investors, who shy away from uncertainty.
“If the perception is we don't know if Alberta is going to stay in Canada, that has immediate economic development and investment attraction impact,” he said.
Political scientist Smythe says Smith’s approach makes her appear as a Trump sympathizer.
“She's already got that suspicion around her with this referendum,” Smythe said. “She claims she’s pro-staying in Canada. But if she moves too far in terms of appearing to be weak in her approach to standing up for Canada vis-à-vis the U.S., that's a problem.”
The Alberta NDP did not make anyone available for an interview Monday, but is holding a press conference in Calgary on Tuesday to call on the government to take steps in response to what it calls Trump’s latest attack on Canadian sovereignty.
"Danielle Smith has approved a separatism referendum to save her political skin from her own separatist base,” NDP leader Naheed Nenshi said in a separate email statement. “This has weakened Canada in front of Donald Trump and the entire world.”
The Opposition is organizing a “Rally the Vote for Canada” tour to encourage electors to vote for Alberta to remain in Canada.

The Delhi High Court has observed that the institution of marriage is quite paradoxical and if the issues between spouses are not resolved quickly, the “better half becomes a bitter half”.
Justice Vimal Kumar Yadav made the observations while allowing a man’s appeal against a trial court’s judgment sentencing him to three years of imprisonment for trying to kill his wife by allegedly forcing her to ingest Baygon spray, a well-known insect killer.
The court, in its August 24 verdict, acquitted Nafe Singh in the case, saying the prosecution’s case lacked cogent evidence about the intention and knowledge as contemplated in Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code. It is highly unsafe to act upon the kind of shaky evidence brought on record, the court said while granting the benefit of doubt to the man.
Mr. Singh and the woman got married in 2000 but relations soured within a year. According to the prosecution, during a matrimonial dispute in 2001, the husband first allegedly tried to force his wife to ingest insecticide from a tumbler, and when that failed, he poured it directly down her throat from the container.
An FIR was registered against the man and his mother. While his mother was acquitted by the trial court, Mr. Singh was convicted for the offence of attempt to murder.
The man denied the allegations levelled against him and contended that there was some matrimonial issue due to his wife’s desire to live with him in a separate house, leaving aside his widowed mother.
The court said one of the most beautiful relationships of humans, that of a husband and wife, becomes one of the most terrible when things go wrong in a matrimonial alliance.
“The institution of marriage is quite paradoxical and a world of extremities. The best, in no time, becomes worst if not handled carefully.
The better half becomes the bitter half if issues are not taken care of and resolved as soon as possible,” the court said.
The court said relationships can go in a totally different, undesirable and unexpected direction if not handled carefully and in time. “The institution of marriage derives its strength from faith, companionship and the trust which the parties repose in each other wherein both sides feel assured and protective,” it said.
‘Conflict zone’
“The troubles in this bond between the spouses not only affect the institution of marriage but the family as well and in turn society too. The relationship founded upon faith, trust and confidence gets transformed into a conflict zone where often, physical violence also creeps in,” the court said. It added that there are recent examples where the spouses have resorted to extreme levels of violence against each other that were incomprehensible some decades ago.

Broken toilets, leaking roofs: Why India's 'cockroach' party wants to fix schools
- Published
The squat one-storey building has recently received a fresh coat of paint and looks respectable from a distance.
But this government-run primary school for girls in Faridabad, a district on the outskirts of the Indian capital Delhi, suffers from a host of problems.
The road outside the school in Khedi Kalan village is dotted with shallow potholes filled with filthy water. Inside, local social worker Satpal Narwat points out the plaster falling from the ceiling.
"It looks new from the outside, but it's crumbling from inside. Four of its eight toilets are unusable and full of trash, while four of the nine classrooms have also been abandoned because they are too unsafe for children," he says, adding that in the rains, "the classrooms get flooded and children have no place to sit".
This is not an isolated case. Many schools, especially in rural India, are starved of funding and in disrepair.
India spends only 4.1% of its GDP on education. While this meets Unesco's lower minimum threshold of 4%, several countries - including France, Germany, Australia, Brazil and the US - spend more than 5% of their GDP on education. Countries like Belgium and Sweden spend even more.
Experts - and the Indian government's own National Education Policy (NEP) - have recommended 6% as the ideal mark for India.
According to official data, 94,000 government schools have closed here between 2014-15 and 2024-25. A report, external by government think-tank Niti Aayog says some were merged as part of efforts to streamline the system, but acknowledges that enrolment has fallen as demand for private schools has risen.
The poor state of government schools is the focus of a new campaign by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The online satirical movement made global headlines for its weeks-long protest in Delhi, which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month.
The protests had erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.
Named #SchoolThikKaro (#FixTheSchool), the CJP's latest campaign is aimed at highlighting the crumbling infrastructure in government schools and pressuring authorities into addressing it.
"Government schools, especially in rural India, have been neglected for many many decades now. So, children who grow up in villages don't have equal opportunities and they end up working in farms or as a daily wage labourer or construction workers," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told the BBC.
"It's only because they don't get the same facilities and the same opportunities that children in big cities get. And that is what we are trying to change by making schools better."
On Thursday, Dipke said he had visited more than 20 rural schools and had "not found even a single good school".
"There were no benches, no bathrooms, no drinking water, no facilities at all. Even animals would not be kept in such a place," he said.
"What I saw was really heartbreaking. This is very similar to what I used to see when I used to visit my village during school summer vacation. And even after 20 years, nothing have changed there."
In recent days, Dipke and other CJP leaders have shared several videos - of leaking roofs, dirty toilets, children sitting on the floor and angry students - with their 26 million Instagram followers.
"We want to ensure that children get benches to sit on, good washrooms and clean drinking water. They should have smart classrooms with digital boards. That is when they will also feel that they are getting the same quality of education as those living in big cities in the country," Dipke said.
The government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi or his Bharatiya Janata Party have not commented on the campaign.
The BBC has also contacted India's education ministry for a response.
Meanwhile, the CJP's protest in Delhi and the campaign to fix schools appear to have emboldened students across India and opened floodgates of complaints and set off localised mutinies against an administration many accuse of being apathetic.
Armed with mobile phones, school students have been shooting and posting videos on social media - some of which have gone viral and prompted authorities to act.
After one video, external of schoolgirls in Raigad, Maharashtra, mocking the condition of the road leading to their school went viral, the local authorities repaired it
In Uttar Pradesh, another video showed students running into the district magistrate's office demanding a road to their school, while a third , externalshowed schoolgirls asking an official whether he would send his own children to a school in such poor condition.
At Delhi's Jantar Mantar, where the CJP held its earlier protest, the group demanded Pradhan's resignation as well as an overhaul of India's education system with greater accountability.
Journalist and author Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay says "by the end of their protest, it was clear that it wasn't just about one exam or one minister's resignation".
"People there were talking about the state of schools and everything that's wrong with them."
Mukhopadhyay says the #FixTheSchool campaign is an obvious next step and "the way people have contributed with videos, pointing out flaws in school infrastructure, is evidence that the movement is gaining ground".
"It can't be Jantar Mantar 2.0 as it will be much slower and a long-lasting movement. But the CJP will get a lot of support for the campaign because there's plenty to talk about that's wrong with the schools," he adds.
One of the biggest problems government schools face is a lack of teachers and other staff, says Chatar Singh, treasurer of the Primary Teachers' Association in Haryana state where Faridabad is located.
Singh is also the head teacher of the primary school in Atmadpur village. Its new building, funded by a private company's corporate social responsibility programme, and students' trophies make it one of the better-equipped schools in the area.
But as we approach the toilets near the school gate, a stench greets me. Singh says the toilets have not been cleaned properly for the past two days because the part-time cleaner - appointed by the government to come in for a couple of hours every morning - has been sick.
But dirty toilets are not his biggest problem – it is the lack of teachers, he says.
For the school's 910 children, there are 40 teachers. But on Wednesday when BBC visited the institution, 30 had been deployed to help with voters' list revision, four others were off sick, leaving only six teachers to manage the children.
"Teachers are hired to teach, but across India, government deploys them to do a lot of non-teaching assignments. They are used for election duty and to conduct Census. Most of my teachers have been on voters' list revision duty since July. It's affecting the quality of education," he says.
Asked why he thinks the government schools are neglected, Singh says, "Do children of bureaucrats and MPs and politicians study in my school? No. They send their children to private schools because they can afford them."
Most students here are children of migrant factory labourers, he says. "And a majority of them are from underprivileged castes and communities. Anyone who can afford sends their children to private school," he adds.
His claim holds true across India. It is visible in the mushrooming of private schools in small towns and villages.
In Khedi Kalan when he was growing up, Narwat says, there were only government schools near him and he got his education there.
The crumbling girls' primary school which he gave me a tour of upsets him because the 62-year-old studied here from 1968 to 1973.
"In those days, this was the only school in the village for both boys and girls," he says. "The school building was relatively new. There were eight rooms and all were filled with students."
He says flooding became a serious problem after the road outside was raised about 15 years ago, leaving the school below road level.
Narwat, who retired as an officer in the state's electricity office two years back, says he sent his children to the same school, but later moved them to a private school because they have better facilities.
Narwat then takes us to the second primary school in the village - this one for boys, just a couple of hundred metres away. Here, classes are operating out of two rooms and a veranda. A second building with three classrooms was declared "condemned" and demolished about five years ago with assurance that a better one would be rebuilt. The patch is now a parking stand for cycles.
Over the years, Narwat has petitioned chief minister, MPs and district officials, and written to the National Human Rights Commission, seeking improvements to the two Khedi Kalan schools. But he says little has changed.
"I send my grandchildren to a private school," he says. "It's very expensive, but they have all the facilities. In village schools, the teachers are on election duty, and there's no library or laboratory."
The CJP campaign has given him some hope that the schools will finally get attention.
"I think the CJP can be a force for good. They've taught people to fight, to not be afraid. The government has all the power and resources. And now they have to perform."

Dronetech startup Airbound has raised $37 Mn (about ₹355 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by US-based investment firm Greenoaks. The round also saw participation from new and existing investors, including food delivery major DoorDash, Physical Intelligence cofounder Lachy Groom, Lightspeed, and Humba Ventures. Airbound plans to use the fresh proceeds to accelerate engineering, commercial-scale manufacturing, and go-to-market initiatives. The latest fundraise takes the startup’s total funding since its launch in 2023 to nearly $50 Mn, it said in a statement. This includes the $8.65 Mn funding round it raised in October 2025 from Groom, Humba Ventures, Lightspeed, and senior executives from Tesla, Anduril, and Ather Energy. Founded by Naman Pushp, Airbound designs and manufactures autonomous drones for transporting goods. Its aircraft use a blended-wing-body tail-sitter configuration, allowing them to take off and land vertically before transitioning to horizontal flight. The Bengaluru-based startup’s flagship TRT drone weighs about 2.5 kg, can carry a payload of around 1 kg, and has a range of approximately 40 km. The startup claims the drone is built using carbon-fibre composites and requires substantially lower thrust than conventional quadcopters. Airbound also operates a proprietary flight control system, RUDRA, which it says enables a single operator to manage more than 100 drones. As Inc42 reported earlier, Airbound was manufacturing about one drone a day in October 2025. At the time, each delivery cost the startup around ₹24, which it planned to bring below ₹5 by scaling production. The Series A funding will now be crucial for testing whether Airbound can achieve those cost reductions while moving from limited healthcare deployments to a commercially viable, high-frequency delivery network. While Airbound now describes itself as an aerospace startup, its immediate commercial focus remains autonomous drone deliveries across healthcare, ecommerce, and retail. The broader positioning reflects its longer-term ambition to develop larger aircraft capable of transporting freight and, eventually, passengers. The startup said the same aircraft architecture could ultimately be used to carry a passenger or around 100 kg of cargo. “We believe in a world where all movement happens in the air. Not some of it. Not most of it. All of it,” Pushp said. Airbound is currently working with hospital chain Narayana Health to transport diagnostic samples between healthcare facilities. The startup claimed that it has completed more than 1,000 autonomous flights under the partnership without any mission failures, reducing transportation times from hours to minutes. Alongside the fundraise, Airbound reiterated its plans to develop a drone delivery network connecting three cities in Andhra Pradesh and gradually scale it to 10,000 flights a day. The network will support healthcare, ecommerce, and retail deliveries. However, the Andhra Pradesh initiative is not a fresh development. Airbound signed an MoU with the Andhra Pradesh Drone Corporation in June to operate across Amaravati, Vijayawada, and Guntur, with a target of reaching 10,000 daily flights by the end of 2026. The startup expects the deployment to serve as a template for expanding aerial delivery networks to other parts of the country. The development comes amid growing adoption of drones for logistics and last-mile deliveries. Startups such as Skye Air Mobility, Redwing Labs, Yali Aerospace, among others, are developing drone-led delivery solutions across healthcare, ecommerce, and other sectors. Investors are also bullish on the segment, as a result of which startups are seeing a lot of interest. For instance, Skye Air Mobility raised $9 Mn earlier this year to expand its last mile drone delivery service. Similarly, IIT Kanpur-incubated dronetech startup EndureAir recently bagged ₹30 Cr in grant support under the Centre’s RDIF scheme to develop its SABAL-200 kg heavy-payload drone. The startup develops drones for defence, surveillance, disaster management and logistics use cases.

Update | August 25, 18:57 IST Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd cofounder Rishabh Telang has moved the Karnataka High Court to quash the FIR filed against him by his brother-in-law and cofounder Deepak Poduval. The Court did not order a stay on the investigation, but sought responses from Poduval and the State on the plea. It further noted that the police had issued Telang a notice under Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and he would not be facing an immediate arrest. The matter is scheduled for a hearing on September 2. Original | August 8, 21:03 IST Deepak Poduval, cofounder of Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd, has filed an FIR against his cofounder and brother-in-law Rishabh Telang at Bengaluru’s Bellandur Police Station, alleging forgery, cheating and criminal conspiracy in connection with the 2016 transfer of certain assets and intellectual property (IP) from the company to Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd, a part of IPO-bound Cult.fit. Poduval alleges that Telang forged his signature on documents used to wind up Cult Fitness without his authorisation including a board resolution, an EGM notice explanatory statement, a shareholder consent, a Form STK-4 affidavit and Form STK-3 indemnity bond, and a chartered-accountant-certified statement of account, as well as statutory financials filed in August 2016.. He further alleged that he did not receive payment arising from the transaction with Cultfit Healthcare, a subsidiary of Cult.fit, and that his 50% shareholding in Cult Fitness was “extinguished without a rupee of consideration”. “From February 2016, I was systematically excluded from management, meetings and financial decisions, despite remaining an equal shareholder and director,” Poduval said. He claimed that he only discovered that the company had been struck off recently after perusing MCA documents and filed the FIR soon after. According to Poduval, the dealings with Cultfit Healthcare were “a premeditated move to run our business through a parallel vehicle while cutting me out.” Telang has denied the allegations, while Cult.fit said neither it nor its subsidiary is an accused in the FIR. Cult Fitness, a Bengaluru-based fitness centre chain, was founded by Poduval and Telang in 2015. A year later, Cultfit Healthcare acquired certain assets and IP rights of the company, including the ‘Cult - The Workout Station’ brand. Responding to the allegations, Telang said the matter would be addressed through the ongoing legal proceedings. “Deepak was fully involved in the transactions with Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd as well as the winding up of Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd, of which I possess multiple correspondence,” said Telang in a statement shared with Inc42 by Cult.fit. He further claimed that the Ministry of Corporate Affairs acknowledged the winding up of Cult Fitness through an email dated March 12, 2020, and alleged that Poduval had received consideration under the transaction. Telang also questioned the timing of the FIR, alleging that it was filed with “mala fide” intentions. He pointed to a property settlement lawsuit filed by Poduval’s wife, who is also Telang's sister, on July 1, 2026. Separately, Cult.fit said that it has not received any communication from the authorities in connection with the matter. “The accused entity, Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd, was a separate independent company of the complainant himself and we did not have any ownership or management control,” it said in its statement. It added that its transaction with Cult Fitness was carried out “under appropriate contractual arrangements and for consideration which was duly paid and also acknowledged by the complainant”. “With this, this acquisition stood consummated and closed,” the company stated. Inc42 has reached out to Poduval for his response. The story will be updated if and when a response is received. The development is the latest instance of legal proceedings involving founders of IPO-bound startups. Earlier this year, former RentoMojo cofounder Ajay Nain moved the NCLT, alleging oppression and mismanagement and seeking to halt the company’s proposed IPO by challenging a share sale completed in 2023. The proceedings were subsequently disclosed in RentoMojo’s DRHP. The latest development comes nearly a month after Cult.fit filed its draft IPO papers for a proposed IPO. The company plans to raise up to ₹950 Cr through a fresh issue of shares, while existing investors are looking to offload up to 17.86 Cr shares through an offer for sale. The total IPO size is expected to be around ₹4,000 Cr. On the financial front, Cult.fit’s net loss narrowed 47.6% YoY to ₹251.8 Cr in FY26. The company’s operating revenue grew 41.5% YoY to ₹1,720.6 Cr. Total expenses jumped almost 16% to ₹2,027.5 Cr. Editor’s Note: The story has been updated to incorporate Deepak Poduval’s statement.

China warns it will safeguard its interests after US widens sanctions against Iran
- Published
China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.
Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.
This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.
China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.
Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."
Bessent described the new measures as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.
He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".
However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".
The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.
Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.
Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.
China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.
"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.
"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

For the first time, the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC) is procuring various assistive devices and mobility aids, including retrofitted petrol scooters, for the Welfare of Differently Abled Persons Department. Nearly 15 tenders have been floated by the TNMSC after the department asked it to undertake the procurements.
The TNMSC was set up with the main objective of ensuring the availability of essential drugs and medical supplies in all government hospitals across the State through a streamlined procedure for procurement, storage and distribution. According to official documents, including the Health Department’s policy note, apart from supplying medicines for government hospitals, TNMSC also procures and supplies medicines required for various veterinary healthcare institutions functioning under the Department of Animal Husbandry.
Officials confirmed that for the first time, the TNMSC was asked to procure and supply various assistive devices by the Welfare of Differently Abled Persons Department. Following this, it has floated online tenders for fixing of rate contracts for supply of various types of battery-operated wheelchairs, sewing machines, tricycles, hearing aids, reflective folding stick and modular reflective folding sticks, modular reading device and electronic Braille readers, standing frame and corner seat, artificial limbs, metal and plastic calipers, magnifier, goggles and braille watches, axillary crutches, elbow crutches and walking device, augmentative and alternative communication system software with tablet and smartphone, and retrofitted petrol scooters, and specially designed retrofitted petrol scooters for spinal cord injuries.
The TNMSC’s Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association permit it to procure assistive devices, officials said. Earlier, such tenders for procurement of the assistive devices and mobility aids were called for by the Welfare of the Differently Abled Persons Department.
“This was an informed decision taken by the department. TNMSC is well-versed in undertaking such procurements, given the technical nature of assistive devices such as hearing aids. These devices should be procured depending on the condition of individuals such as those with spinal cord injuries. This is based on their request, and the TNMSC has the capability and technical expertise and is allowed to make procurements for all requesting directorates,” an official said. They said the TNMSC’s procurements typically include warranty and maintenance support, which could have been another reason for the department to ask the agency to handle the procurement.
Move criticised
The State government’s decision to entrust the TNMSC with the procurement of one-gram gold rings under the ‘Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam’ for babies born at government hospitals had already drawn widespread criticism, with concerns that it dilutes the corporation’s core purpose.
A section of government doctors said TNMSC’s mandate was different, and taking on such additional procurement activities could divert the TNMSC from its primary responsibilities. “There are already delays in procuring essential and life-saving equipment due to administrative reasons. Taking on additional responsibilities will only affect its routine work,” a senior doctor said. Another doctor added that this could compromise the TNMSC’s functioning, affecting the quality of service, and, in turn, patient care in the long run.

What does your Premier League club still need in the transfer window?
- Published
The first weekend of the Premier League season is complete but clubs still have one week of the transfer window remaining to secure last-minute squad additions.
Results are one thing but for many managers and sporting directors their opening match was an eye-opener in what positions need to be strengthened, who is no longer needed and what gaps still need to be plugged.
With the transfer window closing on Tuesday, 1 September at 23:00 BST, BBC Sport takes a look at what each top-flight club still needs and fans also have their say.
Arsenal
Alex Howell, football reporter
The Premier League champions have already strengthened the middle of the pitch with Bruno Guimaraes, the wing with Christos Tzolis and their defence with Ezri Konsa.
But Arsenal are still in the market for a forward and have a long-standing interest in Julian Alvarez.
Although it appears to be a difficult deal due to many factors, the Gunners will be ready to act if there is a chance to get it done.
Watson, Arsenal fan
If you want someone who is Premier League proven, who has won it all from the World Cup to the Champions League, Julian Alvarez looks like the guy that can take Arsenal to the promise land of finally getting over the line in Europe. Especially when there aren't that many elite forwards in the world.

- Al-Hilal open talks to sign Arsenal winger Martinelli 
  - Published11 hours ago
Aston Villa
Nick Mashiter, football reporter
What don't Aston Villa need after a raft of star departures this summer?
Ollie Watkins' transfer saga, with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal trying to sign the striker, leaves Villa looking for a likely replacement with Nicolas Jackson a target.
A winger is also on the agenda while they need a defender after Ezri Konsa's move to Arsenal, and have opened talks for Club Brugge central defender Joel Ordonez after bids for Southampton centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis were rejected.
Amy Finley, Aston Villa fan
It is clear Aston Villa desperately require a striker more than anything right now.
Although I massively rate Victor Lindelof and Pau Torres, the display against Brighton has worried me slightly.
Therefore, I would welcome another centre-back as well.
It looks like we will be OK in midfield once Johan Manzambi is fit and with the addition of Leon Goretzka.
- Watkins' departure would cut deepest - and Villa did not see it coming

- Villa in talks with Club Brugge for defender Ordonez 
  - Published14 hours ago
Bournemouth
Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter
Bournemouth are used to being picked off and will simply be hoping to come through the final eight days of the transfer window unscathed.
It is clear that big clubs are circling for forward Eli Junior Kroupi and midfielder Alex Scott, who the Cherries insist are not for sale.
In terms of incomings, Bournemouth are largely done as they close in on a move for Juventus goalkeeper Michele Di Gregorio.
Brentford
Phil McNulty, chief football writer
Brentford are in the fortunate position of being able to choose their deals carefully after some excellent squad strengthening.
The Bees have been looking at left-back, with West Ham's El Hadji Malick Diouf strongly linked, but it hardly seems a matter of urgency with Keane Lewis-Potter able to play as a wing-back with Rico Henry and Aaron Hickey also in the mix.
There is experienced striking cover in the shape of former England international Callum Wilson and an all-round depth to Keith Andrews' squad that was missing last season.
Do not expect it to be a hectic closing few days in the transfer window.
Michael Johnston, Brentford fan
Another forward option - particularly down the left - would take this window for Brentford from a nine to a 10 out of 10.
Mykhailo Mudryk's name has been doing the rounds in recent weeks and Brentford have history there, having chased him prior to his move to Chelsea.
Get someone like Mudryk in, and I don't think the transfer window could've gone much better for Andrews.
Brighton
Simon Stone, football reporter
It is anticipated Yankuba Minteh will leave for Liverpool, which might create space at Brighton for another forward and Carlos Baleba's impending exit for Manchester United may see the club make a move for midfield reinforcements.
It is possible there may be other exits but, as usual, Brighton will stick to their data driven recruitment plan.
"We must continue to evolve, invest and innovate while remaining true to the principles that have brought us this far," was chairman Tony Bloom's message to fans before the 4-0 win against Aston Villa.
Maz Mirzadeh, Brighton fan
With Baleba's anticipated departure and Minteh looking likely that he might leave as well, we need to bring a defensive midfielder who can bring a physical presence to our midfield and a winger who is proven at the top level.
We have a lot of games this season with European football, so we need to have the squad depth to compete on all fronts if we want to secure a top-10 finish again.
Chelsea
Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter
Chelsea supporters may want another star forward or a new goalkeeper to replace the unconvincing Robert Sanchez, but Xabi Alonso feels his squad is largely complete for this summer.
However, there is a huge amount of work to do to reduce the squad from 39 players to around 25 within the next eight days. That is the priority, as the Blues will not want frustrated players in their squad this season.
Savage Dan, Chelsea fan
Chelsea need to focus more on the outgoings than incoming players.
With no Europe it's important we do not carry a squad that's too heavy, as we won't have too much room for rotation.
If we were to bring anybody in, I think the priority is a top-drawer goalkeeper.
Coventry City
Nick Mashiter, football reporter
Coventry are in the hunt for Mykhailo Mudryk as the Chelsea winger looks to get his career back on track after serving a 20 month suspension for testing positive for banned substance meldonium.
Defensive cover is also likely to be needed by Frank Lampard while players like Luke Woolfenden could leave on loan.
Conna Chahal, Coventry fan
Honestly, I think we have done enough in the transfer window to build a team that can stay up in this league.
Crystal Palace
Alex Howell, football reporter
There has been a lot of change at Palace with the loss of Maxence Lacroix and a new manager starting the season in Pierre Sage.
The Eagles have been building depth for their Europa League campaign but still need a few bodies in the building.
Sage has made clear he wants a senior centre-back and Palace could be pushed to sign another defender too after the injury to Chadi Riad in the first game of the Premier League season against Everton.
Ollie Thomas, Crystal Palace fan
Riad's injury has amplified the need for another centre-back who is first-team ready.
Axel Disasi is a good start, but a bigger, permanent move would be great. That, plus a central midfielder, and we are set.

Everton
Phil McNulty, chief football writer
Everton simply must sign a recognised right-back before the window shuts. It has been a glaring problem for more than a year.
It is a weakness recognised by everyone at the club but either a prime target cannot be agreed upon or is out of reach.
Talented midfielder Merlin Rohl took on the job for the opening game against Crystal Palace, while Jake O'Brien and James Garner have also been pressed into service.
Time to finally make a decision and get one in. Maybe David Moyes will also look at adding another striker with questions still hanging over Beto and Thierno Barry.
Chelsea outcast Liam Delap is one name regularly linked with Everton.
Fulham
Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter
Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa has been clear that he is happy with the club's business so far, but more could be done to make his squad more balanced.
There have been attempts to sign an additional central defender, with a move for Rennes' Abdelhamid Ait Boudlal explored two weeks ago, and that could be a key area the Cottagers look to strengthen.
This is a club that does not operate at the very top end of the transfer market and one that enjoys a deadline-day deal.
John Charles, Fulham fan
It still feels like Fulham need a right winger - whether that is sticking with Oscar Bobb or providing serious competition for him - I think we need to cover for the loss of Harry Wilson's goals.
We also need a right-sided centre-back as there are serious concerns over how Joachim Anderson will fit Arbeloa's new system.
Hull City
Jonty Colman, journalist
It has already been a busy summer for Hull City's recruitment team but the ambitious Tigers are still working on adding two new forwards in Mohamed Ali-Cho and Ilyas Ansah.
There has also been interest from the club in Real Betis winger Pablo Garcia, although that deal has taken longer than hoped after the La Liga side raised their valuation of the 20-year-old. Stoke City's Sorba Thomas is also a player of interest.
A goalkeeper, midfielder and right-back also could be on the agenda for Sergej Jakirovic's side in the final week of the window.
Ryan Frankish, Hull fan
Over the next week, if we bring in a left winger, one more striker - assuming the Ali-Cho deal also gets completed - a central midfielder, an attacking midfielder and a right-back to add depth and challenge Lewie Coyle for the starting spot, we will be in a strong position to compete.
Ipswich Town
Nick Mashiter, football reporter
Ipswich have spent over £150m on 12 new signings since returning to the Premier League.
Boss Gary O'Neil expects more, though, and a striker and a midfielder could arrive at Portman Road.
Fringe players like Anis Memeti could leave as O'Neil shapes his squad.
Leeds United
Simon Stone, football reporter

China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
- Published
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.
Officials in the northeastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.
An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical that is known to cause cancer, for preserving the freshness of food in China is strictly prohibited.
China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.
Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.
Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.
Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.
In a statement issued on Saturday, local authorities in Kangbao county said: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."
Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.
The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.
An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."
China produces well over 30 million tons of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.
Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
- Published
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.
Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.
One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.
Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.
The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.
Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.
The motive behind the attack is unclear.
Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."
Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".
Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.
He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.
Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.
He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.
After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.
Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.
According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

The speed of innovation on the Ukrainian battlefield means frontline troops may need a new drone design within weeks — but the country’s defense industry faces a critical labor shortage that threatens to derail that pace.
Tens of billions of dollars in investments and wartime demand have fueled the creation of thousands of defense companies in Ukraine, but the supply of workers has failed to keep up. Yurii Faraponov, chief operating officer of BlueBird Tech, said his company can’t respond to some frontline requests because he doesn’t have enough engineers.
Another company recently poached a production manager by offering him three times his previous salary, along with paid housing, said Sergii Vysotskyi, vice president of the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries. Some companies are tracking down retired specialists and begging them to return to work.

Gujarat Police want to unify 80,000+ CCTV cameras into one ‘smart surveillance’ network
Participants will test their systems on about 50 CCTV feeds, tracking a designated vehicle and generating real-time alerts, GIS visualisation and movement data.
The Gujarat Police have announced what they describe as the country’s largest hackathon focused on CCTV integration and AI-based video analytics, aimed at developing technology for policing and public safety. The challenge seeks solutions that can unify more than 80,000 CCTV cameras across Gujarat into "one smart surveillance network".
According to hackathon website under the state home department, the Gujarat Police invited students, researchers, freelancers, startups and companies to participate and develop innovative solutions for a robust CCTV surveillance mechanism in the state. A prize pool of ₹37 lakh has been announced, while the hackathon is scheduled for September 10-11 at iHub Gujarat in Ahmedabad.
Here are the four main objectives of the hackathon, as outlined by the Gujarat government:
- Integrate diverse CCTV systems into a unified platform.
- Cross-reference live video feeds with government databases.
- Use AI to identify persons, vehicles and events of interest.
- Generate real-time alerts to support faster and smarter law enforcement.
The Gujarat government has said different departments currently operate independent CCTV systems, with some using cloud-based storage and others relying on local storage infrastructure. The government intends to integrate these cameras into a unified video management and analytics ecosystem.
What is the challenge?
The main challenge is to develop a system that can scale to more than 80,000 CCTV cameras across Gujarat and enable AI-powered analysis of live feeds.
The system is expected to support capabilities such as real-time suspicious-activity detection, automatic number plate recognition (ANPR), vehicle tracking, watchlist matching and cross-camera search. The challenge will test these capabilities using live CCTV feeds and real-world policing scenarios.
How to register and what happens next?
Those willing to participate can register on the Sentinel Gujarat portal. After completing registration, participants will be able to access the details, resources and live camera feeds from about 50 geographically distributed cameras through the Resources page for technical evaluation, according to the website.
Participants are then required to submit their prototype, documentation and architecture details. The submission requirements include:
- An unlisted YouTube link, with video visibility set to “Unlisted”.
- A Google Drive or OneDrive link with access enabled for “Anyone with the link — Viewer”.
- A URL to their hosted platform, along with test login credentials for the screening committee, if applicable.
- A GitHub or GitLab repository link containing the platform source code or relevant components, if applicable.
The technical evaluation will require participants to integrate approximately 50 heterogeneous cameras, track a designated vehicle and provide real-time alerts and GIS visualisation. The system will also be expected to generate movement history and searchable events.
“All eligible submissions will first be assessed against the common evaluation areas. Bonus consideration may then be awarded for meaningful capabilities demonstrated beyond the mandatory requirements,” the site says.
Senior officials react
Some senior police officials and an advocate reacted to the hackathon and what the government aims to achieve with it.
“As far as I know, this is the first time such an event is being conducted on such a large scale. We are bringing together more than 80,000 CCTV cameras and providing participants an opportunity to develop and test solutions using live feeds and real-world policing scenarios. The aim is to use technology and innovation to strengthen our surveillance and response systems,” DGP G S Malik said.
Ajit Rajian, DCP (Crime), Ahmedabad City, also reacted and said that a core team will be formed to oversee the integration of the cameras. "A dedicated command centre will monitor the network and the alerts generated through the AI-based solutions,” he said.
An advocate from Gujarat High Court also reacted, highlighting how integrating CCTV networks and AI analytics will boost policing and public safety. "A system of this scale also raises serious privacy concerns. Clear legal safeguards are needed on access to live feeds, data retention, facial recognition, accuracy, sharing and misuse. Technology should aid law enforcement without enabling indiscriminate or disproportionate surveillance of citizens," said Punit Juneja, an advocate practicing at Gujarat High Court.
What happens after submission?
The process covers choosing an integration model, building and testing the solution, submitting the prototype and planning its scale-up.
Participants will test their systems on about 50 CCTV feeds, tracking a designated vehicle and generating real-time alerts, GIS visualisation and searchable movement data. They must also submit a plan to scale the system to about 80,000 cameras across Gujarat.
Solutions will be assessed on the test case, architecture, analytics, scalability and proof-of-concept readiness, with bonus consideration and special recognition for innovative capabilities.
What is the schedule?
Registration opened on August 4 and the last date to apply is September 7. Shortlisting is also scheduled for September 7.
The hackathon is scheduled to take place over two days, September 10-11, with the results to be announced on the second day.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has proposed a registration system under which a medical practitioner, once registered with a State Medical Council and allotted a Unique Identification (UID) number in the National Medical Register, would be eligible to practise across India without obtaining fresh registration or a licence in another State.
The proposal is part of the draft Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, notified by the NMC on August 11, 2026. The draft seeks to amend the 2023 regulations governing registration and licensing of doctors. The NMC has invited objections and suggestions for 30 days from the date of notification.
Under the proposed system, registration and licensing would be routed through a unified registration portal of the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board. The State Medical Council would continue to scrutinise applications and grant registration and the licence to practise, but the approval would simultaneously be reflected in both the State Medical Register and the National Medical Register.
The UID assigned in the register would incorporate the State/Union Territory code and the practitioner’s State Medical Register number, the NMC said. Once the State Medical Council grants registration and the Ethics and Medical Registration Board allots the UID, the doctor would not require fresh registration or a separate licence to practise in another State or Union Territory.
The draft also proposes automatic electronic synchronisation between the national and State registers so that a change made in one register is reflected in the other. The National Medical Register would serve as a central repository of registration details as well as disciplinary proceedings, including suspension, removal, and restoration of registration.
The NMR would also carry information on whether a doctor’s license is active or inactive, and details of disciplinary action, if any. The Ethics and Medical Registration Board and the NMC would have powers to seek records and monitor State Medical Councils to promote uniformity and transparency in regulation.
The proposal retains the five-year validity of a license. If a doctor does not apply for license renewal within three months of expiry, the registration will be marked inactive, and the practitioner will not be entitled to practise medicine. The inactive status would automatically be reflected in the NMR.
While seeking to create a nationwide registration framework, the draft leaves disciplinary jurisdiction primarily with the State Medical Council in whose territorial jurisdiction the alleged professional misconduct, unethical conduct or medical negligence occurred.
The concerned State Medical Council would have the power to inquire into and decide the matter, and record the outcome against the practitioner’s credentials in the online register. Where disciplinary action is recommended by a State Council other than the doctor’s primary registering council, the action would be reflected in the NMR and automatically updated in the State register of the council of primary registration.
The draft also provides for an appeal mechanism. If a State Medical Council rejects an application for registration, license or renewal, the applicant can appeal to the Ethics and Medical Registration Board within 30 days. The Board would have 30 days to decide the appeal, and if it allows the appeal, its order directing the State Council to grant registration or a license would be binding on the council.
The proposed amendments also revise provisions relating to foreign medical graduates. Their definition would include Indian citizens and Overseas Citizens of India who obtain a foreign medical qualification in modern/allopathic medicine but do not hold an undergraduate medical degree from an Indian institution. The Foreign Medical Graduate Examination graduates who meet the prescribed conditions would remain eligible for provisional registration for internship and registration in the National Medical Register.
The draft also proposes extending temporary registration for foreign nationals undertaking postgraduate or super-speciality courses from a maximum of 12 months to the duration of the course, subject to a maximum of 24 months, followed by a one-year cooling-off period.
Additionally, existing practitioners who do not have a National Medical Register UID would have to update their details on the Ethics and Medical Registration Board portal within a period to be specified by the Board and obtain the UID as a one-time measure. No fee would be charged for this exercise.
The draft notification has not yet to come into force.

Government regulators have spent the last year asking serious questions about Tesla’s electronic, retractable door handles, a cool-looking automotive design flourish that has since been imitated by plenty of competitors.
The handles have been blamed, in the US and in China, for making it difficult for passengers to quickly exit vehicles, and for impeding rescue efforts. A handful of crash victims’ families have even filed lawsuits against Tesla, alleging the door handle designs played roles in their loved ones’ deaths.
Now the door handles have led to Tesla’s largest recall ever—and China’s. The Chinese government is recalling more than 2.9 million Model 3s and Model Ys manufactured in China between 2019 and 2026, the State Administration for Market Regulation announced Friday.
Some of the affected vehicles will be made safer with an over-the-air software update that lowers windows after collisions, making it more difficult for passengers to become trapped inside. But many cars will also need new warning stickers—affixed free of charge—that can help passengers find and operate emergency mechanical door handles. Those handles can currently be hard to identify because they’re similarly colored to the rest of the vehicles’ interiors. The mechanical door handles are especially important when vehicles’ low-voltage batteries fail. (These batteries don’t operate the cars themselves, but power onboard computers, displays, and other accessories, including electronically-powered door handles.)
Tesla didn’t respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Chinese government simultaneously recalled more than 1 million vehicles manufactured by eight Chinese automakers, also for safety concerns related to flush door handles. The other automakers are Beijing Automotive, Chery, Dongfeng, First Auto Works, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, and Xpeng.
Separately, the Chinese government recalled nearly 50,000 imported Tesla Model 3s, Xs, and S’s for insufficiently monitoring drivers using the US automakers' assisted steering technology. The government said the tech increased the risk of collisions. The recall affects some vehicles imported between 2019 and 2026. Some of the vehicles can be fixed with software updates, but some will need new in-cabin cameras that ensure drivers are paying sufficient attention while operating their vehicles.
China has been more aggressive than other countries in regulating new automotive technology. It put in place new rules earlier this year that will soon ban fully retractable door handles in the country. In 2021, a government agency issued regulations more tightly governing the operations of autonomous vehicles, even before that tech had widely hit the road; another agency that same year created specific rules for the data generated by its increasingly software-centric cars.
The US’ top road regulator has started to examine whether it needs new rules governing door handle design, Bloomberg reported last month.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

A recommendation from someone with great taste
Diet Sabya (@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. “Delhi has registered more than 1,700 cases of swine flu this year,” Health Department officials said on Friday (August 21, 2026), as the national capital sees a surge in seasonal influenza cases during monsoon.
On the day, Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and representatives of the Health Department are scheduled to meet Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda and senior officials from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the swine flu situation in the capital.
"A report is being prepared to assess the number of cases and the overall situation. Everything is under control. There is no need for general panic. All government hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate treatment facilities," Mr. Singh told PTI.
The Minister said the government is closely monitoring the situation and has directed all government hospitals to ensure adequate treatment facilities are available.
“Healthcare institutions and officials concerned have been told to keep a close watch on infection patterns, affected areas and potential hotspots,” the Minister said, adding that separate wards are being set up for swine flu patients.
Doctors in Delhi said they are seeing a noticeable surge in number of patients with influenza and influenza-like symptoms, though most cases are mild to moderate.
Dr. Rishikesh Desai, consultant physician in the department of internal medicine at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said the hospital is witnessing a rise in seasonal influenza cases. "Most healthy individuals recover well, but influenza can become serious in older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic diseases," he said.
Dr. Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant in the department of infectious diseases at Fortis Hospital, Gurugram, also recounted a similar situation. "There has been a sudden increase in patients with influenza and influenza-like illnesses," she said. "Most patients have mild to moderate illness and recover well with appropriate supportive care, so there is no reason to panic." Rastogi further said doctors were seeing more prolonged cough and greater intensity of fever this season, possibly due to reactive inflammation of the lungs due to air pollution, particularly from particulate pollutants.
According to medical practitioners, H1N1 infection — commonly known as swine flu — usually presents fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches and fatigue. Those with persistent high fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or worsening symptoms are advised to seek medical attention promptly.
"Vaccination, hand hygiene, avoiding close contact while ill and staying home during the infection period are key to limiting transmission," Dr. Desai said.

‘Who started the fire?’ Burnham challenges Putin on first trip to Ukraine as UK-Russia tensions grow
The UK is providing Ukraine with the blueprints to long-range SCALP missiles, the prime minister announced in Kyiv
Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit out at Russian president Vladimir Putin during his first state visit to Kyiv, amid mounting tensions between Moscow and London.
The British leader chaired his first meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” to emphasise Britain’s continued support for Ukraine through the provision of long-range SCALP missile blueprints.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the move would add “fuel to the fire” and “prevent any progress in the peace process”.
“Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” Mr Burnham hit back in an address to Ukraine’s European allies on Monday.
“Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.
“This can never be the route to victory, and we need to be clear in sending that message. It means doing everything we can all do, and working with our allies as well, beyond this coalition, to dig into our own stocks of air defence... to protect Ukraine from the missiles that are falling now.”
Mr Zelensky and Mr Burnham both delivered speeches outside Kyiv’s St Sofia cathedral on the anniversary of the country’s 35th year of independence.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine,” he said.
The prime minister compared Ukraine’s battle with Russia to the British fight against Nazi Germany, saying: “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century; you hold that flame in the 21st.”
It marked his first foray on the international stage, heading the coalition of the willing group of 34 countries set up by his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, in support of Ukraine.
Tensions between London and Moscow have been mounting for weeks as it emerged over the weekend that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, last month after seven years in the diplomatic post.
The lower-ranking charge d’affaires has taken the lead in his absence, according to an embassy spokesperson talking to The Times.
The latest announcement of support by Mr Burnham means that the British government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information and blueprints on UK components for the long-range SCALP missile. The weapons are the equivalent of the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow.
Last Tuesday, it was reported that British-made drones had been used in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to threaten “consequences” for the support. It warned ominously that the greater the assistance that Britain provided, “the higher price it will pay”.
At the time, Mr Burnham doubled down, saying: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.”
The European Commission, meanwhile, has approved a further €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in financial aid for Ukraine, to be spent on buying defence systems, including air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.
The latest aid package came after €16bn of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35bn had already been disbursed, according to the EU.
“As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it,” EC president Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
In other developments in the war, Russian attacks killed three people near Kharkiv overnight on Sunday, according to the region’s governor, while Moscow claimed debris from a Ukrainian drone killed two children in Russia’s Krasnodar.
