Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Beijing, Aug 25: India on Tuesday conveyed to China the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) for overall bilateral ties as National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi focusing on delimitation of the frontier and sustaining work on trans-boundary cooperation.
In New Delhi, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said Doval and Wang had “candid and in-depth” exchange of views on the India-China boundary question and agreed to continue their work in seeking a “political settlement” of the issue in the context of “overall and long-term interests”.
Doval landed in Beijing on Monday on a two-day visit and his trip is largely seen as part of ongoing efforts by the two neighbours to rebuild their relationship after it came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020.
“The Indian side highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility in the India-China border areas for the continued development and progress of the bilateral relationship,” it said.
Held under the framework of Special Representatives dialogue, the Doval-Wang talks came weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s anticipated visit to India for the upcoming BRICS summit.
Doval and Wang are the designated Special Representative for the talks.
“Under the strategic guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping, and in a constructive and forward-looking spirit, the two Special Representatives had a candid and in-depth exchange of views on the India-China boundary question and agreed to continue their work in seeking a political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests,” the MEA said.
The Indian embassy in Beijing said the two sides “positively reviewed” the ongoing momentum in bilateral relations in line with the vision of PM Modi and President Xi.
"They discussed ways to further expand bilateral cooperation, maintain stability and ensure peace and tranquility in the border areas, and make progress on boundary delimitation, while sustaining the ongoing work on transboundary cooperation," it said.
The Special Representatives (SR) dialogue took place amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.
In his remarks at the meeting, Doval said that normalcy in the ties has been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas.
"I am very happy we are here for the 25th round of talks which are very important, particularly in the wake of the BRICS summit to happen shortly," he said.
"We meet in keeping with the guidance of our leaders, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping, who have given clear and positive direction to our relationship both at Kazan and Tianjin," Doval said, referring to the meetings the two leaders held on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Russia in 2024 and the SCO summit in China last year.
Referring to progress made by the two sides in normalising the ties following the eastern Ladakh military standoff, Doval said the bilateral relationship has been steadily returning to normalcy.
“The normalcy we have witnessed in our relationship has been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas,” he said.
“We have extensively talked about it today just to see how to effectively reinforce and further consolidate our efforts to maintain peace and tranquillity in the border areas,” he said in an apparent reference to differences over the border and Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as South Tibet.
Doval also talked about advances made by the two countries in improving people-to-people ties.
"The successful conduct of Kailash Manasarovar Yatra via Nathu La and resumption of our traditional border trade via all the three passes brought tangible benefits for our people, particularly people living in the border areas,” he said.
The MEA said the sides also discussed bilateral, regional and international issues of mutual interest.
In his remarks, Wang said the China-India relationship has gone beyond the bilateral scope and taken on global and strategic significance.
“It is important for us to step up communication, to enhance mutual trust, to remove disturbances and overcome obstacles. We need to be good friends that enjoy good neighbourliness and be good partners that contribute to each other’s success,” he said.
Wang also talked about adding new impetus to the ties during the talks with Doval.
"I look forward to continuing to have in-depth exchange of views with you on issues of shared interest to better understand each other and to properly handle the boundary question, to not only maintain peace and tranquillity in the border area but also inject new impetus for the bilateral relationship,” he said.
Wang also said the two sides have stayed in regular communication through diplomatic and military channels on boundary affairs, implementing the guidance of PM Modi and President Xi.
Both Doval and Wang are the designated SRs for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to comprehensively address the dispute of the India-China border spanning 3,488 km.
While success eluded it in resolving the boundary dispute, officials on both sides regard the structured mechanism as a useful tool in addressing the recurring tensions between the two countries on various fronts.

Kejelcha breaks men's half marathon world record by 29 seconds
- Published
Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha has broken the men's half marathon world record, winning a World Athletics road race in Buenos Aires on Sunday in 56 minutes 51 seconds.
The 29-year-old previously held the record with a time of 57:30, set in Valencia in October 2024, but lost that to Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in March.
Kiplimo ran 57:20 in Lisbon earlier this year but Kejelcha has now knocked 29 seconds off that time to regain the record, subject to official ratification.
The world track silver medallist in the 10,000m also holds the world record for a men's 10,000m road race.
He also became one of the first men to run a sub-two hour marathon in record-eligible conditions earlier this year when finishing second behind Kenya's Sebastian Sawe in the London Marathon.
Sawe won the record-breaking race in 1:59:30, beating Kejelcha by just 11 seconds.

I Tried the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere
Featured in this article
There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.
I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.
Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.
Updated August 2026: The second-generation Kindle Scribe has been updated to be our pick for students, and prices have been updated throughout.
Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.
Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs.
Looking for more accessory ideas? Check out my guide to all of the best Kindle accessories. Also, don't forget that if the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.
FAQs
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations, and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.
When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.
You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Monday called on Russian President Vladimir Putin, as the two sides discussed bilateral ties and global developments.
Jaishankar, who arrived in Moscow on Sunday, is on a two-day visit to Russia.
It comes ahead of Putin’s expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS leaders’ summit on September 12-13. The meeting assumes significance as India and Russia seek to deepen their economic engagement and expand cooperation in a range of areas.
Earlier in the day, the foreign minister held talks with Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov on ways to further expand bilateral trade and economic cooperation.
“The India-Russia partnership has consistently demonstrated resilience and adaptability,” Jaishankar said at an event which he co-chaired with Manturov. “Even amidst a complex international landscape, our engagement has continued to deepen, reflecting the mutual interest and confidence that define our bilateral partnership.”
During his visit, Jaishankar is also scheduled to meet Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to exchange views on regional and global issues, the External Affairs Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.
The visit comes a month after Jaishankar and Lavrov met in Manila on July 22 on the sidelines of ASEAN-related ministerial meetings, where they reviewed bilateral relations and exchanged views on the Ukraine conflict and the situation in West Asia. Jaishankar had also reiterated India’s “strong concern” regarding the safety of Indian seafarers in the region during his last meeting with Lavrov. (PTI)

Pernia Pop Up Shop’s parent Purple Style Labs’ (PSL) consolidated net loss for the year ending March 31, 2026 (FY26) widened by 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr compared to a loss of ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous year. Operating revenue for the fiscal increased by about 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Including other income of ₹9.2 Cr, the IPO-bound company’s total income for the fiscal rose 14.8% to ₹567.1 Cr. Pernia's gross merchandise value (GMV) for the fiscal year increased 23% YoY to ₹721.6 Cr. The company’s international GMV contribution declined from 28.38% in FY25 to 20.3% in FY26, while US GMV fell from ₹97.4 Cr to ₹76.8 Cr. This comes despite the company opening its New York store in February 2026 and positioning international expansion as a key growth opportunity. Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs operates multi-brand luxury omnichannel fashion platform Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop. Selling via its D2C platform as well as 12 experience centres, the company sells luxury fashion, sourced from 1,109 active designer brands. These designer brands include Seema Gujral, Anushree Reddy, Amit Aggarwal, Rohit Gandhi & Rahul Khanna. The company's product categories span across womenswear, menswear, and others including jewelry, accessories and kidswear, with a focus on wedding and occasion wear. The company served a total of 66,713 customers in the fiscal, down 6% from 70,651 in FY25. It has raised a private equity funding of about $78 Mn till date from investors like Harish Shah Family Office, Masaba Gupta, among others. The company filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) for initial public offering, and the IPO comprises only a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. Pernia’s parent filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI in September 2025 and got the regulator’s approval to proceed with the IPO in January. A huge portion of the net proceeds will be used to fund lease liabilities of Pernia’s Pop Up Stores’ experience center networks, while the remaining will fund sales and marketing expenses till FY30. Zooming Into PSL’s Expenses The company spent an overall of ₹734.5 Cr in the year under review for all its expenses, marking a 31% increase from the previous year’s ₹559.6 Cr. Here is a breakdown of its total expenditure: Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: Spending under this head rose 84.4% to ₹100.7 Cr in the year under review, from ₹54.6 Cr in FY25. Purchases Of Stock-In-Trade: Constituting 47.6% of the overall costs, expenses under this area stood at ₹349.8 Cr, marking a 15.6% increase from ₹302.6 Cr in the previous year. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs including gratuity, wages, provident fund and others stood at ₹82 Cr in FY26, up 23.9% from ₹66.2 Cr in the previous fiscal.

Over the past few years, I have seen a steady stream of patients who have never set foot in a gym, yet present with the kinds of injuries I mostly see in weekend athletes. While the increased awareness about the need to stay physically active and fit is welcome, many young people are now relying on YouTube videos or Instagram reels without fully understanding their body’s limitations.
There is no doubt that home workouts are certainly better than no exercise at all. What began as a necessity during the pandemic has, for many, become a long-term habit and that is a positive development in many ways. However, what concerns me is that many people are training without proper guidance on exercise form, load management, nutrition, or recovery. While the motivation to stay active is commendable, exercising without the right knowledge or supervision can sometimes do more harm than good.
Here are the five most common injuries due to home workouts and how to prevent them.
Shoulder Pain - Rotator Cuff Strain: This is probably the most common shoulder complaint I see in patients who work out at home. It is often caused by overhead presses or push up variations performed with poor shoulder positioning, inadequate shoulder blade control, or the elbows flaring out at an awkward angle.
In most cases, the pain doesn’t begin suddenly. It starts as a dull, nagging ache that many people ignore for weeks. Over time, if left unaddressed, it can progress into a sharp, intense pain that makes simple daily activities difficult,such as lifting the arm, getting dressed, reaching overhead, or even combing hair.
Prevention: Keep your elbows at somewhere between a 30–45 degree angle from your body during pressing movements, and don’t start pushing heavy weights before your shoulder mobility can support the range.
Back Pain: Lower Back Strain: Working out with a rounded spine, especially during exercises such as deadlifts, bent over rows, and even certain sit-up variations is one of the most common causes of back strain. When exercising at home, without a mirror or a trainer to monitor and correct your form, it’s easy to unknowingly round the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Prevention: Take a deep breath and brace the core before lifting any weights, keep the spine neutral and if you feel you cannot maintain the position through full movement, then reduce the weight. I usually tell patients to first do a workout out without weights, just to get the correct posture and form initially, before starting with weights.
Knee Injury: High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has become one of the most popular workout styles today. However, high impact exercises such as jump squats and burpees are also common causes of knee pain, often leading to conditions including patellar tendinitis and ligament strain. This usually happens because people focus on generating maximum height and power during the jump but pay little attention to how they land.
Prevention: A soft, controlled landing is essential to protect your knees during high impact exercises. Ensure your knees track in line with your toes throughout the movement, and increase your jump volume gradually on a week-to-week basis to allow your body time to adapt.
Wrist and Elbow Pain: Exercises such as push-ups, planks, and mountain climbers performed on hard floors with the wrists held in a fully extended position can place excessive strain on the tendons and ligaments around the wrist and elbow. Over time, this repetitive stress can lead to overuse injuries such as tennis elbow, golfer’s elbow, and even wrist ganglion cysts.
Prevention: Use a soft exercise mat and, if needed, a wrist wrap. Make sure the load is distributed evenly across the entire palm. Maintain proper form and listen to your body’s signals. If you experience pain, burning, or increasing discomfort, slow down, or stop rather than pushing through the pain.
Ankle Sprains: Working out on uneven flooring or in confined spaces without adequate clearance can significantly increase the risk of ankle injuries. Poor landing mechanics, awkward foot placement, and repetitive strain on the ankle ligaments are common causes of sprains during home workouts. Even after recovering from an ankle sprain, many people neglect balance and stability training, which is essential to prevent re-injury. Unlike larger joints, the ankle is supported by relatively small muscles and relies heavily on ligament strength, rather than weight training alone
Prevention: Clear a proper flat space before you start, and if your workout involves any lateral movement or jumping, footwear with real ankle support matters more at home than most people assume.
Why this keeps happening
In almost all the patients I see, the root cause isn’t the exercise itself but not following a proper warm-up routine; skipping the basics and starting with advanced variations; ignoring early warning signs of pain because of not being sure how much discomfort is considered normal during exercise.
Pain is one of the body’s most important ways of communicating with you. A little muscle fatigue is normal but a sharp, localised pain that changes how you move is not something that should be ignored.
Preventing long-term complications
- Warm up for at least 5 minutes before any home routine. This should include dynamic stretches and not static ones.
- Work on form before you increase the intensity - a slow, well-controlled rep is better than fast one ending with an injury
- Progress load by not more than 10% a week - this is the common teaching among long-distance runners and the same applies for strength workouts too
- Don’t train through pain - soreness or discomfort is normal but a sharp pain on one side is a sign of concern - if you experience it, then reach out to a medical expert
- Invest in the right mat/shoes
When you work out at home, you are the trainee and you are the coach - so it is you who should watch and correct your form and understand & listen to your body, because an untreated overuse injury can set your fitness journey back by months.
(Dr. Shriram Krishnamoorthy is senior orthopaedic & sports Injury surgeon, Shri Bone & Joint Clinic, Chennai. skshriram@gmail.com)

CIA director ‘makes mysterious visit to Moscow’ with no explanation from Kremlin or Trump
The Kremlin insists it has no further information about the landing
CIA director John Ratcliffe made a short visit to Moscow on Tuesday to meet with Russian officials for talks not announced by the White House or the Kremlin, according to a report.
The large US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III took flight from Riga in Latvia on Tuesday morning before flying across the border into Russian airspace and landing at Vnukovo International Airport in the country’s capital, according to data from Flightradar24.
It is thought to be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia since taking up the position as intelligence chief last January, Axios reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov initially said that he did not have any further information about the aircraft when pressed by reporters on its arrival earlier in the day.
US media, including Axios and CBS citing unnamed sources, later reported that Ratcliffe was on board the plane in order to attend meetings but did not say with whom or what the talks are expected to be about.
The US told Ukraine to suspend strikes while a senior delegation travelled to Moscow ahead of the trip, a source told Axios,
President Donald Trump has not commented on the arrival of the aircraft and no clarification has been provided by any US government body yet.
The heavy transport plane is designed for carrying troops and military equipment and arrived in Latvia on Sunday from the US Camp Springs airbase near Washington DC, according to the flight tracking website.
The Trump appointee has previously described Russia as a “dangerous, lethal adversary”.
The last time a US registered jet took off to Russia from Europe was in January earlier this year when special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held peace talks with President Vladimir Putin on Ukraine.
It follows Andy Burnham’s declaration to provide unwavering support to Ukraine “despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country” during his trip to Kyiv.
The British prime minister called for further economic sanctions on Russia and said that “this is the moment to keep up the pressure” on Moscow.
Tensions have been mounting between Russia and Europe as the Kremlin again rejected any possible deployment of Nato troops in Ukraine, calling the suggestion “unacceptable”.
A meeting of the Coalition of the Willing was held on Monday in order to rally support for Ukraine where the proposal was discussed.
US-brokered negotiations have largely stalled since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has diverted significant resources and time away from the war in Ukraine.
Last month it was reported that FBI director Kash Patel is to be hosted by KGB officials in Moscow in October but the agenda of the visit is yet to be disclosed.

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

China has denounced the threat of US sanctions for its trade with Iran, saying any such measures would be illegal, and warned it would take “all necessary measures” to protect its national interests.
Beijing’s rejection of the US threat of secondary sanctions for any country or entity continuing to trade with Tehran had been predicted. China buys an estimated 80% of Iran’s oil exports and it has defied previous US efforts to limit the flow of revenue to the Tehran regime.
Its statement of opposition raises the question of how far the Trump administration would be prepared to go in confronting China and its financial system in the drive to isolate Iran.
In making the sanctions threat on Monday, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced an initial set of sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels for alleged involvement in trade with Iran, but there were no Chinese financial institutions on the list, despite their involvement in financing the Iranian oil trade. The omission reflected US caution.
Asked why the Trump administration had not declared immediate sanctions and had stopped short of naming potential sanctions targets, Bessent replied: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”
Financial and trade experts say the administration is well aware of the risk of Chinese retaliation before a scheduled summit next month between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. China could strike back through financial markets or with limits on its export of critical minerals.
The spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry, Lin Jian, told reporters on Tuesday: “Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted.
“China has already stated many times that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions. China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests.”
Iran has been economically wrecked by the war and the accompanying US blockade, but it maintained its defiance in response to Bessent’s threats of total isolation.
The economy minister, Ali Madanizadeh, said on state television: “Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack.”
An oil tanker was reportedly hit on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile at the mouth of the strait of Hormuz. Only two commercial vessels were reported to have successfully made the transit through the narrow waterway on Monday.
The declaration of what Bessent called Operation Economic Outcast suggests that the prospects of a resolution to the conflict with Iran are still remote. It also suggests a lean towards economic measures and away from military force after a six-month war that has not brought about the intended Iranian capitulation.
The near closure of the strait of Hormuz and knock-on effect on oil prices and the global economy is a political risk for Trump as congressional elections loom in November.
The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, insisted that further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday.
Bessent called the sanctions campaign unprecedented and compared it to the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.
“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
He said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.
“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”
Bessent said Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”
In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.
Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.”

MV Ocean Winner: Empty lifeboat located in Bay of Bengal, 22 crew still missing
The bulk carrier, carrying about 71,200 metric tonnes of iron ore fines from Paradip port in Odisha to China, sank around 290 nautical miles off Paradip
Rescuers searching for 22 missing crew members of the cargo vessel MV Ocean Winner on Tuesday recovered an emergency beacon and located a lifeboat associated with the Panama-flagged ship, but did not find survivors, the coast guard said.
“ICGS (Indian Coast Guard Vessel) Varad, supported by Indian naval aircraft, additional Coast Guard ships and merchant vessels operating nearby, is conducting an extensive search across the designated area. During an aerial sweep, a naval aircraft detected an emergency beacon transmission and directed Varad to its location, where the beacon linked to MV Ocean Winner was recovered before the empty lifeboat was found,” a Coast Guard spokesperson said.
The 1998-built bulk carrier, carrying about 71,200 metric tonnes of iron ore fines from Paradip port in Odisha to China, sank around 290 nautical miles off Paradip in the deep waters of the Bay of Bengal on August 21.
Two of the 24 crew members were rescued earlier from life rafts, while the remaining 22, including several Chinese nationals, continue to remain missing.
The search operation, coordinated by ICG along with the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre Beijing, has intensified despite challenging weather and rough sea conditions.
Experts suggest that the vessel’s rapid capsize was consistent with bulk cargo liquefaction, one of shipping’s deadliest hazards.
Maritime industry publication, The Maritime Executive, said the speed of the sinking, the early development of a list and the cargo type pointed to liquefaction of iron ore fines. When saturated with water, iron ore fines can shift suddenly inside cargo holds during rolling, causing a vessel to lose stability and capsize rapidly.
The publication noted that at least 29 seafarers died in iron ore cargo liquefaction incidents worldwide between 2007 and 2019.
Paradip Port Authority officials said Odisha has experienced 29% excess monsoon rainfall this season, with heavy rain lashing the coast through July and August.
Captain Manoj Sahoo of Navitech Logistics said considering that the fines were stocked in open space, there was a distinct possibility that they attracted moisture.
“Liquefaction is one possibility. Besides, leaking hatch covers during rough weather could have allowed seawater into the cargo holds, accelerating liquefaction. Ocean Winner was also nearing its life expectancy, considering that it was 28 years old, and ships generally have an operational lifespan of 25 to 30 years. So there is a possibility of structural deterioration,” Sahoo said.
Neither Bothra Shipping, which acted as the loading agent for the iron ore fines nor the Paradip Port Authority officials responded to HT’s queries on liquefaction

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to unveil new economic sanctions on Iran
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil a new round of economic sanctions on Iran on Monday, in what he has described as the "single greatest financial offensive ever."
President Trump has called it an "economic D-Day" and pledged to go after other countries who extend an economic lifeline to Tehran.
In anticipation, the Iranian currency, the Rial, has plunged to a record low.
What are these new sanctions and how much more pressure can they pile on?
The U.S. already has extensive sanctions on Iran, some stretching back almost 50 years, and as recently as June had imposed further penalties for entities that helped Iran evade existing financial restrictions. There has also been a months-long U.S. naval blockade of Iran, which has cut off most goods to Iran from the outside world.
This latest suggestion from President Trump and Secretary Bessent appears to be focused on putting more pressure on the countries and governments — not just the businesses — that host the entities providing cashflow for Iran.
In an editorial for the Financial Times published overnight, Bessent wrote, "our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." He appeared to reference countries that still trade with Iran, saying they should "consider the consequences of doing so."
That includes China, Iran's biggest oil customer, which Bessent criticized last week for historically buying about 90 percent of Iran's oil.
But some analysts question the actual utility of fresh economic sanctions.
Alan Eyre, a former American diplomat who was part of the U.S. negotiating team over Iran's nuclear program until 2015, told NPR's Emily Feng that the U.S. has already targeted "the low-hanging fruit, the mid-hanging fruit, the high-hanging fruit, the tree," and that "there are no new sanctions that are effective."
Iran vows a "seismic" retaliation to any sanctions
Iran's new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state TV over the weekend that Iran would retaliate in a "seismic manner" to Trump's latest attempt at economic warfare. Rezaei, a hardliner who used to lead Iran's Revolutionary Guards, is now a military adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
Rezaei warned Gulf states that any countries partnering in these new economic restrictions would be considered an enemy of — and a target for — Iran.
Since the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran nearly six months ago, Iran has attacked U.S. bases in Jordan and Gulf countries including the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Several have led to serious injuries and fatalities.
Rezaei said Iran would retaliate by further targeting oil tankers that are transiting the Persian Gulf on the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that "not even a single drop of oil will leave the region."
Iran is not currently interfering in these routes, so such actions could further hamper oil supplies. Energy exports from the Gulf region have already suffered the biggest disruption in their history because of the war and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Gulf countries that invested billions on pipelines that can help avoid the Strait of Hormuz, have not yet commented on the U.S. plans for fresh sanctions.
New sanctions will make a dire economic situation worse for ordinary Iranians
Iran has weathered some U.S. sanctions for almost half a century, since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, with ordinary Iranians bearing the brunt of the subsequent economic pain.
The Iranian economy was already struggling when the U.S. and Israel launched this war against Iran in February, with double-digit inflation and currency devaluation. According to the Iranian government agency, the Statistical Centre of Iran, inflation is now at almost 90 percent.
NPR spoke to one 30-year-old Iranian woman, who said most ordinary Iranians are now buying food using a credit system because they do not have enough cash.
"Since I am in debt to the grocery store, I couldn't even buy tomato paste to cook pasta," she told NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi. She did not want to be named for fear of retaliation from the Iranian government.
She said lifesaving medicines like insulin have become too expensive for many, and that daily life is becoming increasingly difficult, with frequent power cuts and unemployment rising.
Economic pain and the high cost of living were among the factors driving Iranians to protest on the streets earlier this year, in demonstrations that were met with a deadly government crackdown.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Good morning. Do you consider the end of August the end of summer? When is an appropriate time to start talking about Halloween? I don’t have the answers, but I do have some news below.
CDC releases latest life expectancy data
In 2024, American life expectancy at birth surpassed pre-pandemic levels, according to new data from the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. Overall, babies born that year could be expected to live to age 79, per the data. That’s up 0.6 years from 2023 and 0.2 from 2019, the last year before Covid-19 started drastically reducing those rates.
A decline in Covid deaths played a major role in the increase from 2023 to 2024, but so did decreases in deaths because of unintentional injuries (the biggest contribution), heart disease, cancer, and homicide.
The case of the mysteriously deleted comments
When Magdeleine Bradford-Butcher heard about a pending White House regulation that would subject federal science funding to increased political intervention, she decided to submit a public comment on the proposal to explain how she has benefited from research funding. Her daughter has cystic fibrosis, as does the daughter of Russell Vought, who directs the White House Office of Management and Budget. “He probably isn’t reading these but just in case: Russell, for the sake of your daughter and mine, please do not make these rules effective,” she pleaded in her comment, mentioning the medication that both children have been treated with.
Then something unusual happened: Bradford-Butcher’s comment was taken down, without explanation. Hers is one of 42 published comments that have been removed, STAT’s Anil Oza reports. Among those, it’s one of 10 that note how Vought’s family has benefited from federally funded research. Read more from Anil on how legal experts reacted to the deletions and what it may mean for future challenges to the proposal.
Can AI surveillance catch hospital drug theft?
Anyone who has ever seen a medical drama knows about drug diversion — when hospital staff skim from or steal a medication that was meant for a patient. “There is diversion going on everywhere,” said Chris Fortier, who previously served as the chief pharmacy officer at Massachusetts General Hospital. “Whether it’s large, whether it’s small, it’s happening. And it’s very, very difficult to identify.”
But machine learning and AI can capture drug diversion by hospital staff at much higher rates than traditional, manual methods, according to a study from the firm Invistics, which has developed its own detection system. Outside experts aren’t so sure and caution that the technology is only as effective as the people using it. Read more from STAT contributor Alexandra Byrne about how well these programs work in reality.
How Trump’s cuts are reshaping America’s health system
The full impacts of the incoming Medicaid cuts won’t be felt for years, but many parts of the health care system are already racing to prepare — especially in rural states, where changes are expected to hit the hardest.
Take Maine, for instance. The state has the nation’s highest proportion of its population living in rural areas and an above-average share of Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries. STAT’s Daniel Payne visited health systems in “vacationland,” and everyone he spoke to expected the state to end up with fewer hospital services once the cuts are fully enacted. Some had seen an impact already.
“The capabilities in the little hospitals just keep declining,” said Tom Judge, the founding executive director of LifeFlight of Maine. “Demand is going to keep going up.”
Daniel traveled to Louisiana and Maine and interviewed dozens of executives, doctors, and policymakers for STAT’s latest series, Unraveled. His stories will explore the consequences of President Trump’s unprecedented cuts to the health care safety net. Read the first installment now.
Turning island life into a laboratory
Cases of — and news about — alpha gal syndrome have surged over the last decade or so. You’ve likely heard of it: the tickborne red meat allergy. Researchers at Massachusetts General Brigham are launching what they call a first-of-its-kind study focused on who develops the syndrome after a tick bite, and why. The study, based on Martha’s Vineyard, will recruit up to 300 island residents and follow them for two years. The island has been transformed by the syndrome in recent years, per Boston Globe reporting.
It’s not the first time a storied Massachusetts island has forged new ground when it comes to tickborne diseases. In 2016, former STAT reporter Ike Swetlitz wrote about how scientists on Nantucket had proposed genetically modifying tens of thousands of mice to stop the spread of Lyme disease. “If we don’t change how we do science for this, we will be violating our democratic ideals,” MIT researcher Kevin Esvelt told Ike at the time. He’s still working on the project, called Mice Against Ticks. Now, the team will reportedly study the mice on a remote island before moving on to Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard.
Reflecting on cancer screening in long-term care
As a cancer epidemiologist, Kim Johnson knows that a diagnosis of stage 4 breast cancer is not very common. So when her aunt, at 78, died of stage 4 breast cancer just three weeks after her diagnosis, Johnson knew that something was off. Her aunt lived in a long-term care facility, but it turns out that there are no major national cancer screening guidelines written for older individuals living in these facilities.
“In reading literature on this topic, I came away feeling that substantial attention was devoted to the harms of screening residents of long-term care facilities, with much less attention to identifying those residents for whom screening may still provide meaningful benefit,” Johnson writes in a new First Opinion essay. Read more about how her aunt’s death made her reevaluate existing guidelines.

Someone generated the image with AI. Genuine vintage photos do exist showing children in car seats suspended outside the driver's side doors of parked vehicles. Despite social media speculation, no historical records indicate people drove cars with children in a seat hanging outside of the vehicle, nor does data suggest parents or guardians left kids hooked onto the door to avoid interior car heat while adults shopped.
In summer 2026, people claimed a image spreading online was a vintage photo of a baby sitting in a car seat suspended outside the driver's door:
(zadraaa accessed via Reddit)
In the example above, posted June 7, a Reddit user captioned (archived) the image, "A 1950s-style baby car seat, reminding us how far safety standards have come. Never leave a child in a hot car while you shop."
The black-and-white image shows a baby suspended in a car seat outside the open window of the driver's door of the vehicle. A house with a stoop and striped awnings is visible in the background.
Other users shared the picture on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Reddit (archived) and X (archived).
In short, the image is fake, generated using artificial intelligence.
Signs of AI in the fake car seat image
The fake car seat image displays numerous signs that generative AI was used to create it. The full-size version has an unusual crispness for photographs from the 1940s and '50s.
As seen in a reflection on the the car's body, the child appears to have three legs and feet (marked 1, 2 and 3 below):
Notice, too, that the car seat is padded on the child's right side, but there appears to be no padding on the side closest to the car. Also, if the seat were removed from the door as configured and attached to a seat inside the car, the child would be facing left or right, not forward. Our research found only vintage car seats designed to face forward or backward.
Speaking of facing forward, the full-size image shows the car parked perpendicular to the curb instead of parallel to it as would be more expected in a residential neighborhood.
The right side of the house in the background (as seen from the street) appears to have an odd mixture of brick and vinyl siding. Had the brick formed into a fireplace and chimney, that might make sense. However, there are windows on that wall, likely indicating no fireplace. (A Reddit user noted (archived) several of these signs of AI.)
Multiple scans of the image with the Google Gemini AI tool returned the same conclusion. Gemini detected the company's invisible SynthID watermark, meaning someone used a Google-created AI tool to create the image: "My analysis of this image indicates that it contains a SynthID watermark, which means that most or all of the content was edited or generated with Google AI."
A reverse image search failed to find any posts with the fake image prior to a March 2026 post (archived) on the Historical Image Facebook page, on which managers shared nothing but content labeled as AI-generated. Snopes messaged the page's managers to ask for more information about the creation of the image. As of this writing, the page has posted no new content since June.
Real pictures of children in car seats suspended outside cars
Reverse image searches did locate similar images that were genuine, i.e., not created with AI or digitally edited.
For example, on Aug. 2, 2026, an Instagram user posted (archived) the fake image alongside an authentic photo showing a boy in a car seat suspended outside the door of a parked vehicle. The caption alleged, without evidence, that people would drive with the child unsafely attached outside the car to "enjoy the view during road trips."
(@explaining.tech accessed via Instagram)
A popular Facebook post (archived) from 2021 showing the same genuine picture from the above post featured a user claiming, also without proof, that people would hook a child car seat outside on a car door to avoid leaving a child inside a hot car while adults shopped.
(A house in the background features a striped awning similar to the AI-generated image. The Google AI tool that created the fake image potentially referenced this genuine photo.)
(American Hot Rodders Show accessed via Facebook)
The car seat in the authentic photo appears to match the Peterson car seat that appeared in a 1955 newspaper advertisement (archived). It cost $3.45.
(Stockton Record via Newspapers.com)
Another authentic picture, which appeared in a 2018 Reddit post (archived), also showed a young boy in a car seat hanging outside a car door. The caption reads, "Early model of a baby car seat." There are others in the picture as well, including a young girl smiling, left, and what appear to be the shadows of two adults on the right side.
(H_G_Bells accessed via Reddit)
A 1945 newspaper ad (archived) displays an illustration of the same or a similar brand of car seat as that pictured immediately above, priced at $1.98. The ad reads in part, "This one slips right over the regular car seat back."
(St. Louis Star Times via Newspapers.com)
Further reverse image searches located websites, for example vintag.es, hosting authentic vintage photos of children seated forward or backward, not left or right, in car seats inside cars.
How we located brands and illustrations
For readers interested in our research process, we found past car seat brands and the above-shown advertising illustrations via a path of online searches.
A Google search for the history of car seats led to an article mentioning the Bunny Bear company. A Newspapers.com search for "Bunny Bear," with quotation marks, as well as the terms "car," "seat" and "baby," led us to a vintage ad (archived) mentioning the Rose Derry company. A Newspapers.com search for "Rose Derry" and "car seat" pointed to another vintage ad (archived) listing numerous children's product brand names. Searches for those brands led to other leads, including the aforementioned car seat ads with illustrations, as well as numerous illustrated patents.
For further reading, we previously investigated alleged vintage photos showing babies in cagelike enclosures outside apartment-building windows.
