Indonesians brave choking smoke to pray for rain as country battles wildfires
PALEMBANG, Indonesia — Authorities in Indonesia's South Sumatra, the province with the highest number of wildfire hot spots, turned to spiritual measures on Tuesday as huge blazes in central and western regions scorched wide areas of forests and peatland, creating a choking haze that blanketed some cities in the world's most populous Muslim-majority country.
The prayer gathering initiative comes as the province faces prolonged dry weather that has heightened the risk of forest and peatland fires.
The latest satellite data from the Environment Ministry showed South Sumatra recorded the highest number of hot spots nationwide with 1,429, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. Forestry Ministry data indicated that nearly 940 square kilometers (363 square miles) were burned in July alone, including over 20 square kilometers (8 square miles) in South Sumatra province.
About 3,000 residents gathered in Palembang, the capital of South Sumatra province, to perform a special Islamic prayer for rain, known as "salat istisqa." They prayed shoulder to shoulder in the courtyard of the governor's office as thick smoke shrouded roads, buildings and public facilities, reducing visibility and forcing motorists to drive with their headlights on during the day.
"We have done everything we can and worked closely with all relevant parties," South Sumatra Gov. Herman Deru said before the prayer. "As people of faith, we are also praying to God to send rain so that life can return to normal."
He also said the public prayer would complement ongoing firefighting and drought-mitigation measures and serve as a moment for residents to unite in confronting the environmental challenges facing the province.
Emergency services have been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia and Brunei, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.
Indonesia is actively intensifying weather-modification operations to help firefighters combat wildfires by inducing rainfall through the dispersal of salt particles into suitable clouds, with 30 aircraft for cloud-seeding and water-bombing operations over Kalimantan, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Indonesian police have arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the forest and peatland fires, while four companies are under investigation for allegedly using fire to clear land at low cost.
Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, triggering hazardous haze that reduces visibility, disrupts land and air transportation and threatens public health.
Fires are a regular problem during the dry season in Indonesia, and the haze they generate has periodically drawn diplomatic complaints from neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.

- The claim that the Trump administration uses a legal loophole to sell protected wild horses to slaughterhouses is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from reporting by The New York Times in August 2026 and was backed by research by animal rights groups that suggested buyers of wild horses sold through the Bureau of Land Management's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter.
- According to its website, it is BLM policy "not to sell or send any wild horses or burros to slaughter," and buyers from the sale program sign a bill of sale saying they will not slaughter or sell for slaughter the animals they buy.
- The Times' reporting brought to light a long-standing issue within the BLM about what to do with excess wild horses and burros. The bureau is bound by law to regulate populations but has historically avoided euthanizing healthy animals due to concerns about public perception.
- Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses.
- Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that more recent buyers have purchased horses from the BLM and sold them for slaughter, the article did not include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administration. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- We contacted the Times journalist who wrote the article and an animal rights group that provided research to ask for additional evidence and await replies to our queries.
In August 2026, The New York Times published an investigation into the Bureau of Land Management's sale of wild horses, titled "Under Trump, Protected Wild Horses Are Going to Slaughter."
Synopses of the Times' findings circulated widely online. For example, one Facebook page wrote (archived):
A heartbreaking investigation revealed that Trump's Bureau of Land Management is systematically rounding up thousands of America's wild horses, then quietly selling them off to buyers who are shipping them to slaughterhouses abroad. Before, the U.S. government rarely sold wild horses. But since Trump took office, government sales have more than doubled.
Versions of the claim also circulated on Threads (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to learn more about it. One reader wrote, "Is Trump really rounding up horses to sell to slaughterhouses?"
The Times article reported how the U.S. government, faced with the ballooning costs of taking care of more than 50,000 wild horses it has rounded up to control herd sizes, sold thousands every year to buyers who purchased the animals for as little as $25 to sell at auction to other buyers that shipped them to slaughterhouses. This was allowed to happen, the Times reported, because selling a wild horse removes its statutory protection from "capture, branding, harassment, or death."
Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers of wild horses sold through the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter, the article didn't include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administrations.
Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses after being sold to private buyers before the start of the Trump administrations.
Snopes contacted Skydog Ranch and Sanctuary, an animal rescue organization that said it tracked animals from BLM ownership to auctions attended by slaughterhouse buyers to ask for additional evidence of the process the Times article described. We also contacted Dave Phillips, who wrote the Times article, to ask what primary evidence he used for his reporting. We await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A BLM spokesperson said in an emailed statement on Aug. 24, 2026:
The Bureau of Land Management does not sell or send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and allegations that individuals are violating federal law or the terms governing the sale of these animals are taken seriously.
The Times article suggested the BLM had found a way to offload its large off-range holding population of wild horses and burros that was effectively sending the animals to slaughter without incriminating the bureau.
The Wild Horse and Burro Program allows the BLM to sell animals that are more than 10 years old or that it has unsuccessfully listed for adoption at least three times. However, the Times reported, "Livestock inspection records show mustangs sold by the government soon ended up on trucks bound for slaughter plants in Canada."
The article focused on one reported buyer from Ohio, who the Times said had bought 500 horses from the BLM in a matter of years. Some of those horses, the article said, later showed up for sale at "an auction in Tennessee frequented by slaughter buyers."
The article also alleged that a week after the Ohio buyer received a shipment of 97 formerly wild mares, an Ohio exporter of animals for slaughter shipped two trucks of horses across the Canadian border. The Times said that, according to one image its reporter had viewed, at least one of those horses had a BLM freeze mark.
The Ohio buyer reportedly spoke to the Times reporter for two hours but "refused to say specifically what had happened to the horses he purchased from the government, other than to insist that none had gone to slaughter." He declined having worked with the Ohio exporter that shipped the two trucks across the Canadian border. The exporter would not comment to the Times on whether he had purchased horses from the buyer.
Without primary evidence — meaning sales documents tracking individual animals from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the auction in Tennessee or from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the Ohio exporter to a slaughterhouse — it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify the claims in the Times article.
Holding costs tie up BLM program budget
The Times article highlighted an issue that the BLM has grappled with for years: how to legally, effectively and tastefully control wild horse populations. According to the bureau's data, wild horse and burro populations exceed the BLM's Appropriate Management Level, meaning the number of animals that can thrive in balance with other public land resources and uses, in nearly all the states where the bureau tracks populations.
The BLM is required by The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 — the same act that protects wild horses and burros from "capture, branding, harassment, or death" — to uphold the AML for the populations it tracks (Sec. 1333b1). Under the Act, the BLM is allowed to euthanize excess animals "in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible" (Sec. 1333b2C). However, a 2008 report by the Government Accountability Office on the BLM's management of "unadoptable" horses found that the bureau hesitated to do this because it was thought to be "unacceptable to the public" (Page 56).
The BLM estimates that wild horse and burro populations, if left unregulated, would double every four years. Therefore, the bureau rounds up and removes thousands of animals from the wild to control populations. Those animals end up in the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program's off-range corrals and pastures. By May 2026, the program reported that it held 58,025 formerly wild horses and burros and that its total capacity for off-range holding was 78,751 animals. According to the program's figures it spent $101 million — 66% of its budget — on off-range holding costs in fiscal year 2024.
A long-standing problem
According to the 2008 GAO report, the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program faced the same challenges then that the Times article highlighted 18 years later. The report said the cost of caring for off-range animals was already overwhelming the program in 2008, and that the program had "limited" options for "dealing with" animals it could not adopt out because it feared the public would not support humanely euthanizing healthy animals (Page 9).
The program had reportedly sold animals since 2005, though at that point also faced issues with animals ending up at slaughterhouses after the sale (Page 43). As a result, the bureau implemented a mandatory "statement of intent" at purchase, which required the buyer to say that they did not intend to sell the animals they bought for slaughter. BLM bills of sale for wild horses and burros still included such a clause in 2026.
The effectiveness of the clause was unclear because the BLM also said on its website about its sales program that it did not track animals after it sold them. The 2008 report noted that the introduction of a "statement of intent" was part of the reason the BLM sold fewer horses than before.
The existence of the "statement of intent" did not deter one buyer, who admitted in a 2015 investigation carried out by the Office of the Inspector General that "most of" the 1,700 wild horses he bought through the BLM between 2008 and 2012 had gone to slaughter.
The GAO and OIG reports suggest that the issue of wild horses and burros ending up at slaughterhouses after BLM sales is documented and predates the Trump administration.
Aside from adoption, sale or euthanasia, the BLM has been pursuing fertility treatment as a way to control populations since 1992 (Page 69). However, the BLM itself and peer-reviewed research have found it comes with its own challenges around finding and accessing animals and keeping up with treatment. According to the BLM, it delivered 921 fertility treatments to wild horses and burros in fiscal year 2025. That same year, it removed 7,853 horses and burros from the wild.
The Times report said that although government experts did recommend wider use of fertility treatment to control populations the recommendation was hard for the BLM to act on because its funds were largely tied up in the removal, holding and care of excess animals.
In sum, while it was not possible to verify the exact elements of the Times' reporting, the article brought to light a complicated issue for the BLM that predated both Trump administrations but nonetheless had lethal consequences for the horses and burros the U.S. government is bound to protect.

Northern Territory police has charged federal Labor MP Luke Gosling with one count of breaching bail conditions less than one month after he was arrested over the alleged assault of the Territory’s administrator, David Connolly.
Gosling was charged with two counts of assault over an incident that allegedly occurred at a cultural festival in Darwin on 18 July.
He appeared before the Darwin local court on 31 July and was released with several bail conditions.
Police released a statement on Tuesday afternoon alleging Gosling had breached one of those bail conditions on 14 August.
“The Northern Territory Police Force has charged the federal member for Solomon, Luke Gosling, with one count of breach of bail,” NT police said.
“Today he was served with a summons to appear in Darwin local court on 30 September 2026.”
A spokesperson for Gosling said the MP would be discussing the matter with his legal team and defending the charge.
 “Neither Mr Gosling or his office have been made aware of the nature of the alleged breach and have been provided no information from police other than a summons.
“On Friday 14th August Mr Gosling did not attend any events at the same time as the administrator.”
The 54-year-old was elected the member for Solomon in 2016, representing Darwin and Palmerston in the Northern Territory.
A former military officer, he is the special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia.
Gosling’s bail conditions included staying at least 50 metres from the administrator’s house, and he was required to provide Connelly’s office with 48 hours’ notice for any event where the pair would both be in attendance.
If the two men were at the same event, the conditions also stated Gosling must remain at least 15 metres from Connelly.
The administrator has a similar function to a state governor.
Assaulting an administrator while they are performing official duties carries a maximum penalty of 14 years in jail under NT law.
The prime minister was contacted for comment. Gosling has previously denied the allegations and denied having any altercation with Connolly.
After his arrest, Gosling wrote on social media that he would focus on his job. He attended parliament in Canberra during the last sitting fortnight.
“I’ve got a job to do, and I’ll be working hard, as always, to serve the people of Darwin and Palmerston,” he wrote on 30 July.
The shadow minister for defence, James Paterson, has again called on Albanese to stand Gosling down from his envoy role after the latest charge.
“Anthony Albanese’s judgment has been exposed again. He should have immediately stood Luke Gosling aside as special envoy when he was first charged with assault,” Paterson told Guardian Australia.
“Now police allege Mr Gosling has breached bail. Surely this is enough for the prime minister to admit he got it wrong and immediately stand down his special envoy until this matter is resolved.”
The leader of the opposition, Angus Taylor, also called for Gosling to be stood down, and said “the case for the prime minister to act is even stronger”.

Americans love SUVs and full-size pickups. President Donald Trump's latest auto tariffs would hit the US's bestsellers with remarkable precision.
In a Monday Truth Social post, the President threatened 50% tariffs on all Canadian-made cars and trucks. The tariffs, which could go into effect on January 1, 2027, will also hit imported steel and automotive parts.
America's second-, third-, and fourth-best-selling vehicles in 2025 — the Chevy Silverado, the Toyota RAV4, and the Honda CR-V — all rely on production plants in Canada. Last year's best-selling vehicle, Ford's F-Series, has also been scheduled to begin Canadian assembly of its Super Duty trucks later this year. The fifth-best-selling vehicle in the US last year, the Ram 1500, has a significant portion of its parts assembly in Canada, too.
"The impact of unworkable tariffs would be felt well beyond Canadian assembly plants," Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive, told Business Insider. "Some of America's most popular vehicles are built in Canada."
Automakers have escape routes — but they aren't simple
Tariff exposure would not be evenly distributed across every vehicle.
Toyota, Honda, Ford, and General Motors also rely on assembly plants in the US to build these high-volume cars. That could allow the automakers to shift some production, David Whiston, an auto analyst at Morningstar, told Business Insider.
Honda, for example, already moved a portion of the Canadian CR-V production intended for US buyers to Ohio in 2025, although its Ontario plant continues to export vehicles to the US.
Still, the timing is difficult for several of these high-volume nameplates. Because of production constraints, RAV4 sales are down 36% this year, following Toyota's redesign of the popular SUV. The automaker is already trying to ramp production at its current factories to meet demand. GM is preparing its Oshawa plant to build its next generation of full-size Silverados. Ford, meanwhile, has spent roughly CA$ 5 billion retooling Oakville to produce Super Duty trucks.
"The math on that just got a lot worse for them with the 50% tariff," Whiston said about the Canadian investments.
White House's solution: Build in America
The White House defended the tariffs as an incentive for automakers to expand US production.
"President Trump has always been clear: if you don't want to worry about tariffs, make your product in the USA," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Domestic and foreign automakers alike, from Ford to Stellantis to Toyota, are investing billions to reshore manufacturing back to America without raising prices for this reason, and other automakers should follow suit."
Those investments do not necessarily replace the Canadian capacity.
The $3.6 billion Toyota investment recently highlighted by the White House will move Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas by 2030. It has no impact on the higher-volume RAV4.
It also remains unclear how the new tariff would be calculated. The current 25% tariff on Canadian vehicles provides a discount for US content. The White House did not directly answer whether the tariffs themselves could affect vehicle prices and availability.
Still time for a deal
Automakers have four months to adjust their sourcing and production plans, and the tariff could still change through negotiations between Washington and Ottawa, analysts said.
"I think a lot is still to happen between now and January 1, so maybe the two countries will work something out," Whiston said.
Keating said the parts tariffs could also reach drivers who aren't shopping for a new vehicle. More expensive replacement parts could raise repair and insurance costs, she said, regardless of where a driver's vehicle was assembled.
"The bigger question is affordability," Keating said. "Any policy that increases costs puts additional pressure on a market where many households already feel that virtually everything costs more than it did a few years ago."
Toyota declined to comment. Honda did not provide a comment by publication time. Ford and GM did not respond to requests for comment.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has publicly addressed his recent private meeting with Jared Kushner, saying he agreed to speak with the president’s son-in-law about the US affordability crisis while making clear that Democrats would continue to hold the Trump administration accountable. In a video posted on X, Jeffries said he wanted to address what he called the “Jared Kushner situation” after reports emerged that the two had met privately in New York. Jeffries said Kushner “asked for a meeting” and that he agreed to sit down with him to discuss the economic pressures facing Americans. Jeffries used the opportunity to draw a distinction between engaging in discussions and compromising on his opposition to President Donald Trump and his administration. “I wanted to talk about the affordability crisis that exists — that is not a hoax,” Jeffries said, appearing to take a swipe at Trump. While explaining why he agreed to the meeting, Jeffries stressed that Democrats would continue pursuing accountability against members of the Trump administration and its allies. “No one is going to get a pass,” Jeffries said, adding that he intends to hold “every single member of the Trump cartel accountable…on day one,” presumably if Democrats regain control of the House after the midterm elections. Without identifying specific individuals, Jeffries said anyone who is “stealing from…shortchanging…or screwing over the American people,” would face scrutiny. The comments come as Democrats prepare for the 2026 midterm elections, with control of the House expected to be a central political battleground. The New York Times reported on Sunday, citing five people familiar with the matter, that Jeffries and Kushner held a private meeting in New York City to discuss possible areas of common ground. The meeting was reportedly organised through a mutual friend. According to the report, the discussions included housing, immigration and the cost of living. Jared Kushner also reportedly encouraged Jeffries to meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Jeffries' public comments appear to confirm that the meeting took place, while framing the encounter as an opportunity to discuss issues affecting Americans rather than an indication of a political alliance. Jeffries also pointed to the issues on which House Democrats have opposed Trump and congressional Republicans, including immigration enforcement by ICE, tariffs, Medicaid and what he described as a “reckless war of choice in Iran”. He also highlighted changes within the administration, saying: “Pam Bondi is gone, Kristi Noem is gone, and we’re just getting started.” The remarks underline Jeffries' broader message that Democrats intend to continue challenging Trump even while engaging with figures close to the administration on issues where they believe discussions could be productive. The meeting has nevertheless prompted criticism from some prominent Democratic supporters and progressive commentators, who questioned the decision to meet Kushner privately. Tommy Vietor, a co-founder of Crooked Media and former Obama White House staffer, criticised the encounter, writing: “Jared Kushner has no actual government job; he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way Rep. Jeffries should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas.” The criticism reflects concerns among some Democrats that engaging with Trump allies could blur the party's opposition to the administration. Jeffries, however, has sought to portray the meeting as part of his effort to address issues such as housing and affordability while maintaining that Democrats will continue to scrutinise the Trump administration and pursue accountability. The story so far: The Union Health Ministry this past week tightened controls on all fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) containing chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine hydrochloride, requiring manufacturers to carry a clear warning that they must not be used in children below four years of age.
What are these two drugs?
Chlorpheniramine is an antihistamine. It can reduce allergy symptoms such as a runny nose and sneezing. Phenylephrine is a decongestant, intended to relieve a blocked nose.
An FDC puts both ingredients into one medicine. Such combinations are commonly encountered in cold/allergy preparations.
The government’s action does not mean every medicine containing either ingredient individually has been banned. The specific regulatory action concerns FDCs containing the two ingredients together.
What has changed now is the rule where manufacturers must put the warning. “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age” — on the label, package insert and promotional literature. The restriction covers manufacture, sale and distribution of these FDCs.
This expands an earlier action. In 2023, India’s Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) had already directed manufacturers of a particular chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine formulation to warn against use below four.
In April 2025, restrictions were imposed on certain FDCs. The August 2026 notification extends the warning requirement to all such formulations.
Why are children under four the focus?
Young children are more vulnerable to medication-related adverse effects because their bodies process medicines differently from adults and because dosing errors can have proportionally larger consequences.
The government’s Expert Committee and Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) concluded that these combinations could pose risks to children below four and that safer alternatives are available.
There is also a broader international concern around giving young children multi-ingredient cough-and-cold medicines. The US FDA, for example, warns that decongestant- or antihistamine-containing cough/cold products can cause serious adverse effects in very young children and notes the risk of accidental overdose when several ingredients are combined.
Does this mean cold medicines don’t work?
Not necessarily. These drugs can relieve symptoms, but they don’t cure the underlying viral infection. Most childhood colds resolve on their own. What doctors have been saying is that while parents may understandably want to make a congested or coughing child comfortable, but more medication isn’t automatically better.
For nasal congestion, relatively simple measures such as saline nasal drops/spray, fluids and a cool-mist humidifiercan help.
The key message is don’t self-medicate a child under four with a chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine combination, even if the product is marketed as a children’s cold medicine.
Check the active ingredients, not just the brand name. Many cold preparations contain several ingredients, creating a risk of accidentally giving the same drug twice through different products.
For fever or discomfort, parents should use medicines such as paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen only according to age/weight-appropriate instructions and medical advice.

Ex-Delhi Police commissioner Satish Golcha to take over as Home Guards' Director General from October 1
The latest order comes ahead of the superannuation of Virender Singh, who has been heading the Directorate of Home Guards.
Senior IPS officer Satish Golcha, who served as Delhi Police commissioner until last month, will take over as Director General of Home Guards, Delhi, from October 1, according to an order issued by the Delhi government on Tuesday.
Golcha, a 1992-batch AGMUT cadre IPS officer, has been transferred and posted as Officer on Special Duty (OSD) in the Directorate of Home Guards until the superannuation of incumbent DG Virender Singh, a 1991-batch IPS officer, on September 30.
He will assume charge as Director General, Home Guards, with effect from October 1, the order issued by the Home Department of the Delhi government said, news agency PTI reported.
Delhi Police will retain Golcha on its strength until he takes over as DG Home Guards.
Also Read: Who is Satish Golcha, Delhi's new police chief? 30+ years in IPS, held many key posts in capital
Golcha took charge as Delhi Police commissioner on August 22, 2025, succeeding Sanjay Arora. He was replaced by 1994-batch IPS officer Anurag Kumar as police commissioner on July 17 this year.
Who is Satish Golcha?
A 1992-batch AGMUT cadre IPS officer, Golcha has held several senior policing and administrative positions during his career. He served as DGP in Arunachal Pradesh between 2022 and 2023. After being transferred back to Delhi, he was appointed Special Commissioner of Police (Intelligence) and later DG, Prisons.
Before his Arunachal Pradesh stint, Golcha served as Special CP (Law and Order, Zone 2) and headed the Delhi Crime Branch. He has also headed several police ranges within Delhi.
Additionally, Golcha served as Director General of Tihar Prisons before becoming Delhi Police commissioner. He took charge as Delhi Police commissioner on August 22, 2025, succeeding Sanjay Arora, and was replaced by Anurag Kumar on July 17 this year.
Golcha belongs to the AGMUT cadre of the IPS, which stands for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram and Union Territories and includes the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi.
The latest order comes ahead of the superannuation of Virender Singh, who has been heading the Directorate of Home Guards.
The Home Guards organisation assists the civil administration and police in maintaining law and order, traffic management and during emergencies and disasters.

German semiconductor major Infineon Technologies AG is acquiring Peak XV Partners-backed C2i Semiconductors to strengthen its power management portfolio for AI data centres and expand its engineering capabilities in India. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction, which is expected to close in the third quarter of calendar year 2026. The acquisition marks a notable development for India’s nascent but rapidly growing semiconductor startup ecosystem, with a global chip major buying a two-year-old, Indian startup. It also highlights the growing strategic importance of India-based semiconductor engineering talent amid rising global demand for AI infrastructure. Founded in 2024 by Vikram Gakhar, Preetam Charan Anand Tadeparthy, and Ramprasad Ananthaswamy, Bengaluru-based C2i builds power management solutions for AI data centres and cloud infrastructure. The startup specialises in software-defined multiphase controllers and smart power stages, which regulate the power supplied to processors. Its software-defined power technology combines power semiconductors with digital controls and software algorithms to optimise power conversion, regulation, and system performance in real time. As increasingly powerful AI processors create rapidly changing power demands, such systems can respond to sudden fluctuations while reducing power losses and maintaining system stability. Infineon said the acquisition would add C2i’s expertise in intelligent digital power management, multiphase controllers, and system-level power architectures to its existing portfolio. It will also expand Infineon’s capabilities in vertical power delivery, including technologies such as Substrate Integrated Voltage Regulators. Vertical power delivery is an emerging architecture that supplies electricity to AI processors through the substrate beneath them, reducing the distance the power must travel and limiting energy losses. “This acquisition will further strengthen Infineon’s leadership in power solutions for AI data centers and create a new center of excellence for digital power technologies in India,” said Adam White, president of Infineon’s Power Systems division. The transaction will combine C2i’s digital power technology with Infineon’s semiconductor portfolio spanning silicon, silicon carbide, and gallium nitride technologies, along with the German company’s manufacturing capabilities and global customer base. Infineon, which develops power systems, automotive chips, microcontrollers, and IoT solutions, employs around 2,800 people in India. It said the acquisition would add specialised software-defined power management expertise to its global R&D network and strengthen its innovation capabilities in the country. Earlier this year, C2i closed its Series A round at $16.7 Mn (about ₹160.5 Cr) after raising additional capital from TDK Ventures. The round was led by Peak XV Partners and also saw participation from existing backer Yali Capital. The deal comes as the Indian government looks to deepen the country’s semiconductor capabilities. Last month, the Union Cabinet cleared the second phase of the Indian Semiconductor Mission, Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of ₹1.28 Lakh Cr to strengthen India’s chip design and manufacturing ecosystem. According to Inc42’s India’s Semiconductor Uprising Report 2026, the country's semiconductor market is expected to become a $155 Bn opportunity by 2031, up from $62 Bn in 2026, on the back of strong policy support and geopolitical shift.

In another time, the MacBook Neo could have caused a substantial realignment of the lowish-end laptop business. Sure, it has shortcomings compared to the MacBook Air, but it could have at least encouraged PC makers to start shipping consistently decent keyboards, screens, and build quality in the Neo’s $599 price window.
The PC makers did start responding, thanks in part to Intel’s actually new non-Ultra Core Series 3 processors (codenamed Wildcat Lake). Intel has resisted its usual compunction to serve the budget market with aging, re-labeled silicon and has created a lower-end, lower-performance processor with the same building blocks (and the same manufacturing processes) as this year’s high-end, high-performance models.
The likes of Dell, Acer, Asus, and Lenovo began hopping on the Wildcat Lake train fairly quickly, announcing would-be Neo competitors. But it felt like most of them were having trouble matching the Neo’s barebones specs, let alone undercutting them. Dell’s XPS 13 started at $599, but only for students. It would be $699 for everyone else. Acer’s Swift Air 14 was announced at $699, too. Sure, sometimes these offered features the Neo didn’t have. But the point of the Neo is that it eschews frills and frippery in favor of nailing the basics.
But even the MacBook Neo ended up being too good to be true. Apple raised its price by $100 three months after introducing it.
Yes, if you want a laptop that feels good, looks good, and performs well here in The Year Of The Unforgettable Memory Crisis, it’s hard to find a good deal, even if you’re willing to settle for a middle-shelf processor, the bare minimum amount of RAM that a modern operating system and browser will reasonably run on, and a meager 256GB or inexcessive 512GB storage drive.
There was one US-announced Wildcat Lake system that has managed to undercut the MacBook Air and the rest of the industry, though. Chinese PC company Chuwi has put together the Unibook, a Wildcat Lake computer with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage that it’s selling for an introductory price of $449 (its “normal” price is listed at $569, but it’s not clear whether or when the price might go back up.)
On paper, that looks pretty good. And in practice, the Unibook isn’t completely without its charms. But “you get what you pay for” applies here in multiple ways, and it’s difficult to imagine recommending this machine to anyone other than a computer geek looking for a weird project PC.
Look and feel

The Unibook looks unassuming at first glance, somewhere in the neighborhood of an Asus Zenbook. It feels like a cop-out to describe something as “nondescript,” but this is a pretty down-the-middle clamshell PC design.
To begin with the good, the Unibook far outstrips the port offerings of the MacBook Neo or the new XPS 13. It offers a pair of USB-C ports, a full-size HDMI port, two 5Gbps USB 3 ports, one USB 2.0 port, a micro-SD card slot, a headphone jack, and even an Ethernet port. I’ve never loved the little folding-out design for Ethernet ports that some laptops use to save a little space—if and when the little hinge breaks, it will start flopping around and looking bad—but so many laptops use thin-and-lightness as an excuse to ship a bare-minimum allotment of ports that it’s nice to see a budget-minded laptop ship with a ton of connectivity options.
The Unibook’s M.2 2280 drive is also pretty easy to replace. Remove the 11 Philips-head screws on the bottom of the laptop, and its bottom pries up with a bit of pressure. If you want a larger drive or just one from a better-known company, it’s easy to put one in (the built-in SSD is made by “HOGE,” a name that means about as much to most North Americans as “Chuwi”). The Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module is also easily accessible; the battery is, too, if you can manage to find a replacement somehow.
Also in the “good” column is the laptop’s perfectly not-bad keyboard. The keys aren’t as firm or satisfying as those on the keyboards in the MacBook lineup or in Framework’s Laptop 12 or Laptop 13, but the typing feel is decent, and the backlight is nice and even. The computer is missing a fingerprint reader (there’s also no face-scanning camera, which means the Unibook has no biometric login option at all), but this is a corner that the MacBook Neo’s base model also cuts.
Judged by the standards of the category, the Unibook’s screen isn’t awful. It’s a 13-inch IPS display panel with a decent 1920 x 1200 resolution and 16:10 aspect ratio, a step up from the 16:9 1080p displays you’ll still find in some ultra-budget systems. But it’s also not very nice by the MacBook Neo’s standards: only 300-ish nits of maximum brightness, pretty noticeable backlight bleeding around the edges (at least on our unit), and around 59 percent coverage of the sRGB color gamut, according to my colorimeter. At that level, colors appear visibly faded or washed-out to the naked eye; I find it particularly noticeable with shades of red and purple.

The mediocre screen was an unpleasant surprise given that this thing advertised 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage when it was announced and on its product page for many weeks (the Internet Archive captures it here). But since then, the company has said that only a higher-specced Unibook 315 actually has a screen with 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage, in addition to an extra P-core on the CPU, 12GB of RAM instead of 8GB, and a 512GB SSD. You still can’t buy this version of the Unibook, though Chuwi says it “may” be available this month and it “may” cost $599.
I run out of nice things to say about the Unibook after the screen. The webcam is usable, insofar as it functions, but the image quality is fuzzy, and it has trouble with white balance. The speakers produce sound under some circumstances (more on that later).
The trackpad is probably the worst of the Unibook’s core features. The actual finger tracking is OK, one gift of the precision trackpad era that endures despite the hardware’s shortcomings. Aside from that, it’s awful—it’s stiff. It’s hard to click. It’s so, so loud. It’s a trackpad that makes you glad for tap-to-click. It’s almost bad enough to ruin the laptop all by itself, though it does have some other help.
Weird software
When you buy a no-name PC, part of what you have to assume is that you are essentially out in the cold with respect to aftermarket software support. Maybe you’ll get some driver and/or BIOS updates directly from the manufacturer, and maybe you won’t! But you should assume that you won’t, and you should assume that whatever driver support page exists might be busted or deleted at pretty much any time. The driver page for the Unibook has not worked even once at any point during the weeks I’ve been using it.
Sadly, Chuwi’s support database was “Working Un-normal” for the entire time I was using the Unibook.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Sadly, Chuwi’s support database was “Working Un-normal” for the entire time I was using the Unibook.

Usually this means putting up with things that feel just a little off or downright weird, like a BIOS that seems to expose every possible setting whether it’s necessary or not, a shortcut to a Windows 7-era Control Panel applet sitting on the desktop by default for some reason, or the system’s pre-installed Microsoft Office 2024 suite.
If you think it’s odd that a $449 computer would come with Microsoft Office pre-installed or that it’s even more odd that Chuwi doesn’t advertise pre-installed Microsoft Office, you’re right. The copy installed on our review unit was definitely activated using a common activation script, something I verified by running the script and checking Office’s activation status.
Security-wise, the Windows install seems to check out, insofar as it meets Windows 11’s Security dashboard’s “enhanced security” baseline (at least, it did after a round of updates and a reboot). Chinese PC makers will occasionally ship a driver, inadvertently or otherwise, that comes with malware on board, so it’s something you need to watch for.
What the Unibook does ship with is all kinds of weird little Microsoft bits and bobs that don’t come with a clean-from-USB Windows 11 install, including a “mobile plans” app (the laptop has no modem, and the app opens to a blank window that does nothing), and the obscure “Microsoft PC Manager” app. The only page I can find for it on what is apparently Microsoft’s actual website is full of bizarre, possibly auto-translated sentence fragments like “Cleanup your system and free up spaces” and “Enhance the efficiency of computer use”). Some Chinese language packs are also preinstalled.
Windows re-installers beware
Normally, I’d treat this sort of PC the same as I’d treat most computers from most OEMs: Blow away the stock Windows installation and control my own destiny. Sure, a “clean” install of Windows 11 isn’t the cruft-removal magic wand that it used to be, but it’s still a good way to make sure you’re dealing mainly with Microsoft’s nonsense and not additional manufacturer-added nonsense on top of that.
For the Unibook, this wasn’t smooth sailing.
As you saw earlier in this review, Chuwi’s support site is currently suffering from an acute case of “Database Working Un-normal.” This made downloading drivers pretty difficult, partly because Wildcat Lake is new enough that Windows Update doesn’t seem to have drivers ready to go.
As a precaution, I replaced the Unibook’s drive with a spare 256GB SSD I had pulled from some other laptop at some point. When I ran into problems getting some of the hardware to work, I switched back to the old SSD and used Windows’ built-in DISM servicing tool to export every single third-party driver installed on the system.
If you need to reinstall drivers onto the Unibook without the benefit of a backup from the existing system, this patchwork also seemed to clear all the exclamation points from the Device Manager:
Generic GPU and NPU drivers from Intel (Wildcat Lake uses the same drivers as Meteor Lake and other Core Ultra/Arc models)
Various Intel chipset drivers (Management Engine, Software Integrated Package, etc.) from Dell’s support page for the XPS 13 DX13260, which is Dell’s similarly specced Wildcat Lake laptop.
A Realtek 8852BE Wi-Fi driver from Windows Update.
If you want a Bluetooth driver other than the generic built-in Windows one, I’ll offer my archived version that I extracted from the laptop—I couldn’t find a serviceable replacement.
But even with a nice, clean Device Manager, sound still wasn’t coming out of the Unibook’s speakers—it didn’t even see that an audio output was installed. By diving into the “System devices” section and selecting a generic audio controller driver, I was able to install an “Intel Smart Sound Technology Bus” device that finally seemed to make Windows recognize the remainder of the not-installed audio drivers, which got everything working again.
For your convenience, I am also including the pile of audio drivers I extracted from the Unibook’s default Windows install here.
The audio problem was also present in Linux, when I tried Kubuntu 26.04 LTS on the system. In addition, the laptop wouldn’t go to sleep when its lid was closed, which put a pretty good dent in the battery life. Some others have had some success getting this stuff working, but it wasn’t something I spent much time on for this review.
Good enough performance, outstanding battery life
Wildcat Lake is Intel’s first genuinely compelling low-end laptop processor in quite a while.
It used to be standard for lower-end laptop CPUs to be cut-down versions of high-end ones, based on the same architecture and manufacturing process. But as manufacturing improvements have gotten harder to do, Intel (and others) have turned to rebranded previous-generation chips to serve more budget-minded systems. Intel’s 12th- and 13th-generation Core processors weren’t especially impressive laptop chips in the first place (mediocre battery life; same GPU as 11th-generation), and getting warmed over and returned to market as the Core Series 1 and Core Series 2 families didn’t make them any better.
Wildcat Lake only has one or two P-cores (one for this version of the Unibook), four E-cores, and one or two GPU execution units. But they at least benefit from being built on the same architectures as the Panther Lake Core Ultra Series 3 processors, including the Intel 18A process for the main CPU die.
Objectively, performance is not impressive. But even a single P-core means a much faster and snappier-feeling computer than you’d get if you used one of Intel’s all-E-cores budget processors, and the Core 3 304 chip is perfectly serviceable for browsing, communicating, or streaming video. The comparison to Apple’s A18 Pro, the MacBook Neo’s chip, isn’t especially flattering for Intel—the Core 3 304 has one fewer P-core and higher power consumption, which means its performance-per-Watt for heavy tasks is pretty bad (it doesn’t use a ton of power, but it takes a very long time, so overall efficiency for these tasks isn’t great.) The Core 3 304’s single-core GPU also looks pretty bad next to the A18 Pro’s.
If you were hoping to play games or edit photos or video, the other blocker is the 8GB allotment of RAM, which was little enough that it kept benchmarks like Cinebench 2024, Cinebench 2026, or many GPU benchmarks from running entirely.
But its saving grace is its battery life—because it uses newer manufacturing tech, Wildcat Lake enables the Unibook’s 53 WHr battery to last for nearly 15 hours while running the PCMark Modern Office benchmark with the screen brightness set to 200 nits. That’s more than enough to make it through a full day away from an outlet.
I’m sorry, but no
The Core Series 3 chip is generally decent, but too many other things about the laptop don’t clear that bar.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The Core Series 3 chip is generally decent, but too many other things about the laptop don’t clear that bar.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
If a computer’s price in 2026 seems too good to be true, it probably is—Chuwi’s Unibook is interesting, but I’d hesitate to recommend it as a primary laptop to pretty much anybody. Some of that comes down to the hardware—mainly the awful trackpad, but also the worse-than-expected screen—and some of it is that you’ll be mostly on your own for hardware and software support after you buy it. A MacBook Neo or even the new Dell XPS might be more expensive, but at least you’ll have someone to call if something goes wrong.
And that’s before you get to the actual specs. The Unibook is a decent showcase for Intel’s Core Series 3 processors, which offer pretty stellar battery life, along with performance that’s more than good enough for basic computing. But 8GB of RAM will severely limit the kinds of apps that run well (or run at all) on a PC, and trying to play anything other than basic 2D games on a laptop like this won’t go well.
The good
Intel Core Series 3 chips (codenamed Wildcat Lake) offer good-enough performance and very good battery life.
Lots of ports.
Good screen size and resolution.
A decent keyboard with a nice backlight.
The bad
Screen is worse than originally promised, with way less than 100 percent sRGB color gamut coverage. 300 nits of peak brightness also isn’t great.
No fingerprint reader or other biometric authentication options.
Poor speakers and webcam quality.
8GB of RAM will slow the laptop down once you open too many apps or browser tabs, and some kinds of apps and games don’t want to run at all.
Broken driver support page (and weird audio setup) makes a clean Windows (or Linux) install more difficult than it should be.
The ugly
Awful, stiff, loud trackpad is a genuine displeasure to use.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

How to turn off Find My iPhone (and when you definitely should)
There are times when turning off Find My is necessary, but you should always have it on otherwise to keep your phone safe.
Apple's Find My service will help you locate your iPhone, iPad or other Apple device that has been lost, stolen or simply misplaced. It relies on Apple's Find My network, which is a crowdsourced system where other people's Apple devices use Bluetooth to detect the location of your item — in some cases, even when it's switched off. It then reports the approximate location of the device to you.
While the feature can be a life-saver, there are instances when you should switch it off. Primarily, Apple recommends disabling Find My before selling, giving away or trading in your device, as well as if you're sending it in for repair. This ensures technicians won't be hampered by security features and can properly run diagnostics to figure out what's wrong with your device. However, disabling Find My at other times will reduce your phone's security.
Disable Find My by resetting your device
If you're selling or giving away your device, the process to factory reset your iPhone (Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase all Content and Settings) is the easiest way to disable Find My. This will ask for your Apple Account password to make sure it's you wiping the device, and automatically disables Find My as part of the reset process.
Importantly, turning off Find My also disables Activation Lock, which links your Apple Account to the device. When Activation Lock is enabled, your device cannot be used without entering your Apple Account credentials, even if someone factory resets it. This means someone who steals your iPhone can't wipe it to resell it.
In case your phone was lost or stolen, erasing it remotely via Find My or iCloud on a computer will not switch off Find My and Activation Lock. Those features will continue protecting your device and letting you track it.
Manually disabling Find My
If you're not planning to factory reset your phone, such as when sending your device in for repairs, you'll have to disable Find My manually. Thankfully, this is easy: go to Settings > [Your Name] > Find My. Tap Find My iPhone and then toggle it off. This option will be grayed out if Stolen Device Protection is enabled, which is the default as of iOS 26.4.
Stolen Device Protection implements additional security measures when your iPhone is away from familiar locations, such as your home or workplace. It's designed to protect your data if someone steals your phone and knows your passcode. Your device will require Face ID or Touch ID to access sensitive info like stored passwords, and it adds a delay before changing crucial settings like your Apple Account password.
If you need to switch off Find My, you first have to disable Stolen Device Protection. You should ideally do this while at home to avoid the aforementioned security delays. To do so, go to Settings > Face ID & Passcode > Stolen Device Protection and toggle it off. To re-enable these features after your device is serviced, follow the same steps to toggle them back on.
Find My also lets you share your location with friends and family; if you disable it, this won't work anymore. If you're concerned about a particular friend having access to your location, removing their access is better than turning off the entire Find My suite. Open the Find My app, tap the People tab, choose the person, and hit Stop Sharing My Location. Unless they're on an "older operating system," they won't be notified that you stopped sharing with them (though they may notice when they don't see your name in the Find My app anymore). And others won't know when you check their location using the app.
What happens when you turn off Find My?
The most obvious answer is also the most important: once you disable Find My, you cannot locate your device through Apple's network anymore. If you lose your iPhone with Find My switched off, you won't be able to check its location through the Find My app on another of your Apple devices or the iCloud site in a browser.
Find My's suite of features also includes Lost Mode, which enables you to display a custom message with your number on the screen for anyone who finds it. This won't be available once the feature is disabled, and Activation Lock will no longer protect the phone either. Because of all this, you should only disable Find My when you're sending your phone to a trusted repair center, and re-enable the feature as soon as you get the phone back.
There's one major scenario in which you should never disable Find My: after you've lost your device, especially if you receive intimidating messages about doing so. There are hundreds of stories on Reddit about people who lost their phones and later received messages demanding they disable Find My. They'll threaten to publish the personal data on your phone, or make up sad stories about wanting to harm themselves because the phone they bought for their child isn't working.
If this happens to you, do not remove the device from your Apple Account. Because of Activation Lock, your lost phone is useless to someone who's stolen it and is trying to resell it — as long as you keep Find My enabled. You can erase the phone to know your data is safe, but don't give these crooks what they want.

Story so far: The Supreme Court on August 20, 2026, has ruled that the police cannot independently investigate offences relating to illegal prenatal sex determination under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994. The responsibility lies primarily with the Appropriate Authority, a specialised body constituted under the law. In a judgment authored by a Bench of Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh, it settles a long-standing disagreement among High Courts over whether the police could register FIRs and investigate such offences because they are classified as “cognisable” and “non-bailable”.
What was the case about?
The case arose from an allegation of illegal sex determination of a foetus at a hospital in Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh.
The District Magistrate, who was the Appropriate Authority under the Act, received information about the alleged practice. A Tehsildar was authorised to conduct a decoy operation. Following the operation, a raid was conducted at the hospital, and an FIR was registered against the doctor and others.
The FIR included offences under the Indian Penal Code as well as the sex-determination law. The accused approached the Allahabad High Court seeking to quash the chargesheet.
The High Court noticed that courts had taken different views on the role of the police in such cases and referred the issue to the Supreme Court.
There were essentially three questions before the Supreme Court: Can the police register an FIR for an offence under the Act? Can they investigate it? And can a Magistrate take cognisance of the offence on the basis of a police chargesheet?
Who is the Appropriate Authority?
The Appropriate Authority is the specialised authority created under the law to enforce the ban on sex selection and regulate the use of prenatal diagnostic techniques.
Section 17 of the Act specifically gives it the responsibility of investigating complaints of violations and taking action.
According to the section, when appointed for the whole of the State or the Union territory, it should consist of the following three members i) an officer of or above the rank of the Joint Director of Health and Family Welfare Chairperson; ii) an eminent woman representing women’s organisation; and iii) an officer of Law Department of the State or the Union territory concerned.
The functions of the appropriate authority includes to grant, suspend or cancel registration of a Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory or Genetic Clinic; to enforce standards prescribed for the Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory and Genetic Clinic; to investigate complaints of breach of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder and take immediate action and to seek and consider the advice of the Advisory Committee.
The Supreme Court therefore held that the law has deliberately placed the investigation of such offences with this specialised authority.
So, can the police register an FIR?
Not for the purpose of independently investigating a violation of the Act.
The complication came from Section 27 of the law, which says that every offence under it is “cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.” A cognisable offence ordinarily allows the police to investigate without first obtaining permission from a court.
But the Supreme Court said that Section 27 cannot be read on its own. It has to be read along with the provisions that specifically give the Appropriate Authority the power to investigate and Section 28, which lays down how a court can take up an offence under the Act.
The Court said, “The language of the statute, more particularly Sections 27 and 28 of the Act when read together, in light of the other provisions and the socially beneficial nature of the Act as also the requirement of sensitivity along with medical and technical know-how, indicates that the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act. This is further made clear by the fact that an FIR once registered cannot be taken to its logical conclusion as per the procedures of this Act. The restriction applies only to offences under this Act and does not restrict the police’s power to investigate or prosecute independent offences disclosed under substantive criminal law (IPC/BNS)”.
The Court held that allowing the police to independently investigate would undermine this specialised system.
It said, “the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act.”
The police can, however, assist the Appropriate Authority when their help is necessary. Rule 18A(3)(iv) says that police involvement should be avoided “as far as possible”. The Court held that this rule has statutory force.
The phrase does leave room for police assistance, but not for an independent police investigation. The Court said that, when involved, the police would have to act “strictly in a supplemental or aiding capacity.”
What happens if there is also another crime?
The Supreme Court has not said that the police have no role whenever a suspected sex-determination offence is involved. The police can investigate a separate offence under the IPC, BNS or another criminal law, even if it arises from the same incident.
For example, if the facts disclose both a violation of the sex-determination law and an independently constituted offence under general criminal law, the two investigations can proceed separately.
The Appropriate Authority would investigate the offence under the special law. The police would investigate the independent criminal offence.
But the police cannot use the existence of another offence as a way of taking over the sex-determination investigation. The Court’s concurring opinion makes the distinction clear: the police cannot use a general criminal offence “as a gateway to take over the PC & PNDT inquiry.”
Similarly, the special law cannot be used to prevent the police from investigating a genuinely separate criminal offence.
Can a Magistrate act on a police chargesheet?
No. This was the third question before the Supreme Court, and the Court’s answer was categorical.
Section 28 says that a court cannot take cognizance of an offence under the Act except through the complaint mechanism specified in the provision. A police chargesheet therefore cannot, by itself, give the Magistrate jurisdiction to take cognizance of a PC &PNDT offence.
The Appropriate Authority has to follow the procedure prescribed under the Act.
The Court concluded that there is a “complete statutory embargo” on taking cognizance except in the situations provided under Section 28.
What is the takeaway?
The immediate impact is on how a suspected illegal sex-determination case moves through the criminal justice system.
If information received by a police station discloses only a violation under the Act, the police should record the information and send it, along with the relevant material, to the Appropriate Authority. They should not independently investigate the offence.
If the information also reveals an independent cognizable offence under the IPC, BNS or another general criminal law, the police can investigate that offence while sending the sex-determination component to the Appropriate Authority.
The Supreme Court has also made clear that a police investigation cannot simply end with a chargesheet for the offence under the Act. Section 28 creates a separate route for bringing such a case before a court.
The ruling does not weaken the prohibition on prenatal sex determination. Instead, it clarifies who is responsible for enforcing it.

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

Gwalior car's kiss marks, tinted glass, loud silencers: Which violations can invite trouble for Delhi-NCR motorists
The Gwalior incident has highlighted motor vehicle laws, especially in the national capital, and the modifications that can land vehicle owners in trouble.
In a bizarre show of love, a woman spent hours leaving 3,400 lipstick marks on her partner’s car, leading him to pay a ₹5,500 fine and receive an order to remove the marks in Madhya Pradesh's Gwalior.
Car owner Aditya Sikarwar told local media that his girlfriend did it as a part of a “foreign trend” and social media stunt. However, none of them was aware that it was illegal.
Traffic police traced the vehicle after it had been on the road for two days and imposed a fine on its owner under the Motor Vehicles Act.
The incident has highlighted motor vehicle laws, especially in the national capital, and the modifications and practices that can land vehicle owners in trouble.
‘Owner cannot freely alter vehicle’
A senior Delhi Traffic Police officer said a vehicle owner cannot freely alter a vehicle after purchasing it from a manufacturer, news agency PTI reported.
"When someone buys a vehicle from a showroom, it complies with the prescribed traffic and motor vehicle guidelines. For any further changes, one has to take permission, which will be examined by the competent authority. Whether the permission should be granted or rejected is decided after verification and on the basis of the reason for which the owner wants to make the change," the officer said.
Under Section 52 of the Motor Vehicles Act, vehicle alterations are subject to regulations, particularly when they result in the vehicle differing from the specifications recorded in the registration certificate or those provided by the manufacturer. In cases where an alteration is permitted, prior approval from the registering authority may be required.
The officer added that owners could face action for modifications that significantly alter a vehicle’s appearance or deviate from its original specifications.
"Any modification that changes or hides the original identity or make of the vehicle, changes its entire colour without the required permission, or involves prohibited fittings such as tinted glass can land the owner in trouble under the Motor Vehicles Act. Depending on the nature of the violation, enforcement authorities can also take action against or impound the vehicle as permitted under law," he said.
Tinted glass prohibited
Among the most common violations of the Motor Vehicles Act is tinting of glasses. According to Delhi Traffic Police, black films or extra tinting are prohibited.
Provisions say that factory-fitted glass must allow at least 70 per cent visible light transmission through the windscreen and rear window and 50 per cent through side windows, according to news agency PTI.
‘Loud aftermarket silencers another concern’
The officer further flagged loud aftermarket silencers as a common violation, particularly among motorcycle owners.
Under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, vehicles must be equipped with silencers and adhere to prescribed noise limits. Owners cannot treat a modified exhaust as a permissible alteration simply because the motorcycle remains otherwise roadworthy.
‘Additional lights, improper use of high beams’
Similarly, vehicle owners can face enforcement action for installing excessively powerful headlights, unauthorised additional lights or using high beams improperly. In densely populated urban areas, high-beam lights can dazzle other road users and are therefore subject to traffic regulations.
The officer also pointed to pressure horns and multi-toned horns as prohibited modifications. Vehicle owners are not permitted to install horns that produce excessively loud, harsh, shrill or alarming sounds, according to PTI.
‘Use of Press’
The use of “Press” stickers or other official-looking markings on private vehicles can also invite scrutiny, particularly when they falsely imply an official status or breach prescribed vehicle-marking rules.
Similarly, owners cannot change the registered colour of a vehicle or carry out major structural alterations at will. Such changes may require approval from the relevant authorities and corresponding updates to the vehicle’s registration records.
The officer said motorists should not assume that a modification is legal simply because it does not interfere with the vehicle’s mechanical performance.
“Every vehicle owner must follow the prescribed traffic and motor vehicle rules. Before making any alteration, they should check whether permission is required rather than making the change first and approaching the authorities later,” he said, as per PTI.
‘Delhi Traffic Police enforcement drive’
Recently, the Delhi Traffic Police conducted a week-long citywide enforcement drive targeting violations that pose a serious threat to the safety of motorists, pedestrians and other road users.
During the drive, 7,675 challans were issued for wrong-side driving, while 22,992 motorists were fined for riding without helmets and 1,568 for triple riding.
The enforcement campaign also focused on e-rickshaws operating at congestion-prone locations. Traffic police issued 7,298 challans to e-rickshaw drivers for various violations and impounded 63 vehicles for offences warranting such action.
The traffic police said it would also launch a citywide operation to identify and take action against vehicles that fail to comply with prescribed norms.
