Huge tornado tears through villages in Southern France as over 300 homes damaged
Social media videos show the huge tornado above Verzeille
A huge tornado has swept through a region of France, causing chaos and destruction in its path.
The weather phenomenon struck Aude in southern France late on Monday, damaging more than 300 homes and injuring 41 people.
Shock social media footage showed the tornado swirling above the village of Verzeille late on Monday. Many of the homes caught up in its path had their windows smashed as a result of the high winds.
The local administration said gusts of up to 117 km/h were recorded, with the strongest winds hitting the commune of Pomas and its 1,000 residents.
The tornado struck just as part of the region was on orange alert. Local authorities said a total of 41 people were injured, 15 of whom were taken to hospital, and 300 homes were damaged.
The tornado formed at roughly 5.20pm on Monday afternoon.
Social media was awash with videos of the large tornado surrounded by dark stormy skies.
"More than 120 firefighters are on the scene" the prefecture of the Aude department said on Friday, adding that "work to make the buildings safe is under way". By 7.30pm on Monday, 2,800 households in the Aude area were still without electricity.
The tornado hit as this summer's intense heatwave gave way this week to thunderstorms in many areas of France.
The country was facing its driest year on record, with wildfire spreading across the country through the summer.
At their peak, fires in France and Spain alone drove some 330,000 people from homes and vacation sites, stretching firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous crises.
Europe is Earth’s fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus climate service. Rising temperatures and prolonged drought dry vegetation, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely.
A study, released by the World Weather Attribution group, found that human-caused warming made the hot, dry and windy conditions that fuelled the fires at least twice as likely in south-western France and at least 20 times as likely in central Spain. The scientists described both figures as conservative estimates.

Massachusetts woman suspected of killing cop husband found dead in apparent murder-suicide
Karen Solomon went missing after her husband, Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon, was found dead
A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Monday, six days after she disappeared from their Massachusetts home, authorities said.
Karen Solomon, who advocated for greater awareness and improved support for police mental health, went missing after her husband, Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon, was found dead at their home shortly before 5.30am on August 18. Authorities had named Karen Solomon as a suspect and said they believed she was armed.
“We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred,” Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said at a news conference on Monday.
Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman’s corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon.
A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it.
On Aug. 19, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple’s home and found her husband’s body.
Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said.
Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband's death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.
Police handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple's Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6 kilometers) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs.
Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First H.E.L.P., which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books, Hearts Beneath the Badge and The Price They Pay, about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders.
In a 2020 interview on the Dr. Phil show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives.
In a statement read by Saucier during Monday's news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers.
“The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless," the family said. “The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”
A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as “a tremendous human being” who was like family.

Prince Harry to leave board of African Parks conservation nonprofit
Prince Harry is stepping down as a trustee of African Parks, a nonprofit managing protected areas in 13 countries
LONDON -- Prince Harry is stepping down as a trustee of African Parks, a nonprofit organization that manages protected areas in partnership with authorities in 13 countries from Chad to Zimbabwe.
Harry, who last week announced he and his family were returning to live in the U.K., left the board of trustees after 10 years of service to the organization, a spokesperson for prince confirmed on Monday.
African Parks said in a statement dated Aug. 19 that the prince’s departure was part of a “governance refresh” in which a Kenyan Supreme Court justice and the president of AGRA, which helps small farmers in Africa, will join the board. The changes take effect Sept. 30.
Harry's departure comes four months after the Indigenous rights group Survival International called on him to resign after it alleged human rights abuses by rangers employed by African Parks. Previously, the prince left Sentebale, the charity he co-founded to fight poverty and AIDS in southern Africa, in March 2025 after relations with the organization's chair broke down.
“We extend our thanks to all the members of the Board who generously volunteer their time in support of our conservation mission — and particularly to The Duke of Sussex, for a decade of committed service to African Parks,” Vas Narasimhan, chair of the African Parks board, said in a statement.
Harry and his wife, Meghan, stepped aside from royal duties when they moved to the U.S. They will not return to royal duties and are expected to live in a non-royal residence outside London.

England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

For Luis DeSantiago, a substitute teacher in Los Banos, California, it started with a few text messages. On March 12, as he was working his other part-time job at a coffee shop, his phone lit up. A fellow barista said there was an AI photo circulating on social media. Her cousin wanted to know if it was DeSantiago.
At first, DeSantiago wasn’t worried—he figured that inappropriate photos violated TikTok’s community guidelines and were usually quickly removed.
“When I finally saw the image, that’s when it felt like a punch to the gut,” DeSantiago tells WIRED. Parts of it resembled a mirror selfie that he remembered taking at a job in college. But instead of his work uniform, he was wearing lingerie. And instead of standing normally, as he had been in the original photo, he was posing suggestively.
The texts kicked off a monthslong saga that crossed two schools and involved students and administrators. And DeSantiago is far from the only educator who’s been victimized this way.
WIRED spoke with three other teachers who allege that their students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI. They say the incidents have been profoundly distressing and disappointing—and in some cases, it’s led them to reassess how they view their work and their relationships with their students.
“This Could Include Other Students”
After he received the texts, DeSantiago began to piece together who might have been behind the image. One account that shared it used their real name in their TikTok profile—it was a student DeSantiago knew from the local middle school, where he regularly filled in. DeSantiago suspected the involvement of two other students based on people who followed and interacted with that account, and his knowledge of student friend groups. He was scheduled to work at that very middle school the next day.
DeSantiago reported the incident to the assistant principal, who assured him that the school would "take care of it.” Later that evening, he decided to look for the image by searching his name on TikTok. He discovered that a different student had created an account impersonating him—it used his name, slightly mispelled, and had the same photo as their profile picture.
Over the next few weeks, DeSantiago says, he went back and forth with school administrators, the parents of the students, and even the police.
“If these students aren't afraid of generating and posting these images of me, I am concerned of what they may be circulating privately through text messages and group chats,” DeSantiago wrote to the principal. “Keep in mind this could include other students as well.”
One student, who admitted to creating the image, was disciplined with in-school suspension. DeSantiago was later told that the image was also shared on Snapchat. But DeSantiago says the image continued to proliferate, and other students began posting it. He says he also received several crude, sexual comments on his TikTok account.
DeSantiago told administrators he didn’t want to take assignments at the middle school “until this matter is fully addressed.” The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
He took a substitute assignment at the local high school, but the problems followed him. During one class, he received an AirDropped photo of the same AI-generated image before it was quickly revoked. He could tell it was circulating among the class.
The principal told him the school was launching an “immediate investigation” and offered to meet with DeSantiago or make the school counselor available, but DeSantiago says he probably won’t return to the district this year.
He tells WIRED that, at least right now, he doesn’t feel safe doing so.
“It Makes You Question Everything”
When fake nude images of nonconsenting adults are disseminated, it could constitute cyberstalking and violate the federal Take It Down Act, which makes it a crime to publish nonconsensual “intimate visual depictions of individuals, both authentic and computer-generated,” on the internet.
In most of the accounts shared with WIRED, the teachers didn't directly report the content to the platforms on which it appeared. Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy shared the company's policies on harassment and sexual content, which prohibit sharing AI-generated or manipulated content to humiliate or sexually harass others. She told WIRED that the company has "established processes" for reporting such content, and that it continues to "develop features and tools designed to support the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." TikTok did not provide comment before publication.
Donna Ballman, a retired employment advocacy lawyer, tells WIRED that if a student creates and shares sexual images of a teacher, it constitutes a “clear case” of sexual harassment in the workplace.
Ballman says that under federal antidiscrimination laws, employers have an obligation to create a workplace free of sexual harassment. In a school, this could mean disciplining the student or moving them to a different classroom. She adds, however, that there's “no blueprint” for how schools need to respond to these incidents. Administrators don’t even have to tell a victimized teacher how a student may have been disciplined.
“They just have to make [and] create a safe environment for the victim,” Ballman says.
One middle school teacher in her mid-twenties tells WIRED that she’s seen so much AI-generated content used to harass teachers that she’s bracing for the next wave. (She requested anonymity because she did not have permission from her school district to speak about her experience.)
Last year, she says, students found public photos of a teacher in her sixties, manipulated them to make it appear that she was committing sex acts, and shared them with each other in a Snapchat group chat.
A few months ago, the teacher says, she learned from a student about a TikTok account impersonating her. It looked AI-generated—her face had the characteristic smoothness of AI-generated content, her mouth was moving unnaturally while speaking, and the sound of her voice didn’t match her own. Some of the videos showed her doing things like skydiving or backflips. But others depicted her talking about sexual acts she performed and enjoyed.
She says she told her principal about the account and that they assured her that they would “see what we can do.” Throughout the day, students continued to warn her about the account. She says that some told her that they knew who made the account—one of their classmates. She says the student was known to have behavioral problems.
“I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me genuinely believed that was my account, and that I was saying those things,” she tells WIRED. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, you guys—that is not me.’” She asked them to report it to TikTok, and she says the account was quickly taken down.
Still unnerved by the incident, she mentioned the TikTok account during the next monthly teacher meeting. A colleague said he had seen a seemingly AI-generated fake video of himself getting arrested, which he believed was generated by the same student.
As days and weeks passed, she says, she became the target of escalating, in-person harassment from this same student, who began “cursing me out, calling me names, telling me to fuck off, calling me a bitch.” She raised it at the next faculty meeting, and the assistant principal said that the same student was calling and texting them in the middle of the night and posting apparent AI-generated photos of them to TikTok.
She says the principal removed the student from her class and tried to limit his access to her. But she says that the harassment continued until the student ultimately left the district, and TikTok removed the account.
She says that these behavioral issues aren’t exclusive to this particular student. “It's kind of unsurprising that we are dealing with that, because these kids just have a hard time,” she says. "I'm just worried about this happening again.”
Other teachers say their experiences have fundamentally changed the way they relate to students.
Alice, who asked to be identified by her first name, works for a UK college that trains students aged 16 to 19 in trades like construction. Her job combines administrative responsibilities, like taking attendance, with the role of a college counselor. She says she individually meets with about 150 students throughout the year and takes pride in being able to be a sounding board, give them advice, and serve as a mentor.
This winter, she says, school administrators told her that a student filed a report claiming two videos were circulating among his classmates. One appeared to be real, and it showed her having a conversation with a student. The other one, they said, appeared to be a manipulated version of the first. But instead of talking to the student, it showed her taking her clothes off and dancing around in what was either underwear or a bikini.
Alice tells WIRED that as a qualified youth worker, part of her job often involves talking about things that students may feel “too embarrassed to tell their parents about,” like drugs, parties, or having safe sex. She says she had several of those conversations with the student she suspected had created the video. The student denied it when questioned by administrators and soon dropped out of the school. (The college did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
“It makes me reflect as well on those conversations, thinking, did he think that he could overstep a line because we were having these discussions?” she says. “It makes you question everything,” she says.
Afterward, the college gave her permission to step away from the class for a few weeks and took steps to educate students about the danger of creating or distributing deepfakes. But when she returned, she says, the atmosphere had chilled.
“I did have a really good rapport with my students—I do have a good rapport with my students,” she says. And she still loves her work. “But it's definitely made me a bit more cautious, a bit more vigilant when it comes to folks.”
“It Crosses the Line”
Like DeSantiago, Arizona-based sixth-grade teacher Luke Red says his students circulated an AI-generated photo of him in the comments of his public TikTok account. The image depicted him and another male teacher kissing each other.
Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok—not for content violations but for being under the minimum age of 13—but says TikTok didn’t remove the accounts. He says that the school immediately launched an investigation and quickly identified the student, who admitted to creating and sharing the image. The student received a three-day suspension—the most severe punishment kids their age can receive for a first-time sexual harassment offense, according to the school district handbook. The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Red tells WIRED that reflecting on the experience “has kind of sent me into a spiral.” His concerns, he says, are not necessarily about what happened to him. They’re more focused on the enthusiastic, permissive culture surrounding AI use among his students.
“It just got to the point where students felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images,” Red says. “Obviously when you're making your teachers do sexual things with these images, that's where it crosses the line.”
Ultimately, he feels more sorry for the students than for himself.
“It's just clear [that] so many kids nowadays just don't understand not only how what they're doing can affect others, but just what happens on the internet and how dangerous it can be,” Red says.

Sudanese medical group accuses rebel group of killing 27 people
Ethnic clashes in southern Sudan have killed 27 people, including four children, a local medical group said
CAIRO -- Four children were among at least 27 people killed in the latest ethnic clashes in southern Sudan, a local medical group said on Tuesday.
The killings were carried out by the rebel Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM-N) in Qardud and Abu Hamama, areas inhabited by the Otoro tribe in South Kordofan, according to the Sudan Doctors Network, which monitors casualty numbers in the war-torn East African country.
Earlier this year, intense fighting erupted between forces linked to SPLM-N and the Otoro tribe, which is a minority group in the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan.
The ethnic standoff, first instigated by land disputes, adds another layer to the country’s ongoing civil war which broke out in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The attacks have forced many people to flee toward Abu Hitan, a nearby village and Kadugli, the largest town in South Kordofan, said the doctors.
The Sudan Doctors Network said in a statement on Facebook that it stressed "that targeting unarmed civilians, including women and children, on ethnic grounds constitutes an explicit violation of international humanitarian law.”
The humanitarian group urged the international community to exert pressure on the SPLM-N leadership to halt attacks on civilians, noting that women were also among those wounded in the latest attacks.
The SPLM-N is a breakaway faction of the SPLM, the ruling party of neighboring South Sudan. Its leader Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, has aligned his fighters with the RSF and joined ranks with the RSF-led parallel government.

It means that, along with England's Kobbie Mainoo, United now have a spread of different attributes across their four-man midfield, three of whom are 22 or younger.

"Come on, that's ridiculous," replied Carrick. "You played football. You understand. That's a ridiculous thing to say."
So, now the midfield is sorted, it is natural for fans to look at the other areas of Carrick's squad that could do with reinforcements; namely left-back.

How many games can Shaw play?
Signing an additional left-back has looked an obvious thing for Manchester United to do.
Luke Shaw started all 38 Premier League games last season. He started at Hull. Of United's past 44 league games, the 31-year-old England international has failed to start just one, the final game of the 2024-25 campaign, four days after the Europa League final defeat by Tottenham – and he went on the post-season tour of Asia immediately afterwards.
But, before that, Shaw's injury record had not been great.
Between February 2024 and April 2025, he played as many games for England (three) as he did for his club. He missed three months at the start of the 2023-24 campaign.
There were calf and hamstring issues but also a feeling Erik ten Hag rushed him back too quickly.
More than anyone, Shaw benefited from a 40-game season, allowing him to prepare properly, largely for one game a week, sometimes not even that.
That preparation time will not be repeated.
Although there are blank midweeks between Manchester United's first three games, if they get through two EFL Cup rounds, they will not have a full midweek without a game, other than during international breaks, until the one that includes Christmas Day.
It is the combination of Shaw's injury record and the crush of games that has led to the feeling another left-back will arrive.
There is no doubt the club like Newcastle's Lewis Hall. At 21, he is the right age profile and ideally suited to challenging Shaw for his place, with the safety net of there being enough games to keep both men happy.
However, Newcastle don't want to sell. It would take a huge offer to persuade them otherwise and Manchester United's powerbrokers have proved on numerous occasions this summer they will not be held to ransom, or overpay, for players.
In addition, how much money do they have to spend?
In published third-quarter financial accounts to 31 March, United confirmed they owed £405.75m in outstanding transfer fees, £171.14m of which was due after more than one year. The club are still to outline what the additional $125m (£91.64m) they borrowed in a wider refinancing announced in June will be used for.
The assumption is £70m for Baleba, equal the sum United paid for Casemiro in 2022 and a figure only exceeded in their history in terms of midfielders by the club record £89m spent on Paul Pogba, is at the top end of what they wanted to pay.
Plenty of alternative left-backs to Hall have been mentioned.
Racing Santander's 19-year-old Jorge Salinas has a €16m (£13.7m) release clause, but is also coveted by Atletico Madrid.
Barcelona's Alejandro Balde was left out of the 5-0 La Liga victory over Elche by coach Hansi Flick, to allow him to "clear his mind" amid intense transfer speculation, with United among those to be linked with the 22-year-old Spain international. Barcelona are said to value him between €30m (£25.66m) and €40m (£34.22m).
With a week to go before the transfer window closes, the situation is thought to be fluid, but caution in United circles around the expectations of a new left-back being signed is being stressed.
A significant sale could change the dynamic.
However, the idea of Marcus Rashford leaving has virtually been ruled out with confirmation he will wear the coveted number nine shirt this season, while the anticipated exit of Manuel Ugarte had to be scrapped when he was injured at the World Cup.
Of Carrick's senior squad, forward Joshua Zirkzee appears surplus to requirements, yet with fitness doubts over Amad Diallo – the club are choosing to offer no clarification on the extent of his injury amid a report he could be out for up to six weeks – it is uncertain whether interest from Serie A will lead to a sale.
Carrick does have options at left-back without bringing anyone else in. Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have both switched flanks in the past, while Baleba, a left-footed player, has played at full-back for Brighton previously.
In addition, Harry Amass was Shaw's back-up during pre-season and the 19-year-old remains at United. But he was not included in Carrick's squad for the Hull trip and the expectation has been he will leave, either permanently or on loan.
Most still think there will be another left-back in Carrick's squad when the transfer window closes on 1 September – but it is by no means certain.

- The claim that the Trump administration uses a legal loophole to sell protected wild horses to slaughterhouses is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from reporting by The New York Times in August 2026 and was backed by research by animal rights groups that suggested buyers of wild horses sold through the Bureau of Land Management's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter.
- According to its website, it is BLM policy "not to sell or send any wild horses or burros to slaughter," and buyers from the sale program sign a bill of sale saying they will not slaughter or sell for slaughter the animals they buy.
- The Times' reporting brought to light a long-standing issue within the BLM about what to do with excess wild horses and burros. The bureau is bound by law to regulate populations but has historically avoided euthanizing healthy animals due to concerns about public perception.
- Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses.
- Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers did purchase horses from the BLM and sell them for slaughter, the article did not include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- We contacted the Times journalist who wrote the article and an animal rights group that provided research to ask for additional evidence and await replies to our queries.
For example, one Instagram user wrote:
America's wild horses are supposed to be protected—not sold into a system that is funneling them to slaughter. Records show the Trump Administration's Bureau of Land Management's wild horse sales more than doubled in 2025, with some horses sold for as little as $25. A New York Times investigation shows that some buyers are taking advantage of a legal loophole, using middlemen to unconscionably sell these beautiful sentient beings to slaughter.
Similarly worded posts circulated on X (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim and searched our site for more information. One popular search term was, "Is Trump killing horses?"
The story originated from reporting in the New York Times about the Bureau of Land Management's sale of wild horses, titled "Under Trump, Protected Wild Horses Are Going to Slaughter."
The Times article reported how the U.S. government, faced with the ballooning costs of taking care of more than 50,000 wild horses it has rounded up to control herd sizes, sold thousands every year to buyers who purchased the animals for as little as $25 to sell at auction to other buyers that shipped them to slaughterhouses. This was allowed to happen, the Times reported, because selling a wild horse removes its statutory protection from "capture, branding, harassment, or death."
Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers of wild horses sold through the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter, the article didn't include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers.
Snopes contacted Skydog Ranch and Sanctuary, an animal rescue organization that said it tracked animals from BLM ownership to auctions attended by slaughterhouse buyers to ask for additional evidence of the process the Times article described. We also contacted Dave Phillips, who wrote the Times article, to ask what primary evidence he used for his reporting. We await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A BLM spokesperson said in an emailed statement on Aug. 24, 2026:
The Bureau of Land Management does not sell or send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and allegations that individuals are violating federal law or the terms governing the sale of these animals are taken seriously.
Times tracked horses sold to Ohio buyer to slaughter auctions
The Times article suggested the BLM had found a way to offload its large off-range holding population of wild horses and burros that was effectively sending the animals to slaughter without incriminating the bureau.
The Wild Horse and Burro Program allows the BLM to sell animals that are more than 10 years old or that it has unsuccessfully listed for adoption at least three times. However, the Times reported, "Livestock inspection records show mustangs sold by the government soon ended up on trucks bound for slaughter plants in Canada."
The article focused on one reported buyer from Ohio, who the Times said had bought 500 horses from the BLM in a matter of years. Some of those horses, the article said, later showed up for sale at "an auction in Tennessee frequented by slaughter buyers."
The article also alleged that a week after the Ohio buyer received a shipment of 97 formerly wild mares, an Ohio exporter of animals for slaughter shipped two trucks of horses across the Canadian border. The Times said that, according to one image its reporter had viewed, at least one of those horses had a BLM freeze mark.
The Ohio buyer reportedly spoke to the Times reporter for two hours but "refused to say specifically what had happened to the horses he purchased from the government, other than to insist that none had gone to slaughter." He declined having worked with the Ohio exporter that shipped the two trucks across the Canadian border. The exporter would not comment to the Times on whether he had purchased horses from the buyer.
Without primary evidence — meaning sales documents tracking individual animals from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the auction in Tennessee or from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the Ohio exporter to a slaughterhouse — it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify the claims in the Times article.
Holding costs tie up BLM program budget
The Times article highlighted an issue that the BLM has grappled with for years: how to legally, effectively and tastefully control wild horse populations. According to the bureau's data, wild horse and burro populations exceed the BLM's Appropriate Management Level, meaning the number of animals that can thrive in balance with other public land resources and uses, in nearly all the states where the bureau tracks populations.
The BLM is required by The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 — the same act that protects wild horses and burros from "capture, branding, harassment, or death" — to uphold the AML for the populations it tracks (Sec. 1333b1). Under the Act, the BLM is allowed to euthanize excess animals "in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible" (Sec. 1333b2C). However, a 2008 report by the Government Accountability Office on the BLM's management of "unadoptable" horses found that the bureau hesitated to do this because it was thought to be "unacceptable to the public" (Page 56).
The BLM estimates that wild horse and burro populations, if left unregulated, would double every four years. Therefore, the bureau rounds up and removes thousands of animals from the wild to control populations. Those animals end up in the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program's off-range corrals and pastures. By May 2026, the program reported that it held 58,025 formerly wild horses and burros and that its total capacity for off-range holding was 78,751 animals. According to the program's figures it spent $101 million — 66% of its budget — on off-range holding costs in fiscal year 2024.
A long-standing problem
According to the 2008 GAO report, the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program faced the same challenges then that the Times article highlighted 18 years later. The report said the cost of caring for off-range animals was already overwhelming the program in 2008, and that the program had "limited" options for "dealing with" animals it could not adopt out because it feared the public would not support humanely euthanizing healthy animals (Page 9).
The program had reportedly sold animals since 2005, though at that point also faced issues with animals ending up at slaughterhouses after the sale (Page 43). As a result, the bureau implemented a mandatory "statement of intent" at purchase, which required the buyer to say that they did not intend to sell the animals they bought for slaughter. BLM bills of sale for wild horses and burros still included such a clause in 2026.
The effectiveness of the clause was unclear because the BLM also said on its website about its sales program that it did not track animals after it sold them. The 2008 report noted that the introduction of a "statement of intent" was part of the reason the BLM sold fewer horses than before.
The existence of the "statement of intent" did not deter one buyer, who admitted in a 2015 investigation carried out by the Office of the Inspector General that "most of" the 1,700 wild horses he bought through the BLM between 2008 and 2012 had gone to slaughter.
The GAO and OIG reports suggest that the issue of wild horses and burros ending up at slaughterhouses after BLM sales is documented and predates the Trump administration.
Aside from adoption, sale or euthanasia, the BLM has been pursuing fertility treatment as a way to control populations since 1992 (Page 69). However, the BLM itself and peer-reviewed research have found it comes with its own challenges around finding and accessing animals and keeping up with treatment. According to the BLM, it delivered 921 fertility treatments to wild horses and burros in fiscal year 2025. That same year, it removed 7,853 horses and burros from the wild.
The Times report said that although government experts did recommend wider use of fertility treatment to control populations the recommendation was hard for the BLM to act on because its funds were largely tied up in the removal, holding and care of excess animals.
In sum, while it was not possible to verify the exact elements of the Times' reporting, the article brought to light a complicated issue for the BLM that predated both Trump administrations but nonetheless had lethal consequences for the horses and burros the U.S. government is bound to protect.

Leeds and Rangers co-owner Jed York has been jailed in Ohio after being arrested for soliciting prostitution.
The 46-year-old, who is also the owner of the San Francisco 49ers, was convicted of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools after pleading no contest to two charges.
In the Ohio legal system, a no contest plea means a defendant accepts a conviction without formally admitting guilt.
York was sentenced to one day in jail on each offence, to be served concurrently, and was given credit for time already served.
York was fined $150 for disorderly conduct and $1,000 for possessing criminal tools.
Court records show the case was brought by East Palestine Police Department and filed at Columbiana County Municipal Court on Monday.
York pleaded no contest to both charges at an arraignment hearing and was found guilty.
Court records also show an expungement request was filed and denied on the same day. This is a request to have records destroyed or sealed so they are not accessible to the public.
According to reports in the US media, other court documents say York responded to an advertisement on a prostitution website placed by undercover officers from a Human Trafficking Task Force in Ohio.
These documents say he arranged to have sexual activity with a woman in exchange for $140 (£103).
In a plea deal, the original charge was reduced to disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools - thought to refer to the phone used to reply to the advert.
Takeover by US consortium
The 49ers were part of the US consortium who took control of Rangers last year but York is not involved in the day-to-day running of the club.
Rangers and Leeds have both said they will not be commenting.
The 49ers said: "As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time."
York became a co-owner of Rangers through 49ers Enterprises, the investment arm linked to the NFL's San Francisco 49ers, where he serves as chief executive and principal owner.
In May 2025, a consortium led by US businessman Andrew Cavenagh and 49ers Enterprises completed a takeover of Rangers after acquiring a controlling 51% stake in the Scottish Premiership club.

Mumbai: The annual Maha Pookalam, the traditional floral carpet created at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) during Onam, will not be held this year after the Railways denied permission citing security concerns.

The event, organised by the All Mumbai Malayalee Association (AMMA) since 2015, had become a prominent feature of Mumbai’s Onam celebrations, adding festivity to one of the city’s busiest railway stations. The organisers said they had approached Railway authorities seeking permission but were informed that the event could not be permitted this year in view of the prevailing security situation.
Dr Swapnil Nila, Chief Public Relations Officer, Central Railway, said the denial was linked to the imposition of Section 144 of the CrPC in the area following a Central Railway Mazdoor Sangh protest held a few months ago in front of the motormen’s lobby at the station.

According to the organisers, the installation has drawn up to 2.6 million visitors over the years, including people from across India and abroad. The event also featured prominently in the media and on social media platforms.

The Nokia 300 Charge doubles as a 10W powerbank

Man Utd close on deal for Brighton's Baleba
- Published
Manchester United are closing in on a deal to sign Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba.
United attempted to sign the Cameroon international near deadline day last summer but were put off by Brighton's valuation, which was in excess of £100m.
However, the price has reduced significantly and after failing in their pursuit of Matheus Fernandes earlier this summer, United have decided to revisit Baleba.
Their initial £60m offer is below Brighton's valuation, but talks are continuing.
The Red Devils have already signed midfielders Andrey Santos from Chelsea for £48m and Youri Tielemans, who joined from Aston Villa in July for £35m.
Mason Mount did excel alongside Santos in the first three games of pre-season, but he has been struggling to overcome a foot problem he suffered against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg on 8 August.
Baleba is expected to be out for another two to three weeks after suffering an ankle injury during a pre-season training camp in Austria.
Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton squad fly to Norway on Wednesday for Thursday's Uefa Conference League play-off first-leg match with Tromso.
Baleba made 35 appearances for Brighton last season, picking up seven yellow cards as a defensive midfielder.
Analysis: Man Utd need the 24-25 version of Baleba
This is an interesting move by United.
On one side, it makes perfect sense. They tried to sign Baleba 12 months ago, so are fully aware of his abilities.
He is the kind of box-to-box player United do not have in their midfield despite the arrivals of Santos and Tielemans.
Baleba wants to make the move and the fee, whatever it ends up as, will be much less than the £100m they were quoted previously.
However, the reason the fee has gone down is the underwhelming form he showed for Brighton last season.
Thirty-one starts and three substitute appearances in the Premier League in 2024-25 became 23 starts and eight substitute appearances in 2025-26, highlighting a dip in form and value to Fabian Hurzeler in a campaign when Brighton secured European football for only the second time in their history.
There was a belief Baleba's head had been turned by United's interest, but Brighton sources last season said they didn't think that was right.
With the transfer deadline approaching, Old Trafford chiefs have made their move.
Carrick must hope he gets the 2024-25 version.
Tactical analysis: how Baleba's versatility and physicality improves United
United have prioritised players of a certain ilk to begin the window. Both Andres Santos and Youri Tielemans resemble Kobbie Mainoo in being technical midfielders that thrive in small spaces, able to rotate and connect well under pressure. This is a deliberate choice with Michael Carrick perhaps taking inspiration from PSG's midfield trio who he has referred to as playing "exactly the kind of football I enjoy".
The introduction of Baleba takes a different approach in looking to address traits the United squad lacks.
With the aforementioned players good on the ball under pressure, they are able to draw opponents onto them before finding teammates higher up the pitch in space. Baleba's ability to carry the ball over large distances makes him a good player to take advantage of these situations.
Defensively, his athleticism allows him to cover for the relative lack of physicality in his potential midfield partners at United who suit playing in small spaces. By tracking back with speed, he provides protection against counter-attacks.
More importantly, his ability to read and jump up to press opponents high has often helped his sides win the ball back close to the opposition's box – resulting in goals. This suits the high-press Carrick has used in pre-season.
If United are pushed deep whilst defending, his defensive intensity, in the form of tackling and closing down, would also help United replace the qualities lost following Casemiro's departure.

It may finally be safe to eat lettuce again after June’s horrifying—and bagged-salad-trust-destroying—cyclospora outbreak. But the summer of ’26’s foodborne illness train rolls on with a new rash of recalls: for salmonella.
The FDA has reported multi-state salmonella bacteria outbreaks tied to jalapeños, granola, dog food, alfalfa sprouts (also featuring E. coli), and something most people probably have in their refrigerator at this very minute: eggs.
Though the eggs being recalled are only from one supplier, Midwest Poultry Services, they were sold under five brand names, including two distributed by one of the country’s largest grocery chains: Kroger and Simple Truth. While this July recall only concerned Kroger stores in Texas, why wait for the next one?
With the advice of two infectious disease experts, I tested what may be the easiest, most universally applicable way to ensure the eggs in your refrigerator are salmonella-free and safe to use—even in raw or near-raw preparations like Hollandaise and pasta carbonara. All it requires is an immersion circulator, a pot of water, and about an hour and a half of your day.
Are All Eggs at Risk?
Salmonella, which can cause fever and severe diarrhea, is not a new problem for eggs.
In fact, “eggs remain the single food commodity most associated with outbreak illnesses,” says Alan Bulbin, director of infectious disease at Catholic Health’s St. Francis Hospital and Heart Center in Roslyn, New York.
Chickens and other poultry commonly carry Salmonella enteritidis, the bacterium most commonly responsible for salmonellosis in people, which can be transferred to the shell from contact with droppings or even deposited inside the egg itself from an infected chicken's ovaries.
It's difficult to tell just by looking if a chicken has salmonella, which is easily transmitted by rodents or wild birds. In fact, at one point, the USDA estimated that 1 out of every 20,000 eggs was thought to be contaminated with salmonella. That means out of the 67 billion eggs produced in the US each year, 3 million eggs could conceivably have dangerous bacteria in or on them. The USDA enacted a 72-page egg safety requirement in 2009 in hopes of eradicating contamination, but clearly, it hasn't happened.
It's good practice to always keep your eggs refrigerated at 42 degrees Fahrenheit or less and wash your hands before and after handling. It's also worth noting that cooking eggs kills salmonella bacteria. As long as your eggs are “cooked thoroughly, with a firm yolk and white,” according to Bulbin, salmonella shouldn't be a concern.
The Raw Truth
But what if you (like me) have kids who cook for themselves, who you know for a fact will never wash their hands after handling eggs? And more commonly, what if you're not fully cooking the eggs? Many recipes, from mayonnaise and aiolis to eggnog and royal icing for cookies, call for eggs that will be consumed uncooked. How can you make sure they're safe to use?
While in-shell eggs aren't pasteurized, all liquid eggs are—the kind in the carton. However, these are just egg whites, not yolks, which means they won't work for many of the above recipes.
If you want to be certain a whole, raw shell egg is free of bacteria, the only way to ensure this is to pasteurize it, which means heating the egg for a long period of time at 130 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, but not cooking it. Because this is tricky, the vast majority of eggs sold in the US are not pasteurized—if they are, you'll know it, as they're more expensive and the carton will indicate as much.
However, there is a way you can pasteurize your own eggs at home—any store-bought eggs, or ones from your backyard flock—with a simple kitchen tool that happens to also make a mean steak or vegetable side dish.
Sous vide immersion circulators actually originated in laboratory settings as a way to incubate cultures and sterilize testing equipment, but chefs discovered them in the 1970s and ’80s as a solution to easily overcooked foods like vegetables and chicken. Vacuum-sealing a chicken breast and letting it cook gently in a water bath results in meat that stays juicy and tender instead of stringy or rubbery.
Part of the challenge with pasteurization is maintaining a precise and consistent temperature without producing a hard- or soft-boiled egg, since eggs cook quickly. (It's also worth noting that pasteurizing eggs denatures the proteins, and so will affect egg whites’ performance—don't expect to be making any pasteurized-egg soufflés or pavlovas.)
I attempted to pasteurize some eggs I bought at Costco using the 3.0 immersion circulator model from Anova, a company that WIRED reviewer Joe Ray says has been “building water baths for the industrial and scientific community since 2003, and circulators since 2007.” He gave this model's predecessor a 9/10 rating in 2013, praising its touchscreen and dishwasher-safe parts.
Though Bulbin said he does not have direct experience with an immersion circulator, he added that it is possible to use it to kill salmonella if used for long enough. “If used correctly,” says Bulbin, “salmonella can be killed in eggs; however, the egg center must be maintained at a similar temperature to pasteurization (135 degrees) for close to one hour. The ‘come up’ time for the circulator to reach the appropriate temperature does not count and will not kill salmonella.”
Sous Vide Solution
With this “come up” time in mind, I set the eggs' time in the circulator bath for 90 minutes—the same time recommended by Anova and Serious Eats, and deemed “sufficient” by Kristin Burkholder, a microbiologist and assistant academic director at the University of New England's School of Biological Sciences.
“We can say that sous vide process will make eggs safer for human consumption,” Burkholder said. “However, it’s important for people to realize that sous vide may not kill all of the salmonella that might be present in the eggs, so people who are immunocompromised or otherwise more susceptible to salmonella infection might want to consider other cooking options to be truly safe.”
She also notes that eggs should be stored in the refrigerator prior to the sous vide process, “because this helps to keep any salmonella that may be present in the eggs from replicating, thus ensuring that starting levels of salmonella are low.”
I attached the Anova to a clean pot filled with water and selected 135 degrees Fahrenheit on the touchscreen. (Burkholder notes that circulators can vary by at least 1 degree, so it's a good idea to double-check with a probe thermometer—and possibly adjust the time for small versus large eggs.)
Once the water reached temp, the circulator beeped, and I added six eggs. The Anova's touchscreen only shows time elapsed, so I set my phone timer and went about my business. (The device has an app, but most features, including timer notifications, are a paid upgrade.) When my phone timer went off, I added the eggs to an ice bath, and once they were cool, cracked one to see how cooked it was.
To my surprise, not much at all—there was some cloudiness to the egg white, but it was pretty minor. I was able to use the eggs just as I would a “normal” raw egg, though due to the denatured proteins, I wouldn't expect any stellar foaming or stiff-peak performance. In all, the immersion circulator is pretty set-it-and-forget-it—it would not be difficult to do this for every dozen eggs I bring into my house, even just for peace of mind.
The Anova is user-friendly and about as simple as it gets—just clip it on a pot full of water and you’re good to go. And it’s not just great for eggs; with a vacuum sealer, you can slow-cook just about any kind of meat or vegetable, with most of that time being hands-off. For the cautious and thrifty among us, a pot is free, of course. Just note that maintaining a steady 135 degrees Fahrenheit for that long requires careful monitoring with an accurate thermometer.

Astronomers have known for decades that an invisible substance permeates the cosmos. Detected only by its gravitational influence on visible objects, dark matter accounts for some 85 percent of all matter, enveloping entire galaxies in great spheroids that branch and interweave to form the scaffolding of the universe.
But the specifications of this grand architecture remain shrouded in mystery. Driven by a ghostly force that scientists call dark energy, the universe is ever-changing, constantly expanding at an accelerating rate.
A new space telescope, launching as soon as August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, will attempt to untangle the nature of these dark intergalactic phenomena. With the resolution of Hubble and a field of view about 100 times as big, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide a new way to look at the universe that could help solve some of the biggest questions in astrophysics.
“An observatory like Roman is intrinsically a discovery machine,” says Julie McEnery, NASA’s senior project scientist for the space telescope. “We're going to find rare things, unusual things, new things, surprising things.”
During its five-year primary mission, Roman will map expansive swaths of space to develop a comprehensive picture of galaxies and dark matter, helping scientists understand how the universe’s largest formations change over time. The telescope, named for the first chief astronomer of NASA, will trace astrophysical structures by measuring subtle distortions of light caused by gravity, allowing scientists to study how dark energy is driving cosmic evolution.
“We’re not measuring the property of something in the universe,” McEnery says of this work. “We’re understanding how the universe we’re in fundamentally works.”
Roman’s sharp, wide view is also expected to capture as many as 200,000 new planets, an extraordinary leap from the roughly 6,300 confirmed exoplanets. The telescope will spot most of these worlds as they block some of the light from their host stars, but its high sensitivity will allow it to detect an additional 1,000 or so by measuring the planets’ gravitational effects on starlight.
Given the space telescope’s powerful resolution and wide area of study, there’s no telling exactly what else it may find.
“The most exciting science from Roman,” McEnery says, “may well be something that we can't even imagine now.”
Whole New Worlds
In many ways, Roman will be a partner to the James Webb Space Telescope. Both primarily observe infrared light, and like Webb, Roman will orbit a point in space nearly a million miles away from Earth called Lagrange Point 2, where the telescopes can effectively block out light from the sun, Earth, and moon.
But where Webb is designed to peer deep into the cosmos, Roman will take a wide view.
“If we consider what the James Webb Space Telescope is doing, it's optimized towards looking at the very distant universe … but just a tiny patch of the sky,” says astrophysicist Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University. “In contrast, Roman is able to look at a large area of the sky at once.”
That broad view will allow Roman to scour hundreds of millions of stars in search of planets. Similar to previous missions, the space observatory will find most of its targets by looking for planets that transit in front of their host stars. This is a highly effective technique to find large planets with short orbits, but to look for different kinds of worlds, Roman will use another trick called microlensing.
When two stars line up one in front of the other, the light from the background star is warped and magnified by the gravity of the star in the foreground. If that foreground star happens to host a planet, Roman will be able to detect how the planet’s gravity further magnifies the starlight coming from behind.
“This method can detect planets that are farther away from their stars than other methods,” says Matthew Penny, an exoplanet researcher at Louisiana State University. “You don't need the planet to complete an entire orbit before you see it.”
Roman is so sensitive to these microlensing effects that it should be able to detect planets with less mass than Mercury. It will also have the ability to spot free-floating “rogue” planets that have been cast away from their stars or that formed alone in the void.
By studying these new populations of planets, scientists can learn more about the conditions that may produce a system like our own and, by extension, a life-bearing planet like Earth.
“Our solar system is potentially quite unique, although we don't really know at this point,” Penny says. “There's a lot of potentially lucky coincidences in the solar system that make life possible.”
Probing the outer regions of planetary systems will provide key missing pieces to this puzzle. For example, the formation of large planets farther from a star may allow smaller planets to form closer in, Penny says, near the habitable zone where liquid water could form.
“Without a complete census of the whole range of possible planets, we don't really know how common planets like Earth are,” Penny says, “or planetary systems like our own.”
The Dark Universe
In addition to many new worlds, Roman’s gaze will fall upon more than a billion galaxies. In particular, it will focus on a population of galaxies between about 2 billion and 6 billion years after the Big Bang.
“One of the things that we try to study is the history and growth of cosmic structure,” Mandelbaum says. “In the very early universe, the matter was almost uniformly distributed. But there were tiny perturbations or tiny regions that were just a fraction more dense or less dense.”
Those slightly denser regions attracted more and more material over time, eventually forming immense clumps of dark matter that scientists call halos. Gas was then driven to the center of these dark matter haloes, where it ignited stars that swirled together to form galaxies.
Roman will create an extraordinarily detailed map of visible galaxies, and it will map the distribution of dark matter with more precision than ever before using a technique called weak gravitational lensing.
“Anytime we have a light ray from one galaxy that has to pass through the universe, including all kinds of structures, to us, the path of that light ray is getting slightly perturbed,” Mandelbaum says.
By comparing those perturbed light rays from many galaxies, scientists can trace the cosmic web of dark matter that surrounds and connects clusters of galaxies. Comparing the maps generated by Roman to observations of the infant universe will allow scientists to study how things have changed over time.
“We're trying to answer fundamental questions about the universe, and it turns out to be incredibly challenging to do that,” Mandelbaum says. “We need really powerful observatories like Roman."
Addressing Cosmic Mysteries
In recent years, three notable aberrations have cropped up in the study of cosmology. The first is that the universe appears to be expanding faster today than it should be, according to models based on the conditions shortly after the Big Bang. The second is that the universe’s matter is distributed more evenly than expected.
And the third is a surprising recent find from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) in Arizona that suggests dark energy, the force driving the expansion of the universe, may be unexpectedly weakening over time.
These three tensions, as scientists call them, each point to an area where the standard model of cosmology may be missing key details.
“It's kind of tantalizing, because there's hints that something is very wrong,” McEnery says.
For each of these unsolved mysteries, Roman will provide valuable data. Regarding the expansion rate of the universe, the space telescope is expected to capture tens of thousands of supernova explosions, several times as many as have been observed so far. Certain supernovae can be used to measure the expansion rate of the universe today, meaning Roman will allow researchers to calculate this value more accurately.
The observatory’s maps of large-scale structures will also give researchers a better sense of the universe’s matter distribution, or clumpiness. And its measurements of dark matter’s gravitational effects will provide a detailed picture of how these structures have grown over time, allowing scientists to test whether the strength of dark energy truly has been changing as DESI suggests.
If it has, “we're pretty much guaranteed to be able to confirm what they're seeing, because it's exactly the thing we were designed to do,” McEnery says.
Roman’s vast view of the universe will reveal countless new details, and as scientists put the immense puzzle together, they may revolutionize our understanding of cosmology.
“We had a major breakthrough in the last century on the very small with the development of quantum mechanics and the discovery of elementary particles,” McEnery says. “Maybe this is the century of understanding the very big.”

Gurugram sewer line breach causes road cave-in at IFFCO Chowk; traffic diverted
In December, GMDA warned the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) about a possible cave-in at the IFFCO flyover
A large sinkhole was formed on the service road after a master sewer line collapsed on Tuesday afternoon at Gurugram’s Iffco Chowk, triggering traffic disruptions at one of the city’s busiest intersections, people familiar with the matter said.
The incident, which comes a day after torrential rains led to waterlogging across the city, took place at about 3pm on a stretch near Westin Hotel when a portion of the service road caved in, leading to a 10 feet by 10 feet sinkhole on the Delhi-Jaipur side. Traffic police barricaded the site and diverted commuters onto alternative routes while emergency repair teams were deployed.
Officials linked the road cave-in to the collapse of a dilapidated sewer line managed by the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA).
GMDA spokesperson Neha Sharma said the authority, alongside the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), moved quickly to secure the location. “The affected area has been barricaded, and the GMDA has issued directions to the agency for the repair of the 1000mm master sewer line in the area. The road repair work will be taken up after the master sewer line is repaired,” she said.
GMDA executive engineer Bhim Arya told HT that the line was part of the master sewer line that runs from Ambience Mall to Rajiv Chowk along the service road of the national highway.
“The repair of the sewage line will be started from Wednesday morning and all efforts will be made to complete the work at the earliest,” Arya said,
The GMDA sewage line had collapsed at Iffco Chowk in 2021 too, just 100 metres from the current cave-in when a large portion of the drain under the Iffco Chowk flyover collapsed, requiring major repair of the drain and the retaining wall of the flyover by GMDA and NHAI.
NHAI officials said the cavity on the left hand side had exposed significant void formation beneath the road, with water accumulation observed inside.
“Preliminary findings indicate that a GMDA master sewer line is running beneath/along the affected location, and possible leakage or failure of the sewer line may have caused soil erosion and subsequent collapse of the road crust,” an NHAI official said.
“We have instructed GMDA to repair it immediately as it poses a risk to nearby structures also, the official said.
Waterlogged roads in Gurugram also led to a vehicle carrying 300 bags of cement getting trapped in Sector 9 when driver could not assess the weakened road surface along a submerged, excavated stretch on a link road to the Dwarka Expressway.
In another case, a heavy sand truck broke through a concrete drain cover, trapping the vehicle on a service lane along the Delhi-Jaipur Expressway.
No injuries were reported.

Why are there so few African players in the WSL?
- Published
Plenty of talent was on show during the Women's Africa Cup of Nations this month - but why do so few players from the continent play for clubs in England?
The Women's Super League is widely regarded as one of the best leagues in the world and Europe's top talent is flooding in.
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas joined London City Lionesses this summer - the latest figure from Spain's World Cup-winning squad to move to the WSL.
It follows past high-profile moves from foreign players, including Australia captain Sam Kerr who made 158 appearances for Chelsea before joining Gotham.
Some of the United States' biggest stars are in the WSL too, including Chelsea duo Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma, Arsenal's Emily Fox and Manchester City's Sam Coffey.
There has also been an influx of Asian talent in recent seasons, with Japan captain Yui Hasegawa becoming one of the WSL's best players at Manchester City.
BBC Sport explores why the WSL has just four African players - Chiamaka Nnadozie (Brighton and Nigeria), Aisha Masaka (Brighton and Tanzania), Rofiat Imuran (London City Lionesses and Nigeria) and Ines Belloumou (West Ham and Algeria).

Where are Africa's biggest stars?
The small representation in the WSL is not because of a lack of talent in Africa.
National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) clubs in America have shown huge interest, spending big money on some of the continent's best players.
Zambia forward Racheal Kundananji became the most expensive women's footballer at the time in 2024 when she joined Bay FC from Madrid CFF for £685,000.
Her compatriot Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride, was voted the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year in the same year.
Cameroon's Wafcon player of the tournament Monique Ngock is at Washington Spirit, where six African international players currently reside.
Temwa Chawinga won the NWSL Golden Boot and Most Valuable Player awards in her first two seasons with Kansas City Current.
Her sister, Malawi captain Tabitha Chawinga, plays for European giants Lyon and helped her country reach the final of Wafcon last week, where they lost to Cameroon.
Michaely Bihina, who was a standout performer in the tournament for Cameroon, plays for Benfica.
Nnadozie, who notably became the first African goalkeeper to be shortlisted for the Women's Ballon d'Or award, joined Brighton last year. The Seagulls goalkeeper ended her season with an FA Cup final appearance at Wembley against WSL champions Manchester City.
What are some of the barriers?
A major barrier for WSL clubs hoping to sign African talent is the Governing Body Endorsement (GBE) criteria set out in the league's registration rules.
Foreign players must earn a minimum number of points in five categories to be eligible for a GBE visa.
The number of caps they have for their national team, appearances in the Women's Champions League and the ranking of their former clubs play a part.
WSL sides also have to compete with the wages and transfer fees being offered by NWSL clubs, who are targeting the best African footballers.
They have to use resources for scouting which, at the moment, is prioritised across Europe.
Another major issue is the lack of coverage given to the domestic game in Africa, as well as issues around Wafcon.
There was confusion in this edition when the Confederation of African Football (CAF) named Channel 4 as the UK broadcast partner, but no matches were shown live in the opening round as an agreement had not been formally reached.
The tournament had also been postponed just 12 days before it was set to kick off in Morocco, eventually taking place three months later.
Switzerland captain Lia Walti, who signed for Brighton this summer, told BBC Sport that, globally, coverage of women's football has room for improvement.
"I think you have to bring the game to the people. You kind of have to force people to watch it. I felt that was how it maybe started in England," she said.
"In a lot of other countries I think they have bad coverage. It's not shown at all, or if it's shown, from where they film the game [makes it look] really poor.
"It affects the way you watch a game. You don't really see the speed, the tactics or anything and you don't enjoy watching the game."

'Africa shouldn't be left behind'
Malawi's magical route to the Wafcon final ensured they will play in the Women's World Cup for the first time next year, alongside champions Cameroon, and semi-finalists Algeria and Morocco.
Tabitha Chawinga believed the Malawi side put their nation on the map and showed their quality.
Speaking to BBC's World Service following their final defeat by Cameroon, the Malawi captain said: "It's really the best. No-one gave Malawi a chance to be in the finals, no-one gave Cameroon a chance to be in the finals.
"But as you can see, we watched fantastic football. There was amazing football from both sides."
Nigeria goalkeeper Nnadozie paved the way in the WSL last year with her move to Brighton.
She told BBC Sport in October her Ballon d'Or nomination made a "big impact" in Africa and put the spotlight on some of the continent's best talent.
"We have so many good players and they just need the opportunity to show what they can really do," she said.
"Very soon, we will have more numbers [in the Ballon d'Or nominations] from Africa. Trust me, there are so many good talents from Africa.
"Some players have had the opportunity to come to Europe but some have stayed back home. I hope in the future, bigger competitions will come to Africa.
"The Under-17s World Cup is in Morocco. This is big evidence that they are doing a lot of great jobs over there. It is just a matter of time.
"Women's football is rising and Africa shouldn't be left behind."

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
- Published
Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going.
Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glass and agates from her business, CindyLouWho2, based in Calgary, Alberta, come from Americans.
But after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed over the weekend and leaders of both countries pledged to slap 50% tariffs on each other's products, business owners on both sides of the border are bracing for the fallout.
With a majority of the items she sells falling under US President Donald Trump's newly imposed tariffs, Baldassi says she will need to add 50% to the price of most of her products to stay afloat.
"It's quite likely that it will wipe out most of my US sales," Baldassi told the BBC. "I expect that at least half of my business will be gone."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged levies starting on 8 September on US steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Trump tariffs went into effect on Saturday, hitting Canadian wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.
'We may get killed'
In Canada, it is not clear how much more severe the impacts will be, since the country has grown somewhat used to the on-again-off-again trade war.
Lind Furniture has been in business for almost 60 years in the Canadian province of Ontario, selling leather furniture to big store clients like Sears and Costco over the years.
Sales dropped when Trump took office in 2025. "As soon as there were tariffs in the air, people put purchases on hold," Michael Saifer, general manager of Lind Furniture, told the BBC.

Now, his concern centres around Canadians' chances for victory.
"Everyone wants to sell to the Americans - they can buy from whoever they want," he said. "I don't know that we're going to win a war with them; we may get killed."
The US tariffs that took effect after talks broke off on Friday apply to about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian exports to the US - about 5% of what Canada ships to the US annually. The levies add to US tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.
Canada would be very exposed if the import taxes multiply on both sides because 70% of its exports are to the US.
Navigating what comes next as both sides are dug in is proving a delicate balance for some business owners.
Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores.
Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff.
"If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said.
He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go.
"There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US.
"Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this."
'It's going to get worse before it gets better'
The impacts are not only being felt north of the US-Canada border. Carney promised his tariffs hitting US products in September will match Trump's "dollar-for-dollar". Details of the countermeasures will be released in the coming days, he said.
For Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing, a clothing store in Portland, Oregon, that means preparing for one of their best-selling items to potentially increase sizably in price.
Osgood creates designs that she has a Montreal-based company transfer onto pillows the couple sells in their store.
Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC.
"Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said.
The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out.
"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said.
While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies.
Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol.
He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to.
"The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.
And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border.
The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state.
The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric".
"We completely understood that," she said.
But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat.
And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear.
"It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."
