Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
- Published
A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.
Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.
The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.
Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.
Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.
She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.
"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.
Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.
"It has been happening for decades."
Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.
The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.
A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.
Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.
As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.
"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.
"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."
Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.
Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.
Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.
"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.
Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.
"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.
Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.
There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.
Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.
About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.
He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.
"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.
In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.
"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."
Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.
"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.
"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."
Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.
Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.
The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.
Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.
"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.
The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.
"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.
The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.
There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.
Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.
Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.
More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.
That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.
In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.
When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

A lung cancer diagnosis has a way of stopping a conversation cold. Families go quiet. Plans get shelved. The assumption, almost universal, is that the outcome is already decided. Often, that assumption is wrong. When the disease is found early, meaningful treatment is possible, curative intent included. The gap between what people believe about lung cancer and what medicine can actually offer has never been wider.
Myth 1: A lung cancer diagnosis is always a death sentence
Where does this belief come from? In India, most patients present in advanced stage, and because of this, the treatment options decrease exponentially. The outcomes families witness reinforce a fatalism that’s hard to shake. Late detection is the problem, not an inherent quality of the disease itself. Lung cancer found at an early, localised stage is genuinely treatable. Surgery with curative intent is possible. The question that matters most is how soon the disease gets diagnosed.
Myth 2: Only smokers get lung cancer
Smoking is the most well-known risk factor, and for good reason. But the picture is more complicated. Prolonged exposure to indoor cooking fuel smoke or second-hand smoke carries considerable risk, as does long-term exposure to occupational carcinogens. Registry data from India has shown a steady rise in cases among women and adults who have never smoked. Adenocarcinoma, now the most commonly diagnosed lung cancer subtype in India, occurs frequently in this group. It also tends to carry specific genetic mutations that respond well to targeted treatment. Any respiratory symptom that doesn’t resolve deserves attention, irrespective of smoking history.
Myth 3: The warning signs will always be clear
This is the myth that probably causes the most harm. Lung cancer is often silent early on, and when symptoms surface, they look like something else entirely. A cough that has outstayed its welcome. Recurring chest infections. Unexplained weight loss, or breathlessness that keeps getting worse. Any of these, persisting beyond three weeks, should prompt clinical evaluation. Some features call for more urgency: coughing up blood, a voice that turns persistently hoarse, chest pain that doesn’t shift. Attributing such signs to the weather or getting older is understandable, but it is also how early lung cancer gets missed.
Why early detection changes everything
The stage at diagnosis is an important factor in how lung cancer plays out. Finding it early and getting it surgically removal with curative intent becomes a real possibility. This is where screening comes into the picture. Low-dose CT scanning picks up small nodules in the lung before a patient feels anything, creating a window for treatment that wouldn’t otherwise exist. Indian health economic research has confirmed this approach as cost-effective for those at highest risk. If you have a long smoking history and are above a certain age, it’s worth asking your doctor about screening.
Treatment can transform outcomes
The treatment landscape for lung cancer has shifted considerably. Molecular testing can now identify specific mutations within a tumour. EGFR and ALK alterations are among the most clinically significant, and therapies designed to target them have extended survival in ways that weren’t possible with chemotherapy alone. For patients whose tumours don’t carry targetable mutations, immunotherapy has opened up another avenue. These are part of standard oncology care in India today. A patient diagnosed now is working with a very different set of possibilities from someone diagnosed a decade ago.
Who should act and when
Anyone with a long smoking history, a close family member who has had lung cancer, or years of exposure to air pollutants at work or at home has reason to discuss their risk with a doctor. That conversation doesn’t need to wait for symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they shouldn’t be left to resolve on their own; in someone already carrying these risks, investigation is the right call.
A diagnosis of lung cancer is not, in itself, what limits a patient’s options. Time is. The treatments available today are genuinely different from what existed a decade ago, and outcomes for many patients reflect that. But none of it matters if the disease is found late. The most important thing anyone can do is take symptoms seriously and act on them early.
(Dr. Rajesh Shinde is director – GI (HPB–colorectal) & thoracic surgical oncology Apollo Cancer Centre – Western Region Apollo Hospitals, Navi Mumbai. drrajesh_sh@apollohospitals.com)

A total of four Indian companies have been sanctioned by the US for importing petroleum and petrochemical products from Iran, the US State Department said in a press release. These companies include Portease Partners LLP and its partners Indrismiya Ashrafmiya Sheikh and Harish Ramachandra Rangi. They facilitated the import of multiple shipments of Iranian petrochemical products Other Indian companies facing action are Sadashiva Overseas Limited; PP Softtech Private Limited, along with its director Prashant Garg; and Prakrutees Infra Impex Private Limited. Sheikh, Rangi, and Garg are all Indian nationals, according to the release. Quick answers to key questions The US sanctioned four Indian firms for importing petroleum and petrochemical products from Iran, which they did knowingly, thus engaging in significant transactions that violate US sanctions against Iran. The sanctions under Operation Economic Outcast are designed to sever Iran's financial lifelines by targeting its revenue sources, particularly from oil, and to hold countries and companies accountable that continue to engage economically with Tehran. The firms sanctioned include Portease Partners LLP, Sadashiva Overseas Limited, PP Softtech Private Limited, and Prakrutees Infra Impex Private Limited, along with their respective directors who facilitated transactions with Iranian entities. The US Treasury described the sanctions as economic asphyxiation to emphasize their goal of blocking all potential revenue sources for Iran, aiming to cripple its economy and pressurize it to change its policies. Operation Economic Outcast threatens countries trading with Iran with secondary sanctions if they do not withdraw their economic activities, thereby increasing the risk for international partners who continue to engage with Tehran. Sadashiva Overseas imported Iranian-origin petroleum products worth around USD 69 million from multiple companies, while PP Softtech and Prakrutees Infra imported USD 25 million each in petroleum products, the press release said. These companies were put on a list for "knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products from Iran," it said. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced 'Operation Economic Outcast', which involved new sanctions aimed at blocking all potential sources of revenue for Iran. The US has also told countries to cut economic ties with Tehran or face retaliation. Bessent described it as an unprecedented campaign to sever Iran's financial lifelines. It broadens the risk of secondary sanctions for entities - which can be countries, businesses or organisations - continuing to do business with Tehran. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott on Monday said in a statement: "Today, the United States took sweeping action against multiple entities, individuals, and vessels enabling the Iranian regime's destabilising activities." "Such activities include attacks against US forces and allies in the region, illicit weapons procurement, cyber intrusions into American infrastructure, and the movement of energy products whose sale funds terrorism globally," he added. Trump threatens to demolish another DC landmark
The Kennedy Center becomes a hostage to Trump’s renaming demands.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is threatening that if he can’t have the Kennedy Center, no one can.
What’s going on? Trump has been trying to get his name back on the John F. Kennedy Center for Performing Arts since June, when it was removed in response to a court order. On Monday night, the Justice Department revealed its latest ploy to make that happen.
In a court filing, the DOJ argued that if its renovation plans for the Kennedy Center aren’t allowed to go forward, “the center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down” and replaced by another structure, “such as a large outdoor amphitheater.”
Tied up in the proposed $250 million renovation are three new tributes to Trump, which the Kennedy Center board (stacked with Trump appointees) voted to add earlier this month: the text “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” and “endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund” on the building’s facade, and the renaming of the Kennedy Center grounds as “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
Those changes are currently being challenged in court by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), who successfully sued to undo Trump’s first renaming of the center. But the Trump administration claims her suit endangers the entire project.
What does Trump’s name have to do with the renovations? According to the DOJ filing, “an order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop.”
“There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure,” it adds.
Is that true? No. Congress already approved $257 million for the renovation last year, which the Kennedy Center board touted in a press release crediting Trump.
And far from being a draw, the Washington Post reported Tuesday, Trump’s previous renaming of the Kennedy Center caused ticket sales and donations to plummet, creating a $23 million deficit even after deep spending cuts.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Apple has announced fresh versions of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktop computers, alongside some new chips: the M6 and M5 Ultra.
Neither Mac desktop has undergone any physical changes on the exterior, but the long-awaited update brings these Macs back into stock after being difficult to buy for most of this year. Importantly, this serves as our first introduction to the M6 chip, which we will likely see much more of in future MacBooks.
Skipping the M5 entirely, the Mac Mini now comes in two flavors: the M6 and the M5 Pro. The M5 Pro is the same chip that's currently found in the MacBook Pro, but the M6 is brand new. It's the first Apple Silicon part to be built on 2-nanometer process technology and also adds extra cores to the mix. This is a 12-core CPU—another first for Apple—broken down into two super cores, four performances cores, and six efficiency cores.
New here are the performance cores, which Apple says are designed to speed up multithreaded tasks while preserving efficiency. Apple claims the M6 is 20 percent faster than the M5 in multithreaded performance and 40 percent faster than the M4.
The M6 comes with a faster GPU too, adding two more cores to the mix for a total of 12 GPU cores. This is also the first Mac Mini to have Neural Accelerators for faster on-device AI performance, a feature that launched in the M5 chip last year. The result is a Mac Mini that Apple claims is twice as fast as the M4 Mac Mini, along with providing higher throughput for gaming. Lastly, the M6 Mac mini also comes with what Apple calls a “dual 16-core Neural Engine," which doubles the peak AI performance.
In addition to the extra performance, however, it also comes with a $200 price increase. The M6 Mac Mini now starts at $899 for the model with 16 GB of unified memory. The Mac Mini can still be configured with up to 32 GB of unified memory, and Apple says the tiny desktop is 40 percent faster, with bandwidth now up to 170 GB per second.
The M5 Ultra Arrives
The Mac Studio is also receiving a significant update. Like the Mac Mini, it still comes in two flavors: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. This is the fourth generation of the Mac Studio to come out, with the M3 Ultra (and M3 Max) model coming out in early 2025.
Apple proudly claims that the M5 Ultra is Apple's most powerful chip ever, and the first to use a “quad-die” architecture. Apple's “Ultra” chips have always connected two Max dies together using using a technology called UltraFusion across a high-speed interconnect. The difference this time is that the M5 Max already had two dies itself, which is where the four dies come from. To keep those four chips running as fast as possible, the next version of UltraFusion increases the inter-die bandwidth to over 4.4 TB per second, allowing the whole array to function as a single CPU.
M5 Ultra Mac Studio comes with four more CPU cores for a total of 36. There are still 80 GPU cores (the same as on the M3 Ultra), but the M5-specific improvements to the GPU apply here for better overall performance.
In a briefing on the Mac Studio, Apple even discussed the ability to connect multiple Mac Studios together over Thunderbolt 5 to run frontier-level LLMs with over a trillion parameters locally, allowing the four systems to share memory. Hypothetically, that allows you to run models locally on a Mac that just weren't possible before. Apparently, four Mac Studios can even be connected in this way to run over a standard wall outlet.
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio are available for preorder starting today and will come with macOS 27 Golden Gate preinstalled. However, systems won't ship until September 22. In a briefing, Apple said this delay wouldn't be reflective of shipping times for these new Mac Mini or Mac Studio systems.

King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says
- Published
King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream.
The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice.
The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago.
His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.
King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia.
The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026.
Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018.
The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence.
Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure.
Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

90,000 forced to flee as raging Reno wildfire tears through neighborhoods
Crews have started to contain a wildfire in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Reno, Nevada
Firefighters are gaining ground on a fast-moving wildfire near Reno, Nevada, after flames destroyed more than 30 homes and forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate or prepare to flee.
The Hawk Fire was 27% contained Monday after holding at roughly 23 square miles following a dangerous surge over the weekend, officials said.
“We are making progress,” U.S. Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein said.
Evacuation orders and warnings remained in place for about 63,000 residents, down from more than 90,000 at the height of the fire. Officials warned that shifting winds could still send flames through dry vegetation toward residential neighborhoods.
At least 32 homes have been destroyed and six damaged, though authorities expect those numbers to rise as assessment teams reach more burned areas. Seven people — three first responders and four civilians — have been injured.
Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve described the speed and intensity of the flames as unlike anything she had witnessed.
“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said. “It took your breath away, in the worst way.”
The fire began Saturday near the California border before exploding in size Sunday. Nevada's governor declared a state of emergency and deployed the National Guard to assist with aerial firefighting operations and secure evacuated neighborhoods northwest of downtown Reno.
Schools across Washoe County were closed Monday to keep roads clear for emergency crews.
Some residents have grown frustrated over restrictions preventing them from returning home, but Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam warned that conditions remain dangerous.
“It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.
Officials said the Hawk Fire is the third major wildfire north of Reno in two weeks. All three were caused by human activity, though authorities have not determined whether the Hawk Fire was started accidentally or deliberately.
The disaster has also complicated preparations for Burning Man, which is scheduled to begin Sunday in the Black Rock Desert. Many festivalgoers traditionally travel through Reno on their way to the event.
Burning Man organizers urged visitors not to take hotel rooms or other resources needed by people displaced by the fire.
“Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” organizers said.
For some residents, the devastation has been painfully familiar.
Crystal Hallock, 53, lost her home to fire for the second time in less than a decade. An electrical fire destroyed her previous home in 2018, and she moved into the rebuilt property the following year.
Hallock fled Saturday with her children, grandchildren and pets as smoke and flames approached. Her ex-husband remained behind trying to protect the property and her vintage Cadillac with a garden hose.
As conditions deteriorated, Hallock pleaded with him over the phone to leave.
“He was saying he can’t breathe, it’s so dark I can’t see, and I’m screaming at him, ‘Leave the car, just leave it,’” she recalled.
The call suddenly went dead.
About 30 minutes later, he called again. He had escaped — and managed to save the Cadillac.
“I’m truly blessed because I have a place to stay with my animals and my grandkids,” Hallock said. “We were all able to get out safely.”
Others had little time to gather their possessions.
“Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie,” said Ruby Delatorre, who returned from a concert to find her neighborhood under evacuation orders.
Another resident, Jon Hanbury, was still waiting Monday to learn whether his home had survived.
“The flames were pretty close to my house, and the smoke was really thick,” he said from a temporary shelter at Reno's convention center.
Despite improving containment, the danger is not over. Warm, dry and breezy weather is expected across western Nevada, with critical fire conditions possible later this week.
The Hawk Fire comes during a punishing wildfire season across the West. More than 50,000 wildfires have been recorded nationwide this year, the highest number at this point in a decade, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

In Summary
- The iQOO Z11 is the latest device in iQOO’s mid-segment Z series.
- The phone comes with a curved display, a sleek design, and specs and features that make it a solid mid-segmenter.
- At its starting price of Rs 34,999, the iQOO Z11 is a great option for those who want a phone that is capable of handling most tasks and has flaunt value too.
iQOO’s latest mid-segmenter sports sleek curves of the display sort, packs in decent, entertainment-friendly specs, manages to squeeze a big battery into a slim frame, and tops it all with a generous serving of AI. But will all this be enough for the iQOO Z11 to click with its target audience in a time of rising prices and declining specs? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
iQOO Z11 looks and appearance: Curved display and a Pixel-like camera bar
The iQOO Z11 is a tall, slim phone that will turn heads with its appearance. It sports a curved display in front and also has curved sides, while on the back is a camera bar that reminds us of the Google Pixel. It is a tall phone at 164.4 mm, although it is very slim at just 7.99 mm, and surprisingly light for its size at just 199 grams – that’s taller, and yet lighter and slimmer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. The front is smooth glass while the back and sides are made of polycarbonate, but they can be easily mistaken for metal or glass. The camera bar on the back is made of aluminum, which gives the phone a very premium feel. It comes with IP68/69 dust and water resistance, so it can easily survive a fall in the water, and has a very reassuringly solid feel to it.
The iQOO Z11 comes in Celestial Blue and Aurora Green shades. Both have a subtly shiny look that shimmers and changes shades in the light, and also have matte finishes that do not smudge or stain easily. We got the Aurora Green shade. This phone has flaunt value without being loud – the curved display and the camera bar give it slim and tall Pixel vibes, which is not a bad thing at all.
iQOO Z11 Spec Sheet and Hardware: Solidly upper mid-segment
The iQOO Z11 comes with a 6.83-inch AMOLED display with a resolution of 2800 x 1260 and a refresh rate of 144 Hz, which is rare at this price point. Sound is handled by a pair of stereo speakers. The phone is the first in the Indian market to be powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Ultra processor, which is supposed to be a steady performer with some gaming ability as well. This is paired with RAM and storage variants of 6 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 256 GB, and 12 GB/ 256 GB. The RAM is LPDDR4X, while the storage is UFS 3.1, which are, like the processor, not top of the line, but actually very capable. The camera bar on the back has a 50-megapixel main Sony IMX882 sensor with OIS, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide, while selfie and video call duties are handled by a 32-megapixel front-facing camera. In spite of being very slim, the iQOO Z11 comes with a large 7025 mAh battery with support for 44W charging, and a 44W charger in the box.
The iQOO Z11 runs on OriginOS 6 on top of Android 16 and comes with an assurance of three years of Android upgrades and five years of security patches. Once again, that’s par for the course for the segment. The phone also comes with not only a number of AI tools (apart from Google’s standard Gemini suite), but also with unlimited AI credits for AI captions and AI creations using iQOO’s tools, basically allowing consumers to use them without restrictions, which is rare to see at this price.
iQOO Z11 cameras: Colorfully pleasant mostly
Photography on the iQOO Z11 is largely a single-camera show – something that is beginning to become the rule in this price segment. The 50-megapixel main camera takes very pleasant snaps with ample detail. Purists might feel that the images come with slightly saturated colors, but mainstream users are unlikely to complain. Even low-light and night photography is impressively colorful. We would suggest shooting videos in the daylight, though, as low-light videos are not the best.
The front camera takes good selfies, with plenty of beautification and skin smoothing by default, although these can be toned down. The ultrawide camera is basically good for a different perspective, but its quality is not the greatest. Portraits are impressive, but lossless zoom is limited to 2x, while digital zoom goes up to 10x. There are plenty of shooting and editing options to let one do more with images, but this is a phone for casual point-and-shooters rather than enthusiasts.
iQOO Z11 performance: Doing it all well, instead of doing a few things brilliantly
The iQOO Z11 is one of the rare phones out there that does many things well. The combination of that large display and very good stereo speakers makes it a great phone for viewing content, whether it is viewing shows and films, reels, or just browsing the Web. The 7050 mAh battery comfortably keeps going for a day and a half of normal use, and the 44W charger gets the phone from empty to full in about 70-75 minutes, with half an hour generally being enough to take the phone up to 50 percent (which is enough to see off a day of use).
The Dimensity 7500 Ultra sails through routine tasks effortlessly, and we were able to switch between 6-10 apps quite easily without any lag. While the phone is not a gaming beast, we were able to play titles like Call of Duty and Asphalt after a few minor tweaks, and even Genshin Impact (with graphics toned down) ran well on the phone. The display and speakers again play key roles here. The phone never heated up excessively either, no matter what we burdened it with.
iQOO Z11 Software and UI: Unlimited AI
OriginOS 6 runs smoothly on the iQOO Z11, and there are plenty of AI tools to play around with. AI Creation is a powerful writing tool, and AI Transcript Assist works perfectly for those who love to have written records of meetings, classes, or lectures (do double-check names, though). There are also tools for AI translation, summaries, and more. They all work very smoothly indeed (though you need to log in to an iQOO account and have an Internet connection for most), with many coming with unlimited usage – something college-goers and AI addicts on a tight budget will appreciate. Of course, one also gets Google’s AI tools such as Gemini and Circle to Search.
While there is some bloatware (most of which can be uninstalled), there are a number of handy utilities and features too, including iQOO DocMaster, which lets one work with multiple document formats, the Dynamic Island-like Origin Island, and the ability to easily share information with not just Android but also iOS devices. The software seems to be a little overwhelming, but is extremely useful once one gets the hang of it. And works smoothly most of the time.
iQOO Z11 Review Verdict: Great for those who want a do-it-all, which also looks good
The iQOO Z11 is available in the following RAM and storage configurations at these prices:
6 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 34,999
8 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 39,999
8 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 44,999
12 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 49,999
Given the trend of insanely high prices, these are extremely competitive. In fact, although some might frown at the relatively modest RAM in the base 6 GB/ 128 GB model, the fact that it is priced below Rs 35,000 could tempt many users. Even at its higher price points, its combination of design, specs, and performance makes it very good value for money at a time when prices are increasing dramatically.
It is this unique cocktail of features that lets the iQOO Z11 hold its own against some very tough competition. The Moto Edge 70 Pro has a more powerful processor and cameras with a higher megapixel count but loses out in the looks department and has a smaller battery. The Redmi Turbo 5 brings a quirky design and a powerful chip to the table but has a smaller display. Another contender is the OnePlus Nord CE6, which comes with a huge battery and a good processor, but loses out in the camera and design stakes.
This tick-all-boxes versatility sums up the iQOO Z11. It may not be the very best in any performance category, but there is actually very little that it cannot do. Want a quick gaming session? It will handle it. Want to check or post on social media? It will handle it. Want to binge-watch shows? It has got your back. Want to send images and videos to your iPhone-carrying friends? It can do that too. Want to get notes and summaries? Its AI will chip in, but it does the job.
The iQOO Z11 is very much a generalist, rather than a specialist in any field. It is a masterly jack of all trades. And a very good-looking one too. One of the best all-rounders you can get for under Rs 40,000 right now.

- Smooth performance
- Very good stereo speakers
- Lots of AI features (some with unlimited usage)
- Good main camera
- IP68/69 rating
- Ordinary ultrawide camera
- Bloatware in OS
- Competition has faster chips and memory

Srinagar, Aug 25: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has said teachers cannot be made solely responsible for determining the future of the Union Territory, arguing that the government must first improve their working conditions, school infrastructure and staffing before expecting them to shoulder greater responsibility for children's futures.
Addressing a gathering of teachers and office-bearers of the J&K Teachers Forum, Omar said teachers already faced an expanding list of responsibilities beyond classroom teaching, including election duties, government functions and social campaigns.
“It is a fact that the future of Jammu and Kashmir is our children,” Omar said. “What will be the future of our children? You all have a very big role in that. But if we put all our responsibility on you and say that what Jammu and Kashmir will be like in the future will be decided by our teachers, then I think that would be a great injustice to you and would put excessive pressure on you.”
He said the role of teachers had become considerably more difficult with the proliferation of smartphones, social media, television channels and, increasingly, artificial intelligence.
“Today, look at what you are competing with. You are competing with phones, social media, channels and so many other things. And now there is a new thing — artificial intelligence,” he said.
Omar said AI had created a new challenge for teachers in assessing whether students were submitting their own work.
“I say, how difficult will it be for a teacher to determine whether an assignment submitted by a child, what they have written, is their own work or whether artificial intelligence helped them?” he said.
The chief minister also criticised the practice of continually assigning additional duties to teachers while their own service-related grievances remained unresolved.
“There is an August 15 function, there is a January 26 function, and the first thing we tell you is: prepare the children, organise a cultural programme, have them march past,” he said.
He also cited International Yoga Day, anti-drug campaigns and elections as examples of duties routinely assigned to teachers.
“When there is election work, we put you in booths in far-flung areas,” Omar said.
“Whenever there is some other work, whenever we have to do something, we do not find anyone else — our eyes fall on you.”
At the same time, he acknowledged that teachers' files did not always move with the same urgency.
“But when your issues come up, unfortunately, I have to say that your files do not move forward as quickly as the files that are moved when we have to post you somewhere else,” he said.
Omar said the government had a responsibility to resolve teachers' grievances relating to transfers, departmental promotion committees and vacancies.
“If you have issues concerning transfers, if you have issues concerning DPCs, if you have issues concerning vacancies, or other matters, then we have to resolve those issues with the same seriousness,” he said.
“And I assure you that as long as Sakina is here and I am working with her, none of your issues will be ignored,” he added, referring to Education Minister Sakina Itoo.
The chief minister also highlighted the disparity between teachers posted in rural areas and those able to secure postings in urban schools through influence.
“Providing education in remote rural schools is not easy. Working there is difficult,” Omar said.
He said some teachers without political or social influence remained in remote schools for long periods, while those with access and influence often managed to remain in urban schools.
“Perhaps they have never even seen a rural school. They work only in city schools,” he said.
Omar also drew attention to the problem of so-called ghost schools, where students remain formally enrolled but do not regularly attend classes.
He said some students enrolled in schools primarily to appear for board examinations while spending much of their time at private tuition centres.
“The teacher comes to school. The teacher wants to do their work. But students enrol there only for paperwork,” he said.
The chief minister acknowledged continuing infrastructure deficiencies, including rented school buildings, unsafe structures and inadequate access to smart classrooms.
“We talk about smart classrooms, but how far have we been able to take smart classrooms to our children?” he said. “Smart classrooms are a distant thing; even today, in some places, we are unable to provide proper school structures.”
Omar said responsibility for those shortcomings rested with the government rather than teachers.
“But these shortcomings are not your fault. They are ours,” he said.
“Repairing infrastructure is not your responsibility; it is mine. Filling vacancies is not your job; it is mine. Strengthening your hands so that you can perform your work properly is the responsibility of me, Sakina and Nasir.”
He urged teachers, meanwhile, to prepare students for a rapidly changing world, saying the pace of change expected over the next two or three decades would exceed that witnessed in recent decades.
“We have made a lot of progress from 1947 to today,” Omar said. “But the world is changing very rapidly. The change that has taken place in the last 30, 40 or 50 years will happen much faster in the next 20 to 30 years.”
“We have to prepare our children for that,” he said, adding that students needed to be equipped to make “a positive contribution to Jammu and Kashmir”.
Omar also addressed concerns over the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET), saying the requirement had not originated with the Jammu and Kashmir government and that his administration had repeatedly opposed its application.
“This is not something that we have created. We have repeatedly tried to fight against it,” he said.
He linked its applicability in Jammu and Kashmir to the post-2019 constitutional and legal changes, saying that because laws applicable across the country now apply to J&K, the TET requirement had also been extended to the region.
“Perhaps the Supreme Court's order so far is that this has to be implemented by August 28. So, for the moment, we have time to take our campaign to the Supreme Court,” Omar said.
He said the government would continue to raise its objections before the Supreme Court.
“As Sakina has assured you, we continue to raise our voice against this here and in the Supreme Court,” he said.
Omar's remarks placed the government's responsibilities alongside those of teachers, arguing that better educational outcomes would depend not merely on what teachers did inside classrooms but also on whether the administration succeeded in improving the broader conditions in which they worked.
“You will be able to do it, you will succeed, only if we succeed,” he said. “If we are able to improve your conditions, if we are able to improve your infrastructure, if we are able to improve the schools, then you will be able to improve the future of the children.”
“If we fail and then tell you, ‘Now you go and fix everything,’ that will not happen,” he said.
Omar also acknowledged financial constraints facing Jammu and Kashmir, saying the government's fiscal position was not as strong as it would like it to be.
“The financial condition of Jammu and Kashmir is not as strong as we would like it to be, so there are some restrictions,” he said.
But he maintained that those constraints could not absolve the administration of its responsibility towards teachers.
His broader message to the gathering was that teachers should be supported rather than burdened with every expectation surrounding education, social development and the future of Jammu and Kashmir.
“This is not your responsibility alone,” Omar said.

Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
- Published
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.
It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.
The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision which severed her right leg.
Fifteen months later, her death, and the silence surrounding it, has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.
In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.
Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.
Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures. Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.
Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.
Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.
Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.
Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.
State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.
VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.
While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.
Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.
In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.
In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

  - Published23 January
- British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall 
  - Published8 April
Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.
Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".
Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.
The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.
"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."
Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.
Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.
This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.
Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.
Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.
On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.
Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.
In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.
But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.
Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.
Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.
"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

Several states will decide voter ID ballot measures this year
A Republican-backed election overhaul, which would add proof-of-citizenship and other identification requirements to the voting process, has stalled in Congress.
But voters in a number of states are weighing in on some of these same issues this year.
Voters in at least six states will decide ballot measures related to voter ID — the largest number of voter ID measures in a single year, per Ballotpedia.
Oklahoma is first up, voting on its proposal during Tuesday's primary runoff. That measure would essentially codify existing voter ID policy in its state constitution. The remaining states — including the swing states of Arizona, Nevada and North Carolina — have measures for this fall's general election that would toughen ID requirements for voters.
The ballot measures follow lawmakers in eight other states making voter ID requirements more stringent this year, according to the Voting Rights Lab, a research group that supports expanded voting access.

- Alaska voters will again decide whether to keep its election system, which includes top-four, all-party primaries and ranked choice general election voting.

Wealth management startup Nexedge Capital has raised $20 Mn (₹191.4 Cr) in its maiden funding round co-led by Mirae Asset Venture Investment and Elev8 Venture Partners. The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, to promote ease of doing business. The amendments seek to simplify regulatory requirements, standardise testing fees and facilitate faster market access for eligible medical devices.
The Centre has eased regulatory requirements for medical device manufacturers by removing the need for a separate licence for outsourced sterilisation and expanding the list of countries and regulatory jurisdictions whose approvals can facilitate waiver of clinical investigation requirements in India, a release issued by the Ministry said on Monday (August 24, 2026).
Under the proposed amendment to Rule 44, manufacturers that outsource sterilisation of their medical devices to a facility holding a valid licence under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, will no longer have to obtain a separate loan licence for the sterilisation activity.
Earlier, manufacturers had to secure a separate loan licence even when the outsourced sterilisation facility itself held a valid licence. The government said removing the duplication would reduce paperwork, administrative burden and compliance costs, particularly for manufacturers without their own sterilisation facilities.
However, a traceability requirement has been retained. Manufacturers will have to mention the licence number of the sterilisation facility on the medical device label. A six-month transition period has been provided to allow companies to modify labels, packaging and related processes.
The government said the change was intended to balance regulatory oversight with ease of doing business by retaining traceability while simplifying the licensing framework.
In another change, the amendment to Rule 63 includes the European Union (EU) among the stringent regulatory jurisdictions recognised for waiving clinical investigation requirements for medical devices that do not have predicate devices in India.
The provision already recognises the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Japan. With the EU now included, medical devices approved in the EU that meet the eligibility conditions can benefit from the waiver provisions in India.
The move is expected to reduce regulatory timelines for eligible importers and manufacturers and facilitate quicker availability of newer medical technologies to Indian patients.
The amendments follow stakeholder consultations and are part of the government’s broader effort to streamline the regulatory framework for medical devices while maintaining standards for their quality, safety and performance.
The changes are also expected to promote greater international regulatory convergence and improve the competitiveness of India’s medical device industry, the government said.

Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
- Published
A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.
The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.
In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.
Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.
The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court – which would include his personal physicians – particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.
They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".
Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".
"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.
"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."
Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.
Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.
Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.
His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.
He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

India’s hockey players have made an emotional appeal to save the Women’s Hockey India League, saying the tournament has played a crucial role in building the confidence of a young team that is on the verge of its best-ever World Cup finish since 1974.
With 11 World Cup debutants in the squad, India has lost just one match against Olympic champion the Netherlands while holding Olympic silver medallist China to a 2-2 draw in their opening game.
India was knocked out of semifinal contention after a goalless draw against Australia and will now play for fifth and sixth place.
The players believe the Women’s HIL has been a major factor behind their progress and fear that its discontinuation could hurt the next generation of Indian talent.
“I think we have done our best to inspire girls in India to hold a hockey stick. People prefer their kids to play individual sports, but this should give them hope,” veteran midfielder Neha, who led the Odisha Warriors to the maiden HIL title in 2024-25, told PTI.
“In the last two years, HIL for women has benefited us a lot. Junior and senior Nationals do not have this level of competition. Women’s HIL has given us players like Baljeet, Sakshi and Rutuja, who are part of this World Cup team. For upcoming players also, we need this league. It should not be discontinued.”
The appeal comes as the revived women’s HIL faces serious financial challenges, including high operational costs, low broadcast and ticket revenues, delayed player payments, and limited sponsorship interest.

India’s captain Salima Tete also stressed the league’s role in widening the national talent pool.
“We have many players from HIL in the Indian team. They get a chance to be selected for the national camp, which is an important opportunity for them,” she said.
“This is just the beginning for us, and there is much more to achieve. For that, HIL is a must so that our talent pool is broadened and the girls get good exposure to handling the pressure of international hockey.”
Sakshi Rana, one of the players to have benefited from the league, said playing alongside experienced stars helped her overcome pressure.
“HIL has given me confidence, which was very useful in this tournament. It is about handling pressure. We have played alongside many veteran players like World Cup topscorer Yibbi Jansen and learnt a lot,” she said.
Navneet Kaur said sharing the dressing room with international stars had removed the fear and hesitation among younger Indian players.
“We have been playing HIL for the last two years and gained confidence from that. We have played with some of the biggest names in international hockey, and after sharing the dressing room with them, the fear and hesitation was gone,” she said.
“That gave us self-belief. We often discuss that they are like us and we can beat them because we have played with them.” Navneet also urged the teams and corporate houses to support the league at a time when its future is under a cloud.

“We have heard that a few teams are pulling out of the Women’s HIL, but at a time when our performance graph is going up, we want to request them to support us. It will be a big setback for women’s hockey and the future crop of players,” she said.
For the Indian players the women’s league is not merely a commercial venture but an important pathway for developing the next generation. Ishika, Sakshi, Shilpi Dabas, and Lalthanluangi are the players who are in the World Cup squad due to their powerful performances in HIL.
With India producing its strongest World Cup campaign in decades, the players believe this is precisely the time to strengthen, rather than discontinue, the competition that has helped them take the next step.
“I request the Sports Ministry and Hockey India to save this league. I also request the corporate sector, which invests huge money in cricket, to support women’s hockey.
“Our league does not require that much money. It is not about money; we need exposure. The Women's Hockey League should survive. We will do even better in the future,” said Navneet, who was player of the tournament last season with the Delhi team.
The inaugural season featured four teams -- Delhi SG Pipers, JSW Soorma Hockey Club, Shrachi Rarh Bengal Tigers and Odisha Warriors. The Warriors were later terminated over non-payment of player dues and franchise fees, with Ranchi Royals replacing them in the second season.
The Ranchi franchise has also since been terminated, with Indian players still awaiting payments.
Last season’s finalist, the Shrachi Rarh Bengal Tigers, is also contemplating withdrawal, citing financial pressure.
Franchise sources said the league is currently not commercially viable. The cost of running both a men’s and a women’s HIL team is estimated at around ₹10-12 crore, including an administrative fee of around ₹1 crore. The franchise fee of ₹2.5 crore has, however, been removed for the third season for the women’s team.

Mumbai: Commuters on the Central Railway's Kasara route will face disruptions for 15 consecutive nights from August 28/29 to September 11/12, as Central Railway will undertake special traffic and power blocks at Titwala to extend the platform and make it suitable for 15-car suburban rakes. The first phase of the work, from August 28/29 to September 1/2, will involve a five-hour-40-minute block every night, from 11.30 pm to 5.10 am, between Kalyan and Vasind on the Up and Down North East lines.
First phase begins on August 28
The first phase will particularly affect late-night and early-morning suburban services between Titwala and Kasara. On August 28/29, several CSMT-Titwala and CSMT-Kasara locals will be cancelled, while services from Titwala towards CSMT and Thane will also be affected. The CSMT-Asangaon local departing at 8.56 pm will be short-terminated at Titwala, while Dombivli-CSMT and Kalyan-CSMT locals departing around 10 pm will be short-terminated at Thane. The last local for Kasara before the block will leave CSMT at 10.47 pm, while the first post-block service will leave CSMT at 4.19 am. The first Kasara-CSMT service will leave Kasara at 3.51 am.
From August 29/30 to September 1/2, further cancellations and short terminations have been planned. Importantly, all Titwala-bound suburban services will be extended to Asangaon, while trains originating from Titwala will originate from Asangaon during the block period. Some services will instead terminate at Thane or Kalyan.
AC locals and daytime services affected
Among the affected daytime services, the 6.30 am CSMT-Titwala AC local and 3.33 pm Dadar-Titwala AC service will run only up to Thane. Other CSMT-Titwala services will be restricted to Thane or Kalyan, while several Titwala-CSMT services will originate from Thane or Kalyan.
Mail and Express trains will also be regulated or delayed. The Gorakhpur-Dadar and Ballia-Dadar Express will be regulated at Vasind or Atgaon on specified nights, while the Jananeshwari Express, Shalimar-LTT Express, Howrah-CSMT Mail and Mau-LTT Express are expected to reach Mumbai 10 to 20 minutes late.

Rejoice, coffee lovers - Pumpkin Spice Latte season is officially brewing at Starbucks once again.
Starbucks 2026 Fall Menu out
The coffee giant as confirmed that its signature Pumpkin Spice Latte (PSL) will return to menus from 25 August, joined by an expanded selection of seasonal drinks and a handful of new additions.
Customers will once again be able to order the Pumpkin Spice Latte hot, iced, or blended.
Other familiar pumpkin drinks are also making a comeback, including the Pumpkin Cream Cold Brew, Iced Pumpkin Cream Chai, and Pumpkin Spice Frappuccino.
This year's menu, however, goes beyond the usual autumn favourites.
Starbucks is introducing the Iced Pumpkin Cream Shaken Espresso, Pumpkin Spice Chai and Iced Pumpkin Cream Matcha, expanding its pumpkin-inspired range across coffee, chai, and matcha drinks.
Pecan is also back on the menu, with Pecan Cortado, Iced Pecan Crunch Latte, and Pecan Crunch Latte returning for the season.
Another notable edition is the banana bread range. The new Iced Banana Bread Latte and Iced Banana Bread Chai bring the flavour of the popular baked treat into Starbucks' seasonal drinks menu.
The chain has also introduced the Chaider, a cider-inspired take on chai designed to offer another autumnal flavour profile.
Seasonal food is part of the launch as well. The menu will include a Chicken Bacon Protein Pocket, Hedgehog Cake Pop, and the returning Pumpkin Cream Cheese Muffin.
The fall menu arrives as the Pumpkin Spice Latte continues to be one of Starbucks' most recognisable seasonal products, with its annual return marking the beginning of the autumn drinks season for many customers.
With new flavours joining long-standing favourites this year, Starbucks' 2026 fall offering combines the familiar appeal of pumpkin spice with newer experiments centred on pecan, banana bread, and chai.

CIA director John Ratcliffe meets with Russian officials in Moscow, reports say
No immediate comment from the CIA or Kremlin
CIA director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.
It would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a U.S. spy chief since Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in November 2021. About three months after that meeting, Putin launched Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
CBS News and Axios reported the visit by Ratcliffe, U.S. President Donald Trump's CIA chief, who served as director of national intelligence in Trump's first term. The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what the talks are expected to cover. ABC News, CNN and the Wall Street Journal also reported the meeting taking place.
The CIA declined to comment, and the Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. last week asked Ukraine not to launch airstrikes around Moscow, St. Petersburg and some northern territories of Russia between Monday and Wednesday of this week because a plane carrying a senior U.S. official would be flying to the Russian capital, said a source familiar with the matter.
The source declined to provide further information. The Financial Times first reported the U.S. message to Ukraine.
On Monday, the U.S. warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, a move aimed at stepping up economic pressure in order to settle the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February.
No U.S. ambassador to Russia
The U.S. has no ambassador to Russia, which maintains a close strategic partnership with Iran involving extensive military, economic and diplomatic ties.
Tehran supplied Moscow with drones for its war against Ukraine.
In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of supplying its version of those drones to Iran.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment reported by Reuters in April said that Russia has aided Iran with satellite imagery for use in targeting U.S. facilities in the Middle East.
Moscow denies providing such assistance and has said it is ready to help resolve the U.S.-Iran conflict.

Donald Trump announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbors with historically strong economic ties.
Trump said that the increased tariffs would start 1 January 2027 on all cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel. He also derided the nation’s tariffs on American farmers, writing on social media that Canada has been “ripping off” the US “for years”.
“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”
In response, Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected.
“It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” he said from Quebec.
“But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” he continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.”
He added that Canada would be ready to move forward with talks “when the Americans go to the negotiating table first with the right attitude toward our industry and a true partnership”.
Trump’s announcement follows the last-minute collapse this weekend of a potential deal to lower tariffs on automobiles and other materials. After Trump imposed another 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports, including hockey equipment and electronics, Carney, rejected the latest deal between the two nations on Saturday.
Carney said that the US “asked too much and they offered too little”, and he has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
Canada and the US have been long-time partners, trading roughly $909bn, according to the office of the US trade representative. But Trump’s second presidential term and his aggressive trade policies have brought the era of “deep ties” between the two nations to a close, Carney said last year, vowing to fight Trump’s sweeping tariffs.

In a significant step to safeguard the health and safety of young children, the government has imposed restrictions on the manufacture, sale and distribution of all fixed dose combinations containing Chlorpheniramine Maleate and Phenylephrine Hydrochloride, mandating a clear warning that these medicines shall not be used in children below four years of age.
Earlier, vide a notification dated April 15, 2025, the government had restricted certain fixed dose combinations (FDCs) containing the two chemical compounds, subject to the same age-specific warning.
The latest notification extends this requirement to all formulations containing these two ingredients.
The decision followed recommendations by an expert committee and the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB).
The government noted that the use of such combinations may pose risks to children below four years of age and that safer alternatives are available.
Manufacturers have been directed to clearly display the warning – “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age – on the label, package insert and promotional literature associated with these formulations.
The notification has been issued under Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and is effective from the date of its publication in the official gazette.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) said India’s security policy must be framed keeping in view emerging global challenges, including geopolitical instability, energy and resource insecurity, supply chain disruptions, rising radicalisation and cyber misinformation campaigns, while urging security agencies to anticipate threats before they become major crises.
Mr. Shah said he had visited all land-border States over the past eight months and shared with them a document outlining a four-pronged border security strategy. Stating that the government aimed to make the country “infiltrator-free” in a short period, he said illegal immigrants posed threats to national security, the economy and demographic balance. “This country is not a dharamshala and only citizens of the country have the right to live here,” he said.
Addressing the valedictory session of the Intelligence Bureau’s National Security Strategy Conference (NSSC), Mr. Shah said the forum should study trends over the next 15-20 years and identify potential security challenges and strategies to counter them. “We have to identify challenges in advance and destroy them before they become major problems,” he said, calling for the creation of an ecosystem capable of delivering a secure, infiltrator-free and narcotics-free India.
Linking national security with the government’s long-term development agenda, Mr. Shah said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of making India a developed nation by 2047 could only be achieved with strong internal security. “If we want to become number one in every field, internal security will have to be strengthened further,” he said.
The Home Minister said previous governments had failed to anticipate problems such as narcotics trafficking, Left-wing extremism and unrest in the Northeast before they became acute, forcing the country to deal with their consequences for decades. He said the government had succeeded in overcoming challenges posed by the three major internal security hotspots, crediting State police forces, Central agencies and the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) for the achievement.
New criminal laws
Mr. Shah said the three new criminal laws would be implemented fully within a year. According to him, their implementation would enable criminal cases to be disposed of up to the Supreme Court level within three years and increase conviction rates by 25%.
On counter-terrorism, the Home Minister called for taking the anti-terror framework “Prahar” from a policy document to everyday practice and urged agencies to dismantle “360-degree terrorist networks”. He cited the coordinated nationwide action against the Popular Front of India (PFI) and its subsequent ban as an example of effective Centre-State coordination.
Mr. Shah also asked State police forces to implement the Narcotics Control Vision Document 2026-2029 and work on the three pillars of “Detect, Disrupt and Destroy” to achieve the goal of a drug-free India. He said the fight against narcotics could be won only through coordinated action by the Union government and all State governments.
Highlighting the role of technology in policing, Mr. Shah said integrated databases linking CCTNS, ICJS, NatGrid and NAFIS had been created. He urged young officers to use artificial intelligence for data integration, analysis and identifying criminal modus operandi to generate actionable intelligence and prevent future threats.
The Home Minister further said the government had strengthened mechanisms against fugitive offenders and that around 274 fugitives had been brought back to India from abroad between 2019 and 2026. He urged all States to work towards ensuring that offenders hiding overseas were brought within the ambit of Indian law.

Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh on Tuesday chaired a review meeting to assess preparations for seasonal influenza, including H1N1, currently the predominant influenza subtype in the city.
Mr. Singh directed officials from the Health Department, Municipal Corporation of Delhi, New Delhi Municipal Council, and Delhi Cantonment Board to ensure adequate medical supplies, including medicines and testing facilities, while intensifying surveillance mechanisms and awareness drives on prevention.
The Capital has recorded 2,308 H1N1 cases so far, as per the Minister’s office. On August 21, the number stood at 1,777.
“I want to reassure the people of Delhi that there is no need for panic. Our health infrastructure is fully prepared and we are continuously monitoring the situation. At the same time, we cannot be complacent. I have directed all agencies concerned to intensify drives on preventive measures,” the Minister said.
Mr. Singh added that the density and connectivity in urban spaces can contribute to the spread of respiratory infections, making timely awareness and preventive action particularly important.
He called for coordinated campaigns involving the Transport Department, Delhi Metro Rail Corporation, and civic bodies.
Meanwhile, the Directorate of Education issued a circular asking all government and private schools to adopt a ‘Healthy School-Healthy Community’ approach and reinforce respiratory hygiene and other preventive practices.
“There is no need for panic. Seasonal illnesses, including influenza, are seen during this period of the year. Our focus is on preparedness, awareness, and timely preventive action,” Education Minister Ashish Sood said.
‘No ICU cases yet’
Dedicated H1N1 wards have been set up at several government hospitals in the city. Dr. Ramesh Chand Meena, Associate Professor (Department of Medicine) at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, said, “We have dedicated beds [for H1N1 cases] and a dedicated section in the ICU. No patients have been admitted to the ICU so far.”
He added that while most healthy adults are recovering well, complications have been reported among the vulnerable sections such as the elderly, children, pregnant women, and those with existing respiratory issues.
