The United States sent 20 deportees to Liberia, who arrived on Thursday as part of 1,200 migrants that the African country will receive under a new deal.
The deportees arrived at the Roberts international airport outside Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is among the largest third-country deportations driven by the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration.
The 1,200 deportees will include African nationals and also nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean, according to Liberian information minister Jerolinmek Piah.
During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberian justice minister Natu Oswald Tweh said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the West African country if they wished.
Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that aren’t their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa.
Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum-seekers back to their home countries.
In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they’ve never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Tuesday announced a fresh organisational expansion, appointing five joint secretaries and two national spokespersons and constituting coordination committees for its north, west and east zones amid its ongoing ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign across States.
It has also launched a legal aid website for its volunteers and supporters, the outfit said in an official statement.

The newly constituted zonal coordination committees for the east (16 members), west (10 members) and north (17 members) zones will be responsible for strengthening the outfit’s field-level activities, coordinating across regions and building a network of local leadership. Mondelez India Foods, maker of Bournvita and Cadbury products, has withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims flagged by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), along with related advertisements from e-commerce platforms, as the regulator steps up action against misleading food claims.
The action is part of a wider drive in which FSSAI has issued more than 150 notices to food companies over misleading advertisements, false claims and labelling violations. Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India and Kenvue are among companies named by the regulator.
Bournvita had come under scrutiny in 2023 over its sugar content and nutritional claims, particularly its marketing to children.
The latest corrective-action drive has also prompted Amway India to remove “100%” from its “100% Pure Coconut Oil” packaging and promotional material and drop the “Energy Drink” descriptor from its caffeinated XS range. Keralam-based Juza Foods has agreed to withdraw claims including “boost immunity”, “support stronger bones” and comparative calcium claims from its baby-food products.
The action follows FSSAI’s May 2025 advisory asking food businesses to discontinue the use of “100%” on labels, packaging and promotional material, arguing that the term could imply absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI has also widened enforcement to e-commerce platforms and food-service establishments, issuing 12 notices to e-commerce companies and more than 30 to food-service establishments, including major restaurant chains.
The regulator’s latest action underlines its focus on ensuring that food claims are substantiated and do not mislead consumers. The challenge, however, will be to ensure sustained compliance after companies withdraw or modify the claims.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

When the NFL season kicks off next month, millions of Americans will gather around their televisions to watch athletes of comic book proportions crash into each other at breathtaking speeds. Inevitably, those players’ heads will smash into each other, leaving them dazed on the field. And according to a major new study, these repeated head-on collisions may eventually lead to a degenerative brain disease for many — if not most — of the players long after they’ve left the field.
Football is dangerous. Parents are finally steering their kids away from it.
A new study found at least one in four former NFL players had CTE at their time of death.
For years now, America has been reckoning with the tension between its love for football and the growing evidence of its dangers. Those concerns can be boiled down to three letters: CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which is the progressive brain disease that can lead to dementia, depression, suicide, and other serious mental health problems.
One major question over the past 20 years has been: Exactly how often does playing football lead to CTE? What are the risks for peewee players versus pros? How quickly does the brain deteriorate once the disease takes hold? And new research, published this week in the British Medical Journal, has provided us with some staggering answers. After analyzing the death records for hundreds of former NFL players, the co-authors concluded that at least 25 percent of the former players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE at the time of their death.
And the actual prevalence could be much higher, but more players’ brains would have to be given over to scientists for a CTE assessment for us to know for sure. Because among the 338 players whose brains were donated and studied, the CTE rate was an astonishing 93 percent. The question is, according to the researchers: Is that percentage skewed because the players exhibiting CTE symptoms were more likely to offer up their brain for research? Or, as the authors suggest is possible, is the real CTE rate closer to 90 percent? Only further research will be able to tell us, but even the latest estimate — one in four — is cause for concern.
It’s a stark reminder of football’s risks, delivered right on the cusp of a new season for pro, college, and high school teams around the country. And according to the Aspen Institute’s annual State of Play report, there are signs that the game’s future may actually be at risk.
More and more American parents are steering their kids away from tackle football. How long can an elite league like the NFL last when the pool of players is getting smaller and smaller — at the same time the scientific evidence of its dangers is becoming clearer and clearer?
The youth football pipeline is drying up
Despite the latest research, the NFL is going to be fine in the short term. Professional football is the biggest TV show in the country: Last year, 83 of the top 100 rated TV shows were NFL games, up from 72 in 2024. The next Super Bowl will almost certainly attract more than 100 million viewers and end up the single most-watched TV program in the US for the whole year. Football is one thing that transcends politics in an increasingly polarized America.
But with each new piece of evidence about the physical and mental costs of playing football, football’s long-term dominance looks less and less certain. Already, if you dig into the trend lines for youth participation, they reveal a real threat to the sport’s future.
Let’s start with the good news for football enthusiasts: Flag football has become more and more popular among kids, supported by investments and promotion by the NFL itself and expert consensus that it’s much safer than tackle, especially when it comes to head injuries. According to the Aspen Institute’s State of Play survey, flag football participation among kids ages 6 to 12 grew by 13.6 percent from 2019 to 2024, while tackle football play dropped 7 percent among the same age group over that time.
But it’s participation among the next age group that may be most revealing. According to the Aspen Institute, tackle football participation rates among Americans ages 13 to 17 — the prime age for middle school and high school teams — decreased 9 percent from 2019 to 2024. It has even fallen behind tennis among the teenage cohort. Many of the tweens who play flag football may never strap on a helmet to play tackle.
Even if fewer kids play tackle football year over year, the sport may still subsist on its promises of upward mobility for people who come from poorer backgrounds. With the recent introduction of compensation for college players, elite athletes can make millions of dollars in income before they even reach the NFL. It may be no surprise, then, that the young people still playing tackle football are more likely to be lower-income and live in conservative states.
Another study found that Black and Hispanic parents, who on average earn less money than their white counterparts, are more likely to see football as a path to college scholarship or even a professional career; the Washington Post reported in 2023 that the proportion of white players at the college level is falling while the percentage of Black players is rising. Football players are often thought of as modern gladiators: participants disproportionately from lower classes aspiring to riches and glory in a violent game for the viewing pleasure of the general public. That’s becoming more and more true as we learn more about its dangers.
As the annual hoopla around the NFL kickoff makes clear, football’s cultural dominance remains unrivaled among professional sports. But this new study has left even me, a lifelong football fan, wondering how much longer it can, and should, last.

From former 'street kid' key to South Africa's police corruption inquiry
- Published
The name of controversial businessman Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption.
The 49-year-old has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts.
In police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, Matlala is giving his side of the story before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel after an earlier hearing last month was aborted.
The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds.
Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November.
He said he did not know senior police officers and politicians personally and denied corruption allegations though he admitted to having made donations for activities related to the African National Congress (ANC), the main party in the coalition government.
But he has not yet been asked to address the wider allegations made at the Madlanga Commission or the accusation that he was part of a drug trafficking cartel, allegedly known as the Big Five.
Matlala may now be a central figure, but he only came to public prominence three years ago when his name was mentioned in news reports around alleged tender irregularities at a state hospital - though he said he had nothing to do with the tender.
What little is known about his early life is based on what he told parliament last year.
He was born in 1976, when South Africa was still run by a white-minority government, and grew up in a township east of the capital, Pretoria.
He told lawmakers that he was for a time raised by a single mother, who he said then "disappeared on me".
"I had to raise myself. I was actually a street kid," he told lawmakers.
He eventually reunited with his mother in 2002, when she was terminally ill.
After she died, Matlala learned that she had been sexually assaulted, which he said was because of her albinism. Myths surround the condition include people believing that having sex with a woman with the condition would cure the men of illness.
After leaving school, he said he started an informal business to make ends meet, which led to various brushes with the law.
In 2001, he was convicted and served time in prison for the possession of stolen goods.
Over the years, he would be arrested for a string of crimes, including house robberies, a cash-in-transit heist and assault. He denied involvement in them all and was either acquitted or had the charges withdrawn against him.
He told the parliamentary committee that his nickname "Cat" was not, as some had suggested, down to his "nine lives" and ability to survive trouble, but because of his large family - he has nine children with his wife.
But things caught up with him in May 2025 when he was arrested and charged with attempted murder, which he denies. His wife is accused of the same crime and also denies the charge. Unlike her husband, she has been granted bail.
He was later charged with corruption over allegations in relation to providing health services to the police - and last month pleaded guilty as part of a deal with the prosecution but has since withdrawn the plea as the agreement has fallen apart.
He told the parliamentary inquiry last year that he turned his life around in 2017, when he registered his first formal business to provide security services.
Matlala said he later expanded his services into healthcare, and this led to him scoring lucrative contracts, first with a hospital and then the police, even though, as he admitted to lawmakers, he had no track record providing healthcare services.
But since last September, as witnesses gave evidence to the Madlanga Commission, allegations that Matlala had a close and corrupt relationship with senior police officers emerged in the public domain.
This included allegations that the now-suspended Police Minister Senzo Mchunu was indirectly receiving financial campaign money from Matlala to fund his "political endeavours". Mchunu denied these accusations.
Matlala has also been accused of having dealings with Mchunu's predecessor Bheki Cele.
Matlala told parliament's inquiry he had paid Cele a 500,000 rand ($31,000; £23,000) "facilitation fee", which the latter had demanded after police returned firearms seized from Matlala.
The businessman alleged that Cele also made other requests, including asking for help to purchase a home and pay for his son's studies, to which Matlala refused to accede.
Cele admitted to MPs that he had known Matlala for a couple of months and had stayed at his rented penthouse in Pretoria on two occasions but denied receiving money from Matlala.
Matlala's relationship with suspended deputy police chief Maj-Gen Shadrack Sibiya has also come under examination.
Both Matlala and Sibiya denied having a close relationship, insisting their dealings were strictly professional.
But testimony given at the Madlanga Commission painted a different picture.
It was alleged that Sibiya had received 20 impalas from Matlala around the same time Matlala was awarded the police contract. Sibiya denied this, saying he would never "receive anything from a service provider".
A witness also alleged that Matlala had bragged about his "close connections with very senior police officials", including Sibiya, following his arrest in May last year.
Matlala's alleged relationship with other senior police officers have also been brought up at the Madlanga Commission.
Brig Rachel Matjeng, who oversaw the controversial police contract awarded to Matlala, told the commission she had had an on-off romantic relationship with the businessman that included lavish romantic presents – among them shots of Ozempic.
Another senior officer, the head of the police's organised crime unit Maj-Gen Richard Shibiri, admitted to receiving a "personal loan" of $4,000 from Matlala which he repaid.
Shibiri, who oversaw anti-gang, narcotics, illegal mining investigations among others in his role, said the money was for repairs to his son's car. He denied having a close friendship with Matlala, despite speaking to him often and advising him on personal matters.
"At no stage was I aware that he was a member of any cartel or that he was a subject of any criminal investigation," he said.
Shibiri and Matjeng have since been fired from the police force.
Matlala's name was also mentioned in relation to an alleged scandal in Ekurhuleni, a local government area just east of Johannesburg.
It was alleged that while Julius Mkhwanazi was Ekurhuleni's acting police chief, he arranged for blue lights and sirens to be fitted on Matlala's personal vehicles.
Mkhwanazi, who has since been suspended, denied the allegations but did admit to receiving money from Matlala, describing him as a "blood brother" during his appearance at the Madlanga Commission.
The startling revelations that have emerged since September, when the Madlanga Commission began, have left people wondering how such things were allowed to happen.
Many South Africans, anxious to understand the mechanics of the alleged corruption, hope that Matlala has the answers as his testimony continues.

In 1886, a young girl was born to S. Narayanaswami Iyer, the Principal of Maharaja’s College, and Chandrammal in the Pudukkottai princely state of Tamil Nadu. At a time when women were forced to live in a world of social limitations, the young girl went on to break barriers in medicine and state administration. This is the story of Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy, one of the most brilliant social reformers in India’s history.
Growing up
Muthulakshmi pursued education with determination and became the first female student to be admitted to Maharaja’s College in Pudukottai. It was not an easy win by any means. Not just the principal but also the students and their parents did not want a woman studying in the men’s college. It was the Maharaja of Pudukottai who admitted her and gave her a scholarship. Even then, as the only woman on campus, she had to go through a trial period of three months. After passing from there with flying colours, Muthulakshmi wanted to pursue a bigger dream — medicine.
In 1907, Muthulakshmi became the first woman to be admitted to Madras Medical College, and she completed her studies with a gold medal. She then went on to become a House Surgeon in the Government Hospital for Women and Children in Madras (both these institutes are in present-day Chennai). She was the first woman house surgeon at the Government Maternity and Ophthalmic Hospital, breaking barriers for generations of women in the medical field. This was just the start of her journey in empowering women through the knowledge and experience she had gained.
Into public life
Dr Muthulakshmi’s medical career did not just give her experience in the field but also helped her understand multiple social issues, especially ones faced by women. This helped her work towards reforms to make societal changes.
Her life in the public sphere properly began when she became the first woman legislator, first woman deputy president of the Legislative Council and the first woman in the Madras Corporation. She used her authority to bring in multiple rights for women, including property rights, laws against child marriage and children’s protection. With personal experience in hand, she also campaigned against the devadasi system, which was trapping multiple girls at a very young age.
With equality and justice as her main principles, Muthulakshmi also advocated for a better educational and healthcare system — especially for women through fee exemptions, scholarships and building hostels. She also created better sanitation facilities, improving the quality of life in many economically backward neighbourhoods.
Legacy left behind
Today in Adyar, Chennai, two institutions stand tall as a testimony to Muthulakshmi’s dedication towards making a better future — Avvai Home and Orphanage, an institution created to shelter, protect, and educate girls and women and Adyar Cancer Institute.
In 1956, Dr Muthulakshmi was awarded the Padma Bhushan not just for pioneering in multiple fields but also for bringing such brilliant reforms while interconnecting multiple fields she was passionate about. Even after her death in 1968, her legacy speaks loudly through the community and reforms she brought in to make education, health, freedom, and respect an everyday reality in society.

2 UN peacekeepers killed in an ambush in South Sudan
Two United Nations peacekeepers have been killed in an ambush in South Sudan
JUBA, South Sudan -- Two United Nations peacekeepers were killed on Monday when armed men ambushed a patrol traveling to a remote area of South Sudan, according to the United Nations Mission in South Sudan.
Others injured in the attack by unidentified people included three peacekeepers, two members of the South Sudanese police and two civilian staff of the mission, UNMISS said in a statement.
The mission said it had deployed a “Quick Reaction Force” to secure the area and support the emergency response after the attack. The patrol was going to the area of Pajut in the state of Jonglei when it came under attack.
“Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel who are serving to support peace in South Sudan is unacceptable,” Anita Kiki Gbeho, the head of UNMISS, said in the statement.
The identities and nationalities of the two peacekeepers killed were not immediately disclosed.
Violence is rampant in South Sudan, where government troops have been combating fighters and militias loyal to opposition leader Riek Machar, who was suspended last year as vice president after he faced charges of treason and other offenses he says are politically motivated. Attacks against peacekeepers are rare.
A 2018 peace deal between President Salva Kiir and Machar, who is under house arrest, has collapsed, leading to fears of a return to full-blown civil war.
More than 450 incidents of violence against humanitarian workers and assets were reported between January and July, more than double the number recorded during the same period last year, according to U.N. figures.
The conflict escalated in December when opposition forces seized government outposts in Jonglei. The government has conducted a counteroffensive since January with aerial bombardments and ground assaults, despite an official commitment to the peace agreement.
The U.S. has urged talks between Kiir and Machar. Earlier this year it called for “urgent action to uphold peace and mitigate the risk of civil war through an immediate return to dialogue among the parties to the 2018 peace agreement.”

In August 2026, after Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic Party primary, a claim circulated online about his mother's supposed ties to terrorist organizations abroad.
According to posts from Republican and right-leaning social media accounts on X and Facebook, Fatten Elkomy allegedly worked for a "terror group" that provided direct financial support to Palestinian militant group Hamas, the Taliban — Afghanistan's de facto rulers, whom the U.S. also has designated a terrorist group — and Osama bin Laden, the founder of the militant group al-Qaida.
This claim is missing significant context. It originated with reporting from The Midwesterner (archived), a conservative news website based in Michigan. The outlet published court documents indicating that from at least 1999 to 2002, Elkomy, El-Sayed's biological mother, worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a former humanitarian aid organization
It was not possible to find any evidence the Islamic American Relief Agency, specifically, knowingly financially supported terrorists and militant groups. The Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA-USA) was a branch of the Islamic African Relief Agency (IARA). It is the latter that the Treasury accused of directly supporting Hamas, the Taliban and bin Laden.
While the Department of Justice convicted several of IARA-USA's former officers for engaging in prohibited financial transactions with Iraq, as further outlined below, no charges of terrorism or knowingly supporting terrorism were ever brought against IARA-USA or its officers.
Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed's campaign, said via email that his biological mother "was working to help orphaned children."
Richner also accurately pointed out that Elkomy, 
Court documents that IARA-USA filed say the agency "provided charitable and humanitarian aid to refugees, orphans, victims of human and natural disasters, and other poor and needy persons and entities throughout the world, with no regard to faith or political affiliation" (Section 9, Page 3). At least one local news report from July 2008 says IARA-USA's website offered an orphan sponsorship program (archived).
It is also worth noting that El-Sayed's campaign website says he was raised by his stepmother and his father, not Elkomy. His campaign team did not answer a question about his current relationship with Elkomy.
Here's what we know about his biological mother's alleged ties to terrorist organizations abroad:
IARA vs. IARA-USA
In 2004, the U.S. Treasury Department deemed the "worldwide network of the Islamic African Relief Agency" a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization that supported Hamas, the Taliban and bin Laden.
The Treasury's 
The federal agency's news release does not state that IARA-USA, specifically, was involved in these actions. However, the Treasury considered IARA-USA part of IARA in its designation and seized IARA-USA's assets.

According to Charity & Security Network, which advocates for humanitarian aid efforts in crisis areas, the government also denied IARA-USA's "repeated requests for release of the frozen funds for humanitarian and disaster aid, including assistance for victims of Hurricane Katrina" (PDF Page 10).
The courts determined that there was enough evidence IARA-USA was a branch of IARA and that it would not "substitute our judgment" for the Treasury Department's, even if the "unclassified record evidence is not overwhelming."
IARA-USA was one of many Muslim charities shut down in the wake of the United States' 9/11 counterterrorism efforts. Civil rights and nonprofit advocacy organizations criticized the government for discrimination and unfairly targeting charities with policies that had "little prospect of stopping terrorism and at the expense of important humanitarian and human rights work" (PDF Page 22).
Justice Department indictments
In 2007, the Justice Department indicted IARA-USA on charges including illegally transferring funds to Iraq. The indictment additionally alleged that someone acting on I
A year later, the DOJ charged IARA-USA and some of its officers with "eight counts of engaging in prohibited financial transactions for the benefit of U.S.-designated terrorist Gulbuddin Hekmatyar," a former prime minister of Afghanistan and militia leader. Specifically, IARA-USA was charged with — but not convicted of — sending approximately $130,000 to a supposed orphanage housed in buildings Hekmatyar controlled.
"This raises the question of when a nonprofit must withdraw support for a charitable project when someone with an indirect relationship is designated as a terrorist," the Charity & Security Network wrote. "In this case, Hekmatyar appears to have owned the land the orphanage and refugee camp are located on, but payments did not go to him."
None of the DOJ indictments indicate that IARA-USA knowingly engaged in terrorism or the financial support of terrorism. The DOJ even makes that clear in one of its indictment news releases about IARA-USA:
It is important to note that the indictment does not charge any of the defendants with material support of terrorism, nor does it allege that they knowingly financed acts of terror. Instead, the indictment alleges that some of the defendants engaged in financial transactions that benefited property controlled by a designated terrorist, in violation of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
IARA-USA and several of its officers ultimately took plea deals and were convicted of transferring funds to Iraq in violation of federal sanctions.
Elkomy's role at IARA-USA
Court documents 
(U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri)
These documents do not prove Elkomy knew anything about any possible criminal conduct, although they do show communication with some of the convicted IARA-USA officials.
In a 2004 news article from the Columbia Daily Tribune, Elkomy said IARA-USA had no terrorist ties.
"I've been working there serving orphans and children with at least one deceased parent, and it breaks my heart they're not going to get any help," the newspaper quoted her as saying.
Elkomy also reportedly told the Daily Tribune that she worked there from 1999 to 2004, and that FBI agents interviewed her for three hours about her work there.
The Midwesterner attributed Elkomy's quote about orphans to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. We could not find that particular news article and it's unclear whether the quote ran in multiple newspapers.
The bottom line
The claim that El-Sayed's mother worked for a terrorist organization is misleading. It is more accurate to say that Elkomy worked for a charity with connections to another charity that was shut down after the Treasury Department accused it of directly supporting terrorists.
The charity Elkomy worked for — the Islamic American Relief Agency, or IARA-USA — was convicted of illegally sending funds to Iraq and indicted on charges of supporting an orphanage an Afghan warlord controlled. There is no evidence Elkomy herself was aware of these actions or was doing anything other than helping orphans, as El-Sayed's campaign claimed.

Healthtech startup Healthify (formerly HealthifyMe) has merged with US-based nutrition care company Berry Street to build an "advanced insurance-covered AI metabolic health platform" for the US market. Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.
Sarcomas in India, are therefore not only a problem of late diagnosis. Some are also operated on before a diagnosis is properly established. A first operation performed without sarcoma-specific planning can make subsequent treatment more extensive, even when the disease remains potentially curable.
A retrospective analysis in AIIMS, Delhi of 157 patients with localised extremity synovial sarcoma found that more than 70% of patients reached a specialist centre only after an unplanned surgery or a recurrence.
It may not look serious
Sarcomas are rare, accounting for about 1% of cancers in adults and roughly 15% of cancers in children. Their rarity is part of the challenge. Most soft-tissue lumps are benign, so neither patients nor clinicians naturally assume that a new lump is a cancer. Yet sarcoma can present with little more than a slowly enlarging swelling.
A soft-tissue sarcoma may appear well circumscribed, but that apparent boundary can be deceptive. Some tumours develop a surrounding pseudocapsule, and microscopic tumour cells may extend into or beyond it. If a sarcoma is removed without appropriate oncological margins, residual tumour may remain in the surgical bed. The operation that follows may then need to remove the previous scar and potentially contaminated tissues and, in some patients, may require more complex reconstruction.
Why unplanned removals are risky
The term ‘unplanned excision’ is used when a soft-tissue sarcoma is removed without appropriate preoperative imaging, histological confirmation or an oncological surgical plan. Evidence does not support the idea that such an operation automatically destroys the chance of cure. However, it can increase the risk of local recurrence and frequently creates the need for a second, wider operation to clear the tumour bed.
The AIIMS synovial sarcoma series illustrates both sides of this problem. Despite more than 70% of patients arriving after an unplanned operation or recurrence, limb salvage was still achieved in 64%. This is an important message for patients: an earlier inappropriate operation is serious, but it does not mean that amputation or treatment failure is inevitable. Prompt referral to a sarcoma team can still preserve meaningful treatment options.
Signs that should trigger a referral
Not every lump needs an MRI or a biopsy. But certain features should make a clinician stop before simply removing it. A soft-tissue mass that is enlarging, is about 5 centimetres or larger, lies deep to the fascia, has suspicious or indeterminate imaging features, or has returned after a previous removal deserves specialist assessment. Current imaging guidance recommends referral to a sarcoma or tumour reference centre before biopsy or surgery, when sarcoma is suspected.
For a suspicious extremity soft-tissue mass, MRI is usually the preferred local imaging test. If malignancy remains a concern, a carefully planned image-guided core-needle biopsy is generally the standard way to establish the diagnosis before definitive surgery. Small, superficial lesions may sometimes be managed differently, which is why the decision should be based on the whole clinical and imaging picture, rather than size alone.
Pain is not a reliable safety signal. Soft-tissue sarcoma can present as a painless lump, and the absence of pain should not reassure someone if a mass is enlarging or has other concerning features. The practical message is simple: a persistent or growing unexplained lump deserves an assessment, not an assumption.
Multi-disciplinary care
Sarcoma is not one disease but a heterogeneous family of cancers with many distinct subtypes. Diagnosis and treatment may require input from musculoskeletal radiology, specialist pathology, surgical oncology or orthopaedic oncology, radiation oncology and medical oncology. This is why major guidelines emphasise assessment in, or in close collaboration with, a specialist sarcoma centre when the diagnosis is suspected.
Image-guided core-needle biopsy has high diagnostic accuracy when it is properly planned and interpreted by experienced teams. The concern that a needle biopsy will routinely ‘spread’ a sarcoma is also misleading. Tumour seeding along a percutaneous biopsy tract is possible, but published data suggest that it is uncommon. The biopsy route should still be planned carefully because the tract may need to be considered during definitive surgery.
Dispelling harmful beliefs
Three beliefs are particularly harmful: that a painless lump must be harmless, that biopsy itself is more dangerous than obtaining a diagnosis, and that sarcoma automatically means amputation. None is a safe assumption. Modern sarcoma care is built around diagnosis before definitive treatment and, for extremity tumours, limb-preserving treatment is possible for many patients.
Better referral pathways between primary care, general surgical services and specialist centres can prevent avoidable unplanned excisions. The goal is not to send every small lump to a cancer centre; it is to recognise the few features that should trigger imaging, biopsy planning and specialist input before the first incision.
The first operation on a suspected sarcoma can shape what becomes necessary afterwards. For an unexplained lump with concerning features, diagnosis and planning should come before excision. Sometimes the most important cancer treatment decision is the one made before anyone enters the operating theatre.
(Dr. Siddharth Turkar is a consultant in medical oncology at Apollo Hospitals Navi Mumbai. drsiddharth_t@apollohospitals.com)

This Optoma laser projector is great for setting up a golf simulator in your living room, but mediocre video quality makes it less appealing for home entertainment.
Great for golf simulation. Continuous operation. Light and portable. Affordable. Easy to configure using the remote.
TIRED
No built-in smart TV OS. Outdated HDMI ports. Passable performance for home entertainment and gaming. Confusing remote for everything but the initial setup.
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.
I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.
Made for Indoor Driving Ranges
Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)
Photograph: John Brandon
For less than $1,300, the GT2400HDR is a reasonable option, especially since it works well as a basic golf sim and costs far less than 4K models that can run $5,000 or more. The GT2400HDR also has some interesting perks that make it ideal for long golfing sessions.
For starters, it’s rated for 24/7 continuous operation. That’s because the laser light source doesn’t need to cool down after a few hours and can last 30,000 hours total. (Optoma does recommend powering the unit off when not in use, though.) The laser light source does not use a bulb, so there is nothing to replace. Heat dissipation is amazingly good, as the projector tends to run cool, unlike some high-end models. The GT2400HDR has an IP6X dust rating, so it’s sealed better than some massive home theater projectors that cost $4,000—ironic, considering that if you’re spending that much, you would expect better dust protection.
The projector's light weight (just under 7 pounds) and portability make it a good match for golf simulation. I found it easy to position the projector on the floor and then use it on a table or even in another room without lugging it around like a massive brick.
I first had to figure out where to place it for the golf sim, though. As a short-throw projector, it should normally sit about 4 feet away from the screen. Since I wouldn’t be using actual golf clubs, I could set it on the floor in my windowless testing room; otherwise, I would have to mount it on the ceiling, away from swinging clubs. The projected image looked big enough that, when I started playing EA Sports PGA Tour, the players looked about as tall as they are in real life.
Photograph: John Brandon
I noticed Optoma offers an app to help with initial setup, but it’s a hassle to use. You have to install the app and sync over Bluetooth, but I found it was easier to just do the keystone adjustment with the included remote. (Also, Optoma did not include the required Bluetooth dongle even though it is normally part of the package.)
Fortunately, keystoning was easy with the remote because, during setup, you can just position the four corners of the image. I ran one HDMI cable for my laptop and one for an AV receiver for surround sound (I used a Yamaha RX300A). In less than 30 minutes, I had the projector running, and I was swinging with the pros at Augusta.
I will say, I had an absolute blast with the setup. I loved the massive screen for golf, and I was pleased I didn’t have to bother with golf clubs, a backdrop screen, netting, or anything else to replicate the experience. If you want to use real clubs and balls, there are quite a few golf sim apps like SkyTrak for both PC and tablets that scan your motion and render a virtual player, although the total cost can add up quickly, including the backdrop and other gear.
Even though I was using a controller to play a video game, I still felt like I was on the links because of the massive size, bright 4,200-lumen rating, and colorful picture.
Photograph: John Brandon
The GT2400HDR only runs at 1080p resolution, but it does so at low latency (only 8.4 milliseconds at 120 Hz). I wasn’t expecting home cinema quality at this price, and golf simulations don’t require subtle color variations like a theatrical movie, which might have scenes that take place at night. You need accurate greens and blues, and the GT2400HDR handled that well.
There are two HDMI ports, which is fairly common, but the projector does not support the latest HDMI 2.1 standard for eARC passthrough audio. That means no Dolby Vision, and if you connect an AV receiver, you could run into compatibility issues. For example, I tried using my Onkyo receiver and had some minor audio glitches.
The projector also doesn’t support Wi-Fi unless you add a streaming device like a Google TV or an Amazon Fire TV. It has a legacy VGA port if your device is still in the dark ages (e.g., an extremely old computer, but in reality it is still widely used for signage, in schools, and as a fail-safe port), both a 3.5-mm input and output, and (in another unusual twist) a 3D Sync port for connecting 3D glasses (which I didn’t test).
Photograph: John Brandon
The remote has one of the most confusing layouts of any projector I have used. It seems like it was designed for a bygone A/V era. There are way too many buttons, and they're very small. There are so many buttons that it all seemed like overkill, especially since you may only use those buttons occasionally. Indeed, once everything is running, I didn’t find the need to use the remote that often.
Performance off Course
Outside of golf simulation, the GT2400HDR was just average in just about every other way. I ran a few typical benchmarks, and the skin tone tests all looked bland and grayed out, as though every face looked the same. There just wasn’t enough dynamic tonal range. In a demo video, mist over a mountain scene blended into the white background and did not look distinct. In a scene involving a fence with green grass in the background—one of the best ways to test color quality—the GT2400HDR made everything look way too brown.
For movies, I watched a scene in The Batman with flares that look shockingly red on higher-end projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max. Here, the reds were too dark, lacked shadow detail, and blended too much into the dark background. In a scene from the 4K Ultra Blu-ray version of Blade Runner 2049, where the main character arrives at a protein farm, several buildings should have rendered in distinct yellows and blues. Instead, the scene looked too grayed out, like a thin veneer covered the entire screen. Of course, it didn’t help that the 4K movie had to be downgraded to 1080p resolution.
Photograph: John Brandon
I won’t harp on these detriments too much, because the GT2400HDR is not meant to compete with a movie theater. I switched to a few more games and found that Red Dead Redemption 2 on an Xbox Series X looked pretty good, if a little too atmospheric. That’s a kind way of saying the contrast is not great. At times, it seemed like the projected image had more in common with an LCD computer monitor than a home cinema projector.
The GT2400HDR disappointed in its handling of what should be impressive updated graphics in Halo: Campaign Evolved. Instead of rich, vibrant-looking trees, they looked too bland, with flat, dull greens. In Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag Resynced, the colors in a level that takes place in Havana should pop when you walk through the town, but the blue tunics, yellow fruit, and green trees lacked vibrancy.
A news broadcast looked dull and bland, as did a World Cup match I rewatched. There’s a theme here: bland and dull colors. However, I was surprised that a dark scene of a character riding a bike in the movie Awake didn’t look terrible. I could make out faces and some colors, which is saying a lot since this scene is hard to render. An entire moonlit scene in House of the Dragon, via the HBO app on a Google TV Streamer, looked completely washed out until I switched to the Vivid picture mode, which helped a bit. It was all par for the course, no pun intended.
I then watched scenes from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 and noticed that Cinema picture mode did help punch up the colors a bit. Super Mario Galaxy lacked the color vibrancy and clarity that it normally has and looked like it was playing on a cheap computer monitor (e.g., poor contrast and less-than-vivid colors). When I switched to The Ark on YouTube TV, the colors looked much better because the show features bright, well-lit interior shots in almost every scene.
In the end, everything I tested and benchmarked on the GT2400HDR looked just OK, but I liked how well this projector works as a golf simulator. It can run all day long for multiple rounds, has low latency to make sure your controller nudges translate to accurate drives, and looks massive and bright on a large projector screen in a dark room. Sure, just about everything else is average, but if you are into golf, this is a good low-cost entry-level option.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic.
“These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added.
Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said.
The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures.
India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala.
National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States.
NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains.
“People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said.

Pogacar's astonishing solo effort punishes Vuelta rivals
- Published
Tadej Pogacar took a huge step towards winning the Vuelta a Espana for the first time and completing his Grand Tour collection as he powered to a resounding victory in the fourth stage on Tuesday.
The Slovenian sped away from his rivals with 50km remaining in Andorra la Vella and finished the 104.8km mountainous stage in two hours 40 minutes 35 seconds, two minutes and 39 seconds ahead of Jarno Widar - the largest margin of victory of Pogacar's Grand Tour career.
He began the day top of the general classification with a nine-second lead and looks increasingly unlikely to relinquish the red jersey, extending his advantage to three minutes and 21 seconds.
"It's super good because now I can be calm and confident for the next days," said Pogacar, who remains on course to become the first rider since 1994 to lead a Grand Tour from start to finish.
"We just keep going day by day and focus on each day after this, because it will be a little bit less stressful for sure.
"I tried with an attack on the climb and I just hoped that I could survive until the finish line. I saw that I could open the gap and I did it and it was pretty tough but a beautiful day out there."
After Monday saw the third stage abandoned because of severe hailstorms in the French Pyrenees, Pogacar began stage four patiently as he sat in the third peloton about 32 seconds behind the leading group.
Lorenzo Fortunato of UCI WorldTeam XDS Astana led across the summit of the first mountain pass to collect the mountain points before Pogacar made his move.
With 50km remaining the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider surged uphill and began his descent from the second climb with a lead of 90 seconds.
From then on the 27-year-old raced alone and completed the longest Grand Tour solo victory of his career, surpassing the 43km benchmark he set on the the Col du Tourmalet last month en route to winning stage six of the Tour de France.
At one point he stretched his lead to almost three minutes, before a chasing group including Widar and fellow Slovenian Primoz Roglic were able to win some seconds back.
Roglic replaces Wout van Aert - who finished 24 minutes and 35 seconds off the pace - in second place in the general classification, with Spaniard Enric Mas in third.
On Wednesday the 173.3km hilly stage five will start in Falset near Tarragona - the site of more severe hail on Monday - and finish in Roquetes as the Vuelta heads south down Spain's east coast.

Centre notifies Keralam as Kerala's new official name ahead of Onam
The Union Home Ministry has notified Keralam as the state's new name from Tuesday. The move brings the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026 into force after the Assembly and Parliament cleared it.
The Union Home Ministry has notified "Keralam" as the new name of Kerala, with the change coming into effect on Tuesday, August 25.
"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of Section 1 of the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026, the Central government hereby appoints the 25th day of August, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force," the Home Ministry said in a gazette notification.
President Droupadi Murmu had earlier this month given assent to the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, turning it into law.
The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on August 11, followed by the Rajya Sabha on August 12.
During the Rajya Sabha debate, Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai said the Kerala Assembly had passed a resolution in 2024 urging the Centre to rename the state.
"The Bill provides that the state of Kerala will be known as the state of Keralam," Rai said.
The state government had sent the Assembly's resolution to the Centre in June 2024. President Murmu subsequently referred the Bill to the state legislature for its views, after which the Assembly unanimously backed it.
The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act changes the state's name to Keralam and makes the necessary consequential amendments to the Constitution.

More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic.
A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four.
In a statement on Thursday, Unicef warned that because the country’s health surveillance systems were fragile, the virus is probably spreading undetected, leaving even more children at risk.
Sandra Martins, the country’s deputy representative for Unicef, said: “This is the first time mpox cases have been reported in Guinea-Bissau, making even a small outbreak a major public health event.”
Mpox is an infectious viral disease that can be transmitted through close contact. There have been more than 2,000 mpox-related deaths among tens of thousands of cases recorded across east, central and west Africa since January 2024.
Health workers say the Clade variants are consistent with viruses circulating in neighbouring countries, meaning that a risk of cross‑border transmission in the region remains strong. The vast majority of confirmed cases are in the Bissau autonomous sector, where the capital is, while one case is in the nearby Biombo area. No deaths have been reported to date.
Dr Magda Robalo, a former health minister who led the country’s Covid-19 response, said that to eliminate the “biggest gaps in the health system right now”, increased surveillance would have to be prioritised and frontline capacity reinforced.
“Even though the numbers are small, new cases have appeared intermittently over several weeks, which means transmission is ongoing,” said Robalo, who is also co-founder of the Institute for Global Health and Development and former director of communicable diseases for the World Health Organization.
The outbreak comes as the country grapples with infrastructure challenges and the aftermath of the suspension of last November’s presidential election by the military, which remains in power. There was no electricity throughout Thursday in Bissau for instance because of petrol scarcity since the weekend.
Many public health laboratories in the region lack equipment to deal with epidemics but have institutional knowledge from handling other crises.
In Guinea-Bissau, that is no different but there is also a sense of urgency, with primary schools scheduled to reopen across the country in September. After the outbreak was declared, community health workers immediately began a door-to-door public awareness campaign with megaphones and translated leaflets, supported by the health ministry and international agencies.
These grassroots initiatives are seen as vital for building public trust in the public health sector. Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick, whose protests against racial injustice a decade ago made him one of the most prominent athlete activists in the U.S., will receive the Muhammad Ali Center’s Humanitarian of the Year award at a ceremony in Louisville on November 7, the organization said on Tuesday.
The center said Kaepernick was selected for his advocacy against racial injustice and for efforts to support underserved communities through his Know Your Rights Camp  and other philanthropic initiatives.
“Colin has used his platform to advocate for equality, human dignity, and social change, even when doing so came at significant personal and professional cost,” said Lonnie Ali, the late boxing champion’s wife and the co-founder, president and chief executive of the Muhammad Ali Center.
Kaepernick began kneeling during the playing of the U.S. national anthem before NFL games in 2016 to protest police brutality and racial inequality. His actions drew widespread support and criticism, turned anthem protests into a national political issue and inspired other athletes to demonstrate.
He last played in the NFL during the 2016 season with the San Francisco 49ers. Kaepernick later filed a grievance alleging teams had colluded to keep him from being signed because of his activism. He reached a confidential settlement with the NFL in 2019.
‘HUMBLING AND A RESPONSIBILITY’
In a statement, Kaepernick said the award carried special significance because of Ali’s willingness to defend his beliefs despite professional and personal consequences.
“Muhammad Ali lived with an uncommon courage to stand firmly in his convictions, even when doing so came at a great personal cost,” Kaepernick said. “To be recognized in his name is simultaneously humbling and a responsibility.”
The Muhammad Ali Center, founded in Louisville by the boxer and his wife, promotes principles associated with Ali’s public life, including respect, confidence, conviction, dedication, giving and spirituality.
Past recipients of the centre’s Humanitarian of the Year award include former NBA player Shaquille O’Neal, singer Christina Aguilera, actor Michael J. Fox, rapper and actor Common, and actors Patricia Arquette and Geena Davis.
The ceremony will also recognize Louisville philanthropists Steve and Amy Trager with the Kentucky Humanitarian Award for their community service.
Six young changemakers from around the world will also be recognized at the 13th edition of the awards, which serve as the centre’s largest annual fundraiser and support its education, youth and community programs.

Israeli defence minister threatens crackdown on kite flying in Gaza saying they will be ‘treated the same as a drone’
Hamas has accused Israel of using the row over kite-flying to justify further attacks on Palestinians
Israel has threatened to shoot down kites sent across its border from Gaza, saying they will be treated “the same as a drone” despite admitting there is no evidence they contain explosives.
Over the past month, several kites have been spotted drifting from Gaza into Israel, sparking alarm in Israeli villages that were attacked by Hamas during the October 7, 2023 assault.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday warned that those responsible for launching the kites would become targets of assassination unless they were halted immediately. The areas that the kites were launched from would also be asked to evacuate, he said.
His warning came on the same day that an Israeli air strike killed three Palestinians on central Gaza on Sunday, including a four-year-old child.
Defence minister Israel Katz said on Monday that any kites or balloons crossing into Israeli territory would be treated as a potential security threat.
“A balloon and a kite shall be treated the same as a drone — with or without explosives,” he said in a statement.
Hamas has accused Israel of using the row to justify further attacks and threats against Palestinians.
“These threats, based on fabricated pretexts, are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people, ultimately threatening children in the Gaza Strip,” Hamas spokesman, Hazem Qassem said.
While Israeli authorities have voiced concern that the paper kites could carry explosives across the border, military inspections of four kites recovered in the area earlier this week found that they did not contain dangerous material, according to theTimes of Israel.
Qassem called on the Trump administration and the Gaza Board of Peace to pressure Israel to stop what he described as continued aggression against civilians.
In Israel however, officials have continued to treat the kites as airborne security threats.
Speaking on a visit to Nir Oz, one of the communities targeted in the October 7 attacks, Israeli president Isaac Herzog said the country “cannot underestimate any sign or any concern from border residents”.
“Residents no longer need to stand in front of the border and ask themselves the meaning of everything that flies in the sky. This is the responsibility of the state. To see, to know, to prevent, and to defend,” he said.
“It is also the responsibility of the international community, the member countries of the Board of Peace, to internalise and understand this principle.”
In 2018, incendiary balloons and kites sent over the border caused fires across hundreds of acres of open fields and farmlands, in what Gazans said was in protest at the Israeli blockade of the Hamas-controlled enclave.
The International Commission to Support Palestinian Rights (ICSPR) has expressed concern over Israel’s targeting of kites, saying it is “an attempt to manufacture a political and military pretext” to facilitate a “return to genocidal war and forced displacement.”
Gazans say that the kite flying remains one of the few pastimes left for children in the enclave’s sprawling, overcrowded displacement camps. Much of the enclave was reduced to rubble during Israel’s war in Gaza.
Umm Mohammed, a mother from Gaza City, told Reuters that she was worried her son could be hurt.
"Every summer, my kid, Ahmed, 10, and the kids in the street fly those kites to entertain themselves, but I will not allow him to, not anymore," she said.

More than one in two anti-tuberculosis prescriptions assessed in healthcare settings outside India’s National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) did not conform to recommended treatment standards, according to a new systematic review and meta-analysis.
Published in the Indian Journal of Tuberculosis, the PRAMAN India study analysed 34 studies conducted between 1991 and 2024, covering 3,834 real-world anti-TB treatment records. The pooled prevalence of faulty prescriptions was 53.3% (95% CI: 42.2–64.1%).
The study also found a significant long-term decline in faulty prescribing. Weighted linear regression showed an average reduction of 1.38 percentage points a year (P=0.013). The crude prevalence fell from 68.6% in studies from 1990–1999 to 32.6% during 2020–2024.
Millions of prescriptions affected
The researchers estimated that about 2–3 million anti-TB prescriptions could be incorrect every year in India’s non-programmatic healthcare sector, based on private-sector treatment volumes. This translates to roughly four to five potentially faulty prescriptions every minute.
The estimate is not a direct count of prescriptions issued nationally, but an extrapolation based on the volume of TB treatment provided in the private sector.
The burden was not uniform across the country. In the regional analysis of 3,817 prescriptions, Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Maharashtra and Uttarakhand recorded faulty-prescription rates above the overall crude prevalence of 50.8%.
Five of the 10 States with the highest TB case notifications, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Delhi were among those with rates above this overall prevalence. The study notes that these States also account for a disproportionate share of private-sector TB drug sales, giving them particular importance for TB control.
Differences between providers
The study also examined whether prescription quality differed according to provider type. Faulty prescribing was 59% in studies that included both allopathic and indigenous practitioners, compared with 51.1% in studies involving allopathic practitioners alone.
However, the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.74), meaning the study does not establish that one provider group had a higher rate of inappropriate prescribing.
Gyanshankar P. Mishra, associate professor of respiratory medicine at Indira Gandhi Government Medical College, Nagpur, and corresponding author of the study, said the reasons for inappropriate prescribing may be more complex than deliberate deviation from treatment guidelines.
“Some gaps may reflect evolving evidence, changes in treatment guidelines and inadequate access to updated recommendations,” he said.
This is particularly relevant in TB, where treatment recommendations have evolved over time and standardised regimens are periodically updated.
Need for intervention
The researchers also used machine-learning-based modelling to estimate future trends. For 2025–2030, the projected prescription error rate was 49.7% ± 9.0%, with a median of 50.7% and a modelled range of 37.1% to 62.1%.
The authors stress that this is a model-based projection and not an observed national prescription rate.
The concern is not only whether a prescription matches a guideline. The study’s discussion notes that faulty prescriptions can compromise treatment efficacy, prolong infectiousness and contribute to drug resistance, potentially undermining TB elimination efforts.
The researchers therefore recommend strengthening links between private providers and the NTEP, including Public-Private Mix models, continuing medical education, prescription-quality audits and feedback, digital clinical decision-support tools and timely referral to programme-based services.
“For every patient with TB, irrespective of where they seek care, the treatment needs to be standardised,” Dr. Mishra said.
He said sustained engagement with private providers and dissemination of updated treatment recommendations could help address prescription gaps.

European rights court orders Turkey to free imprisoned businessman
- Published
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ordered Turkey to immediately release Osman Kavala, an activist and philanthropist who has been detained in prison for almost a decade.
Kavala was sentenced to life behind bars in 2022 for charges related to nationwide protests in 2013 and a failed coup attempt three years later.
Since his initial arrest and detention in 2017, rights groups and Kavala himself have maintained that the charges against him are politically motivated.
The ECHR on Tuesday ruled that his continued detention was unlawful and that his rights to a fair trial, freedom of expression and association had been violated.
"The measures taken against the applicant... had been predominantly motivated by an ulterior purpose, namely, to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender, and to silence him," the court said in its ruling, external.
The court also found that Kavala's aggravated life sentence amounted to "inhuman and degrading treatment".
Rights advocates and opposition groups say President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has increasingly weaponised the judiciary to target critics and rivals.
The court said Kavala's case had exposed a "systemic problem" in Turkey of the "detention and prosecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists", adding that there were "structural shortcomings which affected the guarantees of independence and impartiality of the judiciary".
The Turkish government has insisted the country's courts are independent.
- Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison 
  - Published26 April 2022
- The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West 
  - Published25 November 2021
Kavala, 68, became a symbol of a government crackdown on civil society in Turkey following his arrest in October 2017.
He and others were accused of orchestrating and financing anti-government protests in 2013, which started in Istanbul's Gezi park before spreading across Turkey.
The demonstrations posed the first serious challenge to the rule of Erdogan, who was Turkey's dominant prime minister at the time and became its directly elected president the following year.
Human rights group Amnesty International says prosecutors falsely alleged that the Gezi park protests were an attempt to overthrow the government.
In 2019, the ECHR demanded Kavala's immediate release, describing his detention as arbitrary and politically motivated. Turkey did not implement the ruling.
He was initially acquitted in February 2020 but within hours was rearrested on new charges of being part of a failed military coup in 2016.
His acquittal over the Gezi Park protests was overturned in January 2021, and he was sentenced to life in prison in April 2022 - a conviction now declared "null and void" by the ECHR.
Reacting to the latest ECHR ruling, Amnesty International's Eve Geddie said: "This obstruction of justice must end. Turkey's authorities, including judicial and prosecutorial, must act to free Osman Kavala immediately and unconditionally."
Kavala was born in Paris and educated in the UK. Before being thrust to prominence, he ran a cultural centre.
Erdogan has previously accused Kavala of being an agent of the Hungarian-born US billionaire George Soros.
Turkey has refused to comply with the two previous ECHR rulings on Kavala's case, and it is not clear whether Ankara will implement the court's third binding ruling.
The case remains one of the most serious recent flashpoints between Ankara and Strasbourg.
The Council of Europe oversees how its 46 member states execute ECHR rulings. It has the power to freeze a country's membership or suspend its voting rights if it is found to have seriously violated the rule of law.
Even though Turkey has failed to comply with several key ECHR decisions, it remains a founding member, engages with the system and has not broken ties.
A meeting of the Committee of Ministers in mid-September is likely to prioritise the Kavala case, but it remains to be seen whether it will debate harsh punitive measures.
