Japan eyes blockchain for instant stock, government bond settlement, Nikkei reports
Aug 26 : Japan is preparing to set up a payment infrastructure to enable instantaneous settlement of transactions in stocks and Japanese government bonds using blockchain technology, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Wednesday.
The Financial Services Agency, the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Japan and financial institutions will launch a study group this summer and are expected to formulate a development plan around the beginning of 2027 at the earliest, the report said.
The plan is expected to cover the design of the blockchain to be used, the division of responsibilities among agencies and institutions, and a road map for future work, it added.
Operations could begin within a few years, with the system potentially up and running in the early 2030s, if the plans are formally approved, the report said.
The instant payment system could also extend to international remittances, the report added.
In Japan, cash settlement for stock trades occurs two days after execution, while JGB transactions are settled the day after.
A real-time settlement system would bridge the gap between a trade and its cash settlement, allowing investors to reinvest proceeds from asset sales almost simultaneously.

Dolly Parton, country music legend, actor and philanthropist, dies at 80
The songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 transcended generations, geography and politics
Dolly Parton, the country music icon whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, has died, her nephew Brian Seaver said in a video shared on her Instagram page. She was 80 years old.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday ordered the lowering of flags across the United States for a week, calling Parton’s death a “true loss for millions of people”.
“Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away,” Trump posted on his Truth Social network.
“There has never been anyone like her, and never will.”
Known for her curvy physique, massive blonde wigs and skin-tight outfits that served her self-deprecating wit, she was among the most beloved personalities in music and beyond – the rare celebrity whose appeal transcended generations, geography and politics.
She wrote hundreds of songs, including classics “Jolene”, “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You”, that totalled more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams. Parton, who plucked bejewelled banjos, guitar and dulcimers with her long fingernails during performances, was a generous philanthropist and successful businesswoman whose projects included a theme park in the Smoky Mountain foothills near her birthplace.

IIT Delhi Students Protest MSc Student's Suicide, Demand Compensation And Probe Into Harassment
A ongoing student protest has erupted at the IIT Delhi campus following the suicide of 31-year-old MSc Physics student Hrishikesh Kumar. Protesting students accuse the institute's administration and specific faculty members of severe harassment, claiming that denial of hostel accommodation, project allocation, and course withdrawal permissions contributed to the tragedy. The agitators are demanding a compensation of Rs 1 crore for the victim's family, the immediate resignation or suspension of the accused deans, and a completely independent external investigation into the incident. Students expressed distrust toward the five-member inquiry committee formed by the IIT director, alleging it is biased. Protesters highlighted a troubling trend, asserting that eight students have died by suicide within the campus over the past 30 months due to intense academic pressure and administrative apathy. Meanwhile, counter-claims emerged from within the campus suggesting outside groups are attempting to politicise the tragedy, though core student groups vow to continue demonstrations until all their demands are formally met.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

What will it take to stop the England hangovers?
- Published
Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour.
The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.
If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.
Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.
To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.
In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".
Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.
It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.
Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.
As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.
Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.
There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.
But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.
Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.
Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.
For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.
Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.
And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.
As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?
Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?
Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.
Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.
Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?
Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.
